context.title: Two-Dish Rice Meals in Hong Kong
body: Two-dish rice shops have become a familiar sight in many Hong Kong neighbourhoods. Customers choose two ready-made dishes, add rice and receive a hot meal within minutes. Office workers and students often value the low price, short waiting time and wide choice, while some diners also associate the food with simple home-style cooking.

The meal has attracted attention beyond its practical value. Online posts now review unusual combinations, compare portion sizes and introduce small independent shops. However, frequent customers may need to consider salt, oil, nutritional balance and the waste created by takeaway containers. Shops also face pressure to keep prices affordable while paying rent and maintaining food quality.

Some tourism promoters believe two-dish rice could be introduced as an everyday Hong Kong food experience. Bilingual labels, smaller tasting portions and neighbourhood food maps might help visitors order confidently. Others warn that promotion should not turn an ordinary community meal into an expensive attraction. Any plan should therefore protect affordability, explain the food clearly and respect the people who rely on it every day.

context.source_line: Original mock article written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Financial Literacy among Teenagers
body: Financial literacy means understanding how to budget, save, borrow and make informed choices about money. Teenagers now encounter digital wallets, online shopping, subscription services and targeted advertising at an early age. Although cashless payments are convenient, they may also make spending feel less real and make it harder to notice how quickly small purchases add up.

Students can build practical habits without having a large income. They may record daily expenses, separate needs from wants, set a weekly limit and save part of any allowance before spending the rest. Comparing prices and waiting before making an online purchase can also reduce impulsive decisions. An emergency fund, even a small one, provides protection when an unexpected cost appears.

Schools could strengthen financial education through realistic tasks rather than definitions alone. Students might prepare a monthly budget, compare bank products, identify misleading advertisements or discuss the risks of borrowing. Parents and community organisations could contribute examples from everyday life. Effective education should help young people ask questions, understand consequences and make independent decisions instead of simply telling them never to spend.

context.source_line: Original mock article written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Online Dishonesty
body: People do not always present an accurate picture of themselves online. Some edit photographs, exaggerate achievements or hide sponsorships because they want attention, approval or commercial success. Others share false information as a joke, repeat a claim without checking it or use artificial intelligence to produce convincing material that they then present as their own work.

Online dishonesty can damage trust even when no money is lost. A friend may feel betrayed after discovering that a personal story was invented, while a misleading health or financial claim can cause real harm. Edited images may also create unrealistic expectations about appearance and lifestyle. However, not every alteration is equally serious, and users should consider purpose, context and likely consequences.

Protection begins with careful habits. Users can check the original source, compare several reliable reports, examine dates and images, and pause before forwarding surprising claims. Platforms can label advertisements and manipulated media, while schools can teach verification skills. If a friend posts something false, a private and respectful conversation may be more effective than public embarrassment, unless the content creates an urgent risk to others.

context.title: Food and Drink Trends on Social Media
body: A food or drink can become fashionable within days when short videos make it colourful, unusual and easy to recognise. Matcha drinks and desserts are one example. Their bright green appearance works well in photographs, while influencers can introduce new combinations to large audiences. Repeated online exposure may persuade customers to try a product even before they know much about its taste or origin.

Viral attention can create opportunities for cafés, farmers and small food businesses. Shops may develop new products, attract younger customers and introduce aspects of Japanese tea culture. At the same time, sudden demand can raise ingredient prices, encourage waste and reward appearance more than quality. Businesses that expand too quickly may struggle when the trend moves on to something else.

Responsible promotion should give customers useful information as well as attractive images. Influencers can identify paid partnerships, explain ingredients and avoid unsupported health claims. Producers can offer different sweetness levels, reduce unnecessary packaging and distinguish traditional matcha from products that merely use its colour. A lasting market will depend on quality, cultural respect and repeat customers rather than a brief burst of online popularity.

context.title: E-commerce and Local Retail
body: Online shopping allows customers to compare products, order at any hour and receive purchases without travelling. It can help people with limited mobility and give small sellers access to customers beyond their neighbourhood. Yet buyers cannot always inspect goods before paying, and misleading reviews, complicated returns, excessive packaging and impulsive purchasing remain common concerns.

Physical shops provide services that websites cannot fully reproduce. Customers can try products, ask questions and receive an item immediately. Local shops may also give a district its character and provide informal contact among residents. Their difficulty is that rent and staff costs are high, while online competitors can operate with wider stock and frequent discounts.

Traditional retailers could combine personal service with useful digital tools, such as online catalogues, simple ordering and collection in store. District promotions and loyalty programmes may encourage repeat visits. Government support might include practical training, grants for digital improvement and policies that reduce barriers for small businesses. The aim should not be to prevent online shopping, but to preserve genuine choice and a varied local retail environment.

context.title: Introducing Hong Kong Cinema to International Students
body: A group of international students will visit your school, and your class plans to introduce them to Hong Kong cinema. Local films are known for energetic action, distinctive urban locations, martial arts, comedy and stories about family or community life. They can show visitors aspects of Cantonese language and Hong Kong identity that ordinary tourist information may not capture.

Choosing suitable films requires care. Action and visual storytelling can cross language barriers, while youth or family films may offer themes that students easily understand. Older films can provide valuable cultural history. However, subtitles may not carry Cantonese wordplay, local references or differences in tone. Fast editing, unfamiliar social customs and violent content may also make some titles less suitable for a school audience.

The class could select short clips from several genres and provide a brief introduction before each one. A glossary, discussion questions and information about filming locations would help visitors follow the stories. The programme should represent Hong Kong cinema fairly instead of suggesting that one famous star or one genre defines the entire industry.

context.source_line: Original mock article written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Introducing Robotaxis in Hong Kong
body: Robotaxis are vehicles that use cameras, sensors, maps and computer systems to travel without a driver controlling every movement. Supporters argue that they could provide round-the-clock service, reduce accidents caused by tired or distracted drivers and improve transport for people who find it difficult to drive. Hong Kong's dense road network, however, would be a demanding environment for the technology.

Crowded junctions, pedestrians, road works, heavy rain and narrow streets can create situations that are difficult to predict. If a robotaxi causes an accident, responsibility may be shared among the operator, software developer and vehicle owner. Passengers may also worry about cybersecurity, privacy and what happens when the system fails. Existing taxi drivers could face disruption to their livelihoods.

A cautious introduction could begin with limited routes, low speeds and trained remote support. Clear safety standards, insurance rules and public reporting would be essential. Similar technology might later assist buses, airport shuttles or delivery vehicles, especially on fixed routes. Whether robotaxis improve transport will depend not only on technical ability but also on public trust and integration with mass transit.

context.source_line: Original mock article written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Tipping Culture in Hong Kong
body: Tipping is expected in some places but remains less central to everyday service in Hong Kong, where restaurants often add a service charge. People may still give extra money to hotel staff, delivery workers, taxi drivers or others who provide unusually helpful service. A tip can express appreciation directly and may encourage workers to give careful, friendly attention.

Problems arise when an optional reward becomes a social obligation. Customers may feel uncertain about whom to tip and how much, especially if a service charge is already included. Workers in visible roles may receive more than kitchen staff or cleaners who also contribute. Employers might even rely on tips instead of providing fair and stable wages.

If tipping becomes more common, businesses should state their policy clearly. Digital payment systems could allow a genuine 'no tip' choice without embarrassment, and restaurants could explain whether tips are shared. Good service should still come from training, professional standards and proper pay. Hong Kong must therefore decide whether tipping would improve appreciation for service workers or simply add cost, pressure and confusion to ordinary transactions.

context.title: Home Remedies
body: Many families use simple home remedies for minor problems. Warm drinks, rest, steam, herbal teas or familiar foods may bring comfort when someone has a mild cough, sore throat or stomach discomfort. These remedies are convenient, inexpensive and often passed from one generation to the next, so they can carry cultural as well as practical meaning.

A remedy that feels familiar is not automatically safe. Some ingredients can cause allergies, interact with medicine or be unsuitable for children, pregnant people or patients with particular conditions. More seriously, a person may mistake an urgent illness for a minor one and delay professional treatment. Claims shared online can make this risk worse when they are not supported by reliable evidence.

People should distinguish supportive self-care from medical treatment. They can check ingredients, use moderate amounts and seek qualified advice if symptoms are severe, unusual or persistent. Health education can respect family traditions while explaining warning signs and scientific evidence. Home remedies may have a useful place in daily care, but they should not be presented as guaranteed cures or complete replacements for doctors and prescribed treatment.

context.title: Student Entrepreneurship
body: Your school is considering a student business fair. Suggested stalls include handmade gifts, tutoring services, simple snacks and digital design. Students would choose one idea, prepare a small budget and operate the stall for a limited period. The activity is intended to develop creativity and practical skills rather than to encourage students to make large profits.

Running even a small business can teach planning, communication, pricing and problem-solving. Students may gain confidence when customers value their work. Difficulties include balancing orders with homework, controlling costs, following food-safety or copyright rules and handling complaints. A popular idea can also become stressful if demand is greater than a student can manage.

Parents and schools can provide guidance without taking control. Workshops could cover budgeting, honest advertising, customer privacy and basic legal responsibilities. Teachers might approve plans, set spending limits and arrange safe selling spaces, while parents could offer advice and emotional support. Clear rules should protect students from financial loss and excessive pressure. Success should be judged by what students learn, not only by how much money a stall earns.

context.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Workplace
body: Artificial intelligence can sort information, produce routine documents, answer common questions and control machines. As these systems improve, data-entry, basic customer service and repetitive production work may change substantially. AI can help employees complete some tasks more quickly, but a job usually contains several responsibilities, so transformation may be more common than complete replacement.

Machines still struggle with genuine empathy, moral responsibility and unpredictable situations. They can also produce confident but inaccurate answers. If workers accept results without checking them, mistakes may spread into reports, decisions or customer advice. Other concerns include confidential data, unfair bias, unclear ownership of generated work and the gradual loss of human skills.

Workplaces need rules that match the risk of each task. Staff should verify important output, protect personal information and know when a human decision is required. Training can help employees use AI as an assistant rather than a substitute for judgement. Employers should also explain how roles may change and support affected workers. The central question is not simply what AI can do, but what people should remain responsible for.

context.title: Choosing a Major
body: Choosing a field of study can influence a student's learning experience and future opportunities, but no single factor provides a perfect answer. Interest and ability matter because a demanding programme requires sustained effort. Students should also examine course content, teaching methods, entry requirements, cost and the kinds of work or further study that graduates pursue.

Some programmes become popular because they are linked with professional status, stable employment or new industries. Media attention and salary expectations can make a subject seem attractive even when students know little about the daily work involved. Popularity may also increase competition for places and create pressure to follow a trend rather than consider personal suitability.

Parents can offer experience, financial guidance and emotional support, but their expectations may become too influential. Schools can help through counselling, subject tasters, workplace visits and conversations with current students or professionals. A good decision should combine reliable research with self-understanding. Students also need to remember that careers change, and a degree is one stage of development rather than a guarantee of lifelong success.

context.title: Online Examinations
body: Online examinations can reduce printing, simplify the collection of scripts and provide fast results for questions that can be marked automatically. Students may type, use multimedia material and sit an assessment when travel to school is impossible. Digital records are easier to store, but these advantages depend on reliable systems and fair access to equipment.

An unstable connection, device failure or platform error can interrupt a high-stakes examination. Home environments differ, and not every student has a quiet room or suitable computer. Schools may also find it difficult to protect privacy and prevent unauthorised help. Long periods on screen can disadvantage students who type slowly or need particular support.

Before using online examinations, schools should provide practice sessions, technical assistance and loan devices. Rules must explain identity checks, permitted materials, data protection and what happens after a disconnection. A backup paper or rescheduling procedure can prevent technical faults from deciding a student's result. Online assessment may suit some subjects and purposes, but practical, artistic and extended handwritten tasks may still require different methods.

context.source_line: Original mock article written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Can Money Buy Happiness?
body: Money can provide food, housing, healthcare and freedom from some forms of worry. In a city with high living costs, financial security understandably matters to many families. Yet an increase in income does not always create a lasting increase in happiness. Expectations may rise, comparison with others may continue and greater wealth can bring new responsibilities or fear of loss.

Many important sources of well-being cannot simply be purchased. Trust, friendship, health, purpose and a sense of belonging develop through time and attention. Expensive possessions may bring brief excitement, but people soon become used to them. This does not mean that money is unimportant; rather, its effect often depends on whether basic needs are secure and how it is used.

People can strengthen well-being through relationships, exercise, rest, creative activity, volunteering and achievable personal goals. Simple experiences may be especially valuable when they are shared or meaningful. Society can also reduce unnecessary comparison by recognising different definitions of success. A balanced view accepts that money can remove hardship and create opportunities while rejecting the idea that wealth alone guarantees a satisfying life.

A well-designed space can offer quiet zones, private booths, accessible furniture, secure storage and clear booking systems. Rules should cover calls, guests, cleanliness and the handling of sensitive information. Community events can be optional rather than constant. Co-working is most useful when it gives members genuine flexibility: places for focused work, collaboration and private discussion instead of one fashionable open room for everyone.

context.title: Relationships between Parents and Teenagers
body: Teenagers often seek greater independence while parents remain responsible for their safety and education. This difference can create emotional distance even when both sides care about each other. Busy schedules, school pressure and constant phone use may reduce opportunities for relaxed conversation. Teenagers may also fear criticism and therefore keep worries or interests to themselves.

Common sources of frustration include comparisons with other children, repeated questions, strict control of friendships and online activity, and decisions made without listening. Parents may see these actions as protection, while teenagers experience them as a lack of trust. Arguments become harder to solve when either side interrupts, raises old complaints or treats one disagreement as proof of a person's character.

Families can reduce conflict by choosing a calm time to talk, explaining reasons and agreeing on boundaries that can change with age. Regular meals or shared activities create contact without forcing serious discussion every time. Teenagers should communicate plans honestly, while parents should listen before offering solutions. The goal is not to remove every disagreement but to handle differences without damaging respect or closeness.

context.title: The 'Ugly-cute' Trend
body: The term 'ugly-cute' describes characters and products that combine awkward, strange or imperfect features with a playful appeal. Collectible figures such as Labubu have helped bring this style to a wide audience. Their unusual appearance stands out in photographs, while limited editions, surprise boxes and social-media communities add excitement to buying and exchanging them.

For teenagers, the trend may make beauty feel more flexible and show that charm does not require perfect symmetry. Collecting can provide a hobby and a way to connect with friends. However, pressure to own rare items may encourage overspending, comparison and speculative resale. Some buyers may value popularity or price more than design, and constant promotion can make a temporary trend feel essential.

The popularity of ugly-cute products suggests that people can enjoy imperfection, humour and strong personality in design. At the same time, a commercial trend does not automatically change deeper attitudes towards human appearance. Consumers should consider why they want an item, how much they can afford and whether the product has lasting meaning for them. Creative industries can learn from the trend without relying only on artificial scarcity.

context.source_line: Original mock article written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Note-taking Skills
body: Taking notes requires students to select important ideas, connect information and express it briefly. Writing by hand can slow the process enough to encourage thought, while digital tools allow quick searching, rearrangement and the addition of links, images or recordings. Simply copying every word, however, is unlikely to produce useful notes in either format.

Different subjects may need different methods. A timeline can clarify history, a labelled diagram may suit science and a two-column page can separate key ideas from examples or questions. Colour can highlight a small number of categories, but too much decoration may consume time without improving understanding. Students should review and correct notes soon after a lesson.

Technology can support learning through shared documents, handwriting tablets, speech-to-text and reminder systems. It can also create distraction or encourage students to save material they never read again. Schools can demonstrate several note-taking strategies and let students compare what works for them. Strong study habits combine clear notes with active recall, practice questions, discussion, regular review and enough rest rather than treating note-taking as a complete solution.

Easy access to green space improves city life, but large visitor numbers can damage trails, disturb wildlife and create litter or fire risks. Maintaining parks also requires public land and long-term funding. Visitors with limited mobility or little outdoor experience may find some routes difficult, while extreme heat and sudden weather changes can create safety problems.

Promotion should therefore encourage responsible visits rather than simply more visits. Schools could organise guided walks, conservation projects and beginner-friendly route planning. Clear transport information, multilingual signs and digital trail guides would help new visitors. Campaigns should explain preparation, waste reduction and respect for wildlife. Success should be measured through appreciation and protection of nature, not only the number of people arriving at popular viewpoints.

context.title: Raising Hong Kong's Retirement Age to 70
body: Hong Kong, like many societies, has a growing proportion of older residents. One proposal is to raise the retirement age to 70. Supporters argue that people are living longer, many remain healthy and experienced workers can continue contributing. A later retirement age may also reduce pressure on pension systems and help sectors facing labour shortages.

Opponents point out that health, income and working conditions differ greatly. A desk-based professional may be able to work longer than someone in a physically demanding job. Compulsory later retirement could limit rest, family care or opportunities for younger workers. Some employees may wish to continue, while others need a secure way to leave work earlier.

Public support would probably depend on flexibility. Options could include voluntary extensions, phased retirement, part-time roles, retraining and protection against age discrimination. Employers would need to adapt workplaces and judge performance fairly rather than assuming that every older worker has the same ability. The debate is therefore not only about one number, but about choice, financial security and how different generations can participate in work with dignity.

Rules should therefore respond to specific harm rather than ban photography everywhere. Clear signs, marked photo zones and better crowd management may solve some problems, while serious cases could require penalties. The challenge is to protect privacy, safety and neighbourhood life without preventing responsible visitors from enjoying and sharing public places.

context.title: One Screen Cannot Do Every Job
body: Smartphones have become the main digital device for many young people. They are portable, relatively affordable and able to handle communication, banking, entertainment, navigation and quick searches. Improved cameras and mobile applications have made tasks that once required several separate devices possible from one pocket-sized screen. For everyday use, a phone may seem more convenient than a personal computer.

Yet convenience is not the same as suitability. Writing a long report, comparing several sources, editing detailed images or managing a spreadsheet is often easier with a keyboard, a larger display and desktop software. Students who depend only on phones may be able to consume information quickly but find it harder to produce complex work or organise many files.

The future is therefore unlikely to be a simple victory for one device. Phones may replace computers for more routine tasks, while laptops and desktops remain important for study, creative work and professional use. Schools must consider whether students have fair access to suitable equipment and teach them to choose the right tool rather than use the newest one automatically.

body: For many young people, the smartphone is their camera, map, wallet, television and main way of going online. It is cheaper and more portable than a laptop, and most everyday tasks—messaging, shopping, banking and watching videos—can be completed with a few taps. As phones become more powerful, some families no longer see a reason to own a separate computer.

Nevertheless, a small screen is not ideal for every task. Writing a long report, analysing a spreadsheet, editing a video or comparing several sources is usually easier with a full keyboard and a larger display. Relying only on phones may also create an educational gap: students can consume information easily but struggle to produce complex work. Instead of asking which device will completely replace the other, consumers should consider which tool is appropriate for each task and whether shared computers can provide affordable access.

context.title: Why Weekenders Are Heading North
body: Short trips from Hong Kong to Shenzhen have become an attractive weekend choice. Faster cross-boundary transport allows visitors to reach shopping centres, restaurants, parks and entertainment venues without taking a flight. Many travellers also believe that food, personal services and family activities offer good value, so a day trip can feel like an affordable change from their normal routine.

Shenzhen’s appeal is not based on price alone. New districts, large indoor attractions and rapidly changing technology give repeat visitors something different to explore. Digital payment, online booking and recommendations shared on social media make planning easier. At the same time, crowded checkpoints, unfamiliar applications and differences in service expectations can create inconvenience for some travellers.

Hong Kong businesses cannot compete simply by asking residents to stay. They need to offer experiences worth choosing, such as neighbourhood events, creative packages, family discounts or late-night activities linked to local culture. Better service and clearer value may encourage residents to divide their leisure spending between both cities rather than treating the choice as a competition with only one winner.

context.title: Is Learning to Drive Worth It in Hong Kong?
body: For some Hong Kong residents, driving offers privacy, comfort and direct access to places that are difficult to reach by public transport. It can be especially useful for families with young children, elderly relatives or heavy equipment. Learning to drive may also provide a practical skill for travel or future employment, even if a person does not immediately buy a car.

The disadvantages are equally clear. Vehicles, fuel, insurance, tolls and parking are expensive, while traffic and limited parking spaces can turn a short journey into a stressful one. Hong Kong’s rail and bus networks already serve most urban areas, so many teenagers see little need to spend time and money on lessons before they can afford a vehicle.

Whether Hong Kong is car-friendly depends on whom the transport system is designed to serve. Policies that make driving easier may increase congestion and pollution, but policies that discourage cars can inconvenience people with genuine needs. Young people should therefore consider cost, safety, environmental impact and future usefulness before deciding whether a driving licence is an important step towards adulthood.

context.title: Understanding the Fears Teenagers Carry
body: Teenage fears are not limited to obvious phobias such as heights, insects or enclosed spaces. Many students worry about examination results, disappointing their families, speaking in front of others or being rejected by friends. Online comparison can make these concerns feel more serious because young people repeatedly see carefully edited versions of other people’s success and appearance.

Fear can be useful when it warns someone about real danger, but it becomes harmful when it prevents normal learning, relationships or daily activities. Avoiding every uncomfortable situation may provide short-term relief while making the fear stronger. Adults sometimes dismiss teenage worries as unimportant, which can leave a young person feeling ashamed or unwilling to seek support.

Helpful responses depend on the seriousness of the problem. Talking to trusted friends, parents, teachers or counsellors can make a fear easier to understand. Gradual practice, reliable information and healthy routines may also build confidence. Schools should create a climate in which asking for help is treated as responsible behaviour, while serious or continuing anxiety receives professional attention.

context.title: Wildlife Tourism: Protection or Performance?
body: Animal encounters are sold as unforgettable travel experiences. Visitors may watch dolphin shows, ride elephants or camels, photograph captive wild animals, or join tours that promise close contact with creatures in their natural habitat. Such activities can create jobs and fund conservation, especially where local communities have few other sources of income.

The same industry can also cause serious harm. Animals may be trained through fear, kept in unsuitable spaces or forced to interact with visitors for long hours. Even apparently harmless wildlife watching can disturb feeding and breeding when boats, vehicles or crowds move too close. Tourists often cannot tell whether an operator’s conservation claims are genuine.

Responsible tourism requires more than choosing an activity that looks educational. Travellers should examine how animals are housed, whether physical contact is necessary and where the money goes. Governments can set welfare standards and punish misleading operators, while communities can design smaller tours that protect habitats. A successful activity should improve the long-term well-being of both wildlife and local residents.

context.title: From Bands to Solo Stars
body: Popular music once depended heavily on bands whose members developed a shared sound and public identity. Today, individual performers can record at home, collaborate remotely and reach listeners through short videos or streaming platforms. This makes it easier for solo artists to enter the market without waiting for a record company or several band members to agree on every decision.

Bands still offer something distinctive. Live instruments, different personalities and visible teamwork can create performances that one singer cannot easily reproduce. Groups may also divide the work of composing, arranging and interacting with fans. However, disagreements, higher touring costs and the difficulty of maintaining a stable line-up can make a band harder to manage.

Social media affects both types of performer. A memorable clip may introduce unknown musicians to millions of viewers, but algorithms can reward appearance and constant posting more than musical skill. Trends change quickly, and artists may feel pressure to produce short, attention-grabbing content. The future of pop music will depend on whether audiences continue to value strong songs and live performance alongside online popularity.

context.title: Self-Care Is More Than a Day Off
body: Self-care is often presented online as buying treats or escaping from responsibilities, but its basic purpose is to maintain physical and mental health. Enough sleep, regular movement, balanced meals, supportive relationships and time away from constant notifications can help students manage pressure. These habits are simple to describe but difficult to maintain during busy school terms.

A school Self-Care Month could introduce practical activities rather than one-off slogans. Short exercise sessions, sleep workshops, quiet spaces, peer-support training and guidance on seeking professional help could serve different needs. Activities should avoid suggesting that students are personally responsible for every problem when workload, family pressure or bullying may also affect well-being.

Participation is more likely when events are private, flexible and free from judgement. Student leaders can help choose relevant activities, but teachers and health professionals should provide reliable information. Success should not be measured only by attendance. The school should also ask whether students feel safer requesting help and whether healthy routines continue after the campaign ends.

context.title: Can a Personality Test Choose Your Career?
body: Online personality tests have become popular among teenagers because they provide quick labels and attractive descriptions. Career advisers sometimes use structured questionnaires to help students discuss whether they prefer independent work, social interaction, careful routines or creative problem-solving. A result can give a student helpful vocabulary for describing strengths and possible working environments.

Problems arise when a test is treated as a final answer. People may respond differently depending on mood or experience, and broad categories cannot capture every ability, value or circumstance. A teenager may avoid an interesting subject because a result says it does not match one “type”. Employers may also use weak tests unfairly when judging applicants.

Career choices should combine several kinds of evidence. Students can speak to advisers, interview workers, try short courses, volunteer, complete internships and reflect on subjects they enjoy. Personality tests may begin a conversation, but they should not close it. The most useful plan allows interests and skills to change as a young person gains knowledge and real experience.

context.source_line: Original mock website written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Bamboo Above the Streets
body: Bamboo scaffolding has long been a familiar feature of Hong Kong construction and festival work. Skilled workers can transport and assemble bamboo quickly, even around buildings with irregular shapes. The material is light, flexible and renewable, and generations of practitioners have developed specialised knowledge about selecting poles and tying strong joints.

Its cultural value does not remove the need for strict safety. Weather, damaged materials, poor platforms or incorrect ties can endanger workers and people below. Safety depends on trained workers, suitable protective equipment, regular inspection and clear control of the area around a site. Simply changing to another material would not eliminate careless planning or weak supervision.

Hong Kong must decide how traditional knowledge should continue in a modern industry. Training programmes can preserve skilled techniques while updating them to meet current standards. Public education may help people understand the craft without romanticising risk. The strongest approach would judge bamboo and metal systems by evidence, use each where appropriate and make worker protection the first requirement.

context.title: What Is Really Inside an Energy Boost?
body: Coffee and energy drinks are easy for teenagers to buy and are often associated with studying, sport or staying awake. Both may contain caffeine, while many energy drinks also contain large amounts of sugar and are marketed with exciting images. A temporary feeling of alertness can make these products seem useful during examination periods.

Too much caffeine may disturb sleep, increase nervousness and cause headaches or a rapid heartbeat. Poor sleep can then make a student rely on another drink the next day. Effects differ by body size and the amount consumed, so a large serving designed for an adult may be unsuitable for a younger person. Mixing several caffeinated products also makes intake difficult to judge.

A school health club could compare labels, explain serving sizes and promote alternatives such as water, rest and better study planning. Education may be more effective than a simple ban, which can make products seem forbidden and attractive. However, age limits, warning labels or sales restrictions may be justified for high-caffeine drinks if clear health evidence supports them.

The final decision should reflect a student’s needs and resources rather than the idea that a gap year is automatically adventurous or impressive.

context.title: Giving Clothes a Second Life
body: Cheap and rapidly changing fashion encourages people to buy more clothes than they regularly wear. Unwanted items may be stored for years or thrown away even when they remain usable. Better options include repairing, altering, swapping, donating or selling garments, although each choice requires time and a reliable way to judge condition and quality.

Second-hand fashion is becoming more visible in Hong Kong through online platforms, charity shops and small vintage businesses. Buyers may save money, find unusual designs and reduce waste. Social media has also changed the image of pre-owned clothing by presenting it as creative and environmentally responsible rather than simply an option for people with limited budgets.

Concerns about hygiene, fake branded goods and inconsistent sizing still discourage some shoppers. Clear photographs, washing standards, honest descriptions and simple return rules can build trust. Schools and community groups could organise swap events or repair workshops, but promotion should not encourage another form of excessive shopping. The main goal is to use clothing for longer and buy more thoughtfully.

context.title: Which Language Should Students Learn Next?
body: Learning another language can help Hong Kong students communicate during travel, understand another culture and prepare for study or work. Some choose a language because of music and entertainment, while others consider business links, family background or future education. Motivation matters because progress requires regular practice over a long period.

Schools deciding which language to offer must look beyond popularity. They need qualified teachers, suitable materials and enough students to sustain the course. Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, French, Spanish and other languages may each serve different interests. Choosing only the language believed to have the greatest economic value could ignore student enthusiasm, while following a short-lived trend may waste resources.

Classroom lessons provide structure, but real improvement also comes from songs, films, reading, online exchanges and conversation. Digital tools can increase access, although students need guidance to judge quality and protect privacy. A successful programme should set realistic goals and help students continue learning independently rather than promising fluency from a few lessons each week.

body: A travel agency has offered the school one free group adventure: swimming near sea turtles in Australia, exploring a volcanic cave in Iceland, or viewing a clear night sky in Morocco. Each trip promises a rare experience, but excitement alone is not enough to decide which students should join or how the school should prepare them.

The marine trip requires confident swimming and careful protection of wildlife. The cave visit may involve cold weather, uneven ground and strict safety equipment. Stargazing could offer cultural exchange and science learning, but long travel and unfamiliar conditions may concern families. Cost beyond the free package, insurance, health needs and environmental impact must also be considered.

Students asking for parental approval should present accurate information rather than hide the risks. Training, supervision, emergency plans and regular communication can make a proposal more convincing. The best choice should offer educational value to the whole group and remain accessible to students with different abilities. Participants could later share their learning with the school so that the benefit extends beyond a small number of travellers.

context.title: Could a Beehive Belong at School?
body: Urban beekeeping has appeared on rooftops, in community gardens and at some schools. A managed hive can help students observe pollination, insect behaviour and the connection between food and local ecosystems. Honey production may attract attention, but the deeper educational value comes from collecting evidence and caring for living creatures responsibly.

Keeping bees on a school campus also creates real concerns. Some students may be allergic or frightened, neighbours may worry about swarms, and inexperienced handling can harm both people and bees. A hive needs a suitable location, trained supervision, protective equipment and a plan for holidays, extreme weather and disease.

Before installing a hive, the student council should consult specialists, families and nearby residents. Alternatives such as planting bee-friendly flowers, monitoring wild pollinators or visiting a professional apiary can teach similar lessons with less risk. If the project proceeds, access should be controlled and participation voluntary. The school should treat bee welfare and public safety as continuing responsibilities, not just problems during the launch.

context.title: Should Campus TV Add Subtitles?
body: Subtitles can make school television programmes easier to follow in noisy places and more accessible to viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing. They may also help students learn unfamiliar words, identify names and understand speech delivered in a second language. A written record can make announcements clearer when audio quality is poor.

Producing accurate subtitles takes time. Automatic systems may misunderstand names, accents or subject vocabulary, while manually checking every line creates extra work for the Campus TV team. Subtitles can also cover important visual information if they are badly placed. Fast live programmes, music performances or shows built around visual humour may need a different approach.

The club could begin with news, interviews and educational features where accuracy has clear value. Students should choose readable size, timing and colour, then ask viewers with different needs to test the result. Subtitles do not have to be added in exactly the same way to every programme. A flexible policy can improve access without making production demands impossible for a student team.

context.title: Personal Shopping in an Age of AI
body: A personal shopper helps clients choose products that suit their needs, budget or style. The job may involve researching items, visiting stores, arranging fittings and explaining alternatives. Teenagers with strong communication skills could gain useful experience through supervised part-time work, but they would also need reliability, product knowledge and respect for customer privacy.

Artificial intelligence can already recommend products from browsing history, answer routine questions and create virtual images of clothing. Such tools may make shopping faster, yet they can repeat biased data, encourage unnecessary purchases or misunderstand a client’s feelings. Human staff remain useful when a decision is personal, expensive or difficult to explain through a list of preferences.

Shopping will probably combine digital and physical services rather than move entirely in one direction. Customers may research online, try items in a store and receive advice from both software and staff. Future personal shoppers will need to use technology without becoming controlled by it. Their value will depend on trust, judgement and the ability to understand needs that a customer has not expressed clearly.

context.title: Hong Kong in Ninety Seconds
body: A tourism video contest has asked students to create a short film for young visitors to Hong Kong. Famous views such as Victoria Harbour can establish the location quickly, but a video made only of familiar landmarks may look like many existing advertisements. Street markets, hiking routes, neighbourhood food and creative spaces could show a wider range of experiences.

Activities should be visually interesting and realistic for visitors to try. The team might follow a low-cost day across several districts, introduce local snacks, compare city and countryside, or ask young residents for recommendations. Music, captions and a clear story can hold attention, while accurate transport and accessibility information makes the video useful rather than merely attractive.

Filming in a busy city requires preparation. The team must consider weather, crowd noise, permission, privacy and the time needed to move between locations. Drones or risky camera positions should not be used simply for dramatic shots. A successful entry will present Hong Kong honestly, avoid stereotypes and make viewers curious enough to explore responsibly.

context.title: Why Old Games Still Find New Players
body: Classic video games such as Super Mario Bros remain popular even though their graphics and controls are simpler than those of modern titles. Clear goals, memorable music and carefully designed challenges allow new players to understand them quickly. Older players may also return because the games are connected to childhood memories and can be shared across generations.

Video games have stayed popular by changing with technology. Online play, mobile devices, live streaming and independent developers have brought games to wider audiences. At the same time, familiar characters and older design ideas are repeatedly remade or re-released. This mixture of novelty and recognition helps the industry attract both experienced players and beginners.

Future games may use more realistic virtual worlds, artificial intelligence and movement-based controls, but technical power will not guarantee enjoyment. Cost, privacy, excessive play and age suitability will remain important concerns. The most successful games are likely to combine new forms of interaction with the qualities that made classic games last: understandable rules, fair challenge and a reason to try again.

Schools can teach students to check an organisation’s official website, compare claims across sources and ask a trusted adult before accepting an opportunity. Social media can open a door, but real preparation still requires study, practical experience, reflection and conversations with people who understand the work.

context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style practice article based on the verified 2024 Paper 4 topic (not the official passage):
context.title: Museums Without Walls
body: Museums once depended mainly on visitors walking through their doors. Today, many institutions also place paintings, objects and historical records online. A digital collection can reach students who live far away, support people who cannot travel easily and allow fragile items to be examined without being handled. Zoom tools, audio commentary and searchable labels can make details easier to notice.

Online access, however, is not the same as standing beside an original object. A screen cannot fully show its scale, texture or the atmosphere of a gallery. Digital projects also require careful photography, accurate descriptions and long-term technical support. If the experience becomes only a quick slideshow, visitors may look without understanding.

Local museums therefore need to connect rather than separate the two formats. Online previews can arouse curiosity, while guided activities, workshops and changing exhibitions can give people reasons to visit in person. The key question is how technology can widen access while preserving the special value of a real museum visit.

body: A digital museum allows visitors to examine high-resolution images, three-dimensional models and recorded stories without travelling. Students can rotate an ancient object, zoom in on small details and return to an exhibit after class. Online access also supports people who live far away or find a physical visit difficult.

A virtual tour cannot reproduce the scale, texture and atmosphere of seeing an original object in a gallery. Some users click quickly without reading, and advanced features may exclude people with older devices or slow connections. Museums must also pay to photograph, describe, translate and securely store their collections.

The strongest plan may connect the two experiences. An online preview can build curiosity before a visit, while maps, captions and audio can support visitors inside the museum. Interactive games can invite exploration if they respect the subject. The purpose is not to replace the building, but to give more people a meaningful way into its collection.

Convenience may hide difficult working conditions. Delivery workers face traffic, bad weather and pressure to arrive quickly. Some pay for their own bicycles, fuel and repairs, yet receive no guaranteed hours, sick leave or protection when orders are scarce. Low delivery fees can make meals attractive to customers while shifting costs and risks to workers.

Possible improvements include minimum payments, accident insurance, rest facilities and clearer rules about employment status. Apps could also group nearby orders and encourage reusable packaging to reduce waste. Consumers, restaurants and platforms all benefit from the service, so the discussion should consider how responsibility can be shared fairly.

context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style practice article based on the verified 2024 Paper 4 topic (not the official passage):
context.title: When a Building Divides Opinion
body: A building can be useful, historically important and still be disliked for its appearance. People may object to a strange shape, ageing concrete or a colour that clashes with nearby streets. In a dense city, one large structure can influence an entire skyline, so arguments about beauty often become arguments about identity and public space.

Demolition is not always the best answer. A controversial building may represent the design ideas of its time or contain memories shared by a community. Replacing it creates waste and can remove affordable facilities. On the other hand, serious safety problems, poor access or an impractical layout may make renovation expensive and difficult.

A fair decision should consider more than a popularity vote. Planners can examine structural condition, cultural value, environmental cost and the needs of people who use the site. Public consultation and creative reuse may turn an unpopular building into a useful landmark. The challenge is deciding which faults can be improved and which justify replacement.

Travel can also introduce local culture to a wider audience and encourage residents to see familiar places with fresh interest.

Too many visitors can create different problems. Popular districts may become crowded, rents can rise and everyday services may focus more on tourists than residents. Natural areas and historic buildings can be damaged when large groups arrive at the same time. Noise, waste and disrespectful behaviour may weaken local support for tourism.

Destinations have tried entry reservations, visitor charges, limits on new hotels and campaigns that explain local customs. Hong Kong could apply different measures to busy attractions rather than one rule for the whole city. Good management should protect residents and the environment without making visitors feel unwelcome or excluding travellers with smaller budgets.

Supporters say the technology could improve punctuality and help the network respond more quickly to passenger demand.

Before introducing driverless trams, operators could run supervised trials and publish clear safety results. Accessible boarding, multilingual announcements and space for wheelchairs should be part of the design. The aim should be to modernise an icon of Hong Kong without losing public confidence or the character that makes tram travel distinctive.

context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style practice article based on the verified 2024 Paper 4 topic (not the official passage):
context.title: Why Certain Foods Feel Special
body: Comfort food is not simply a type of dish. It is food connected with safety, memory or care. A bowl of congee may remind someone of being looked after at home, while a familiar snack may recall school days or celebrations. During stress, people often choose such foods because the taste is predictable and the memory is reassuring.

Many popular comfort foods are high in salt, sugar or fat, but this does not mean they must be banned. Portion size, frequency and preparation method matter. A home-cooked soup or fruit-based dessert can provide comfort without becoming an everyday unhealthy habit. Different generations may also choose different dishes because their memories and lifestyles are not the same.

Food offers temporary relief, but it cannot solve every cause of stress. Exercise, sleep, conversation and time outdoors may support mental health for longer. A balanced approach should allow people to enjoy meaningful foods while recognising when eating is replacing other forms of care.

Two services also mean more equipment, staff training and licences. If neither side is managed well, the business may feel confusing rather than convenient.

A successful owner should identify a clear group of customers and design the space around their needs. Reliable Wi-Fi, comfortable seating, transparent prices and a booking system may be more important than unusual decoration. Partnerships with local clubs or charities can also build a community. Good intentions are not enough. Donated food must be within date, stored at the correct temperature and clearly labelled. Privacy also matters: people should be able to receive help without being photographed or treated as a publicity opportunity.

A school could begin with a limited collection of sealed dry food or partner with an experienced charity. Students might organise inventories, create multilingual safety notices and explain why reliable small donations are more useful than occasional large campaigns. The project should be judged by whether it meets community needs safely and respectfully, not simply by how many items are collected.

Smell is personal, so one scent may attract some visitors and upset others. Strong food, exhaust fumes or wet-market odours can be described honestly without suggesting that the whole city is unpleasant. A display should also avoid artificial scents that trigger allergies or overwhelm people in a closed space.

An event stall could use sealed scent containers, photographs and short recorded stories from residents. Visitors might match smells to districts or vote for the scent that best represents Hong Kong. Choosing only three requires balance: heritage, everyday food and nature could each have a place. The goal is to make visitors curious about the stories behind the smells, not just test whether they like them.

Students may be drawn to jobs they already see in films or social media, while overlooking occupations with strong demand but less publicity. Salary matters, yet working conditions, training time, job security and personal interest also influence a sustainable career choice. Some roles will change through automation rather than disappear completely.

A school job fair can help by offering short demonstrations, conversations with workers and honest information about qualifications. The arrangement also places heavy demands on families. Adults need subject knowledge, time and suitable materials, while students still need friends, teamwork and contact with viewpoints beyond the home. Assessment and progression must be planned carefully. In a small flat or a household where adults work long hours, flexibility may be harder to achieve than it appears.

Online courses have made home learning easier, but technology does not replace teaching or social development. Community classes, sports and regular professional guidance could reduce some weaknesses. Homeschooling may suit a limited number of students in Hong Kong, yet it should be judged by learning quality and wellbeing rather than presented as automatically easier or better.

body: Typing and voice input have reduced the amount of handwriting people do each day. Clear writing can help a reader, while forming letters may support memory and fine motor control.

Calligraphy adds an artistic and cultural dimension. It asks writers to slow down, control pressure and pay attention to shape and spacing. For some people it is a link to tradition; for others it is a quiet creative activity. Beautiful writing, however, should not be confused with intelligence, and students with motor difficulties should not be unfairly judged.

A school club could teach basic techniques, compare writing systems, create cards and signs, or invite a local artist to demonstrate. Digital tablets could also show how traditional skills can be adapted. The club should focus on expression and improvement rather than perfect handwriting, making the activity welcoming to beginners.

Harvested food could be used in cookery lessons, sold for a charity project or shared with a community organisation, provided hygiene rules are followed. context.title: A Short Rest at School

A school trial could use bookings, a twenty-minute limit and clear hygiene rules. Students should learn that pods are not a substitute for healthy sleep habits. title: Mascot Design Contest for the Cross Harbour Race
source_note: 2024 HKDSE English Language Paper 4 past-paper topic. Title, Part A task and prompts, and Part B question order were cross-checked against a scanned full paper; official HKEAA sample-performance material independently confirms selected versions. The context below is original practice material, not the official passage.

context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style practice article based on the verified 2024 Paper 4 topic (not the official passage):
context.title: A Face for the Cross Harbour Race
body: The Cross Harbour Race combines open-water swimming with a famous city view. Organisers want a mascot that can appear at the event and on shirts, bottles and souvenirs. A successful character should be easy to recognise from a distance, work in both flat images and costume form, and express energy, courage and connection with Victoria Harbour.

Choosing an animal simply because it is cute may not be enough. A dolphin or fish links clearly to water, while a lion can represent Hong Kong spirit but may be less connected to swimming. Designers should consider local identity, safety, colours, movement and whether the image appeals to children and adults without copying an existing character.

The group could sketch several options, test them with students and explain the meaning behind each feature. The final mascot should also work in small digital icons and be practical for a performer to wear. Good design supports the event rather than distracting from athletes, and gives spectators a friendly symbol they can remember.

part_a.instruction: Your teacher wants your class to enter a mascot design contest for the Cross Harbour Race. Your group is meeting to discuss ideas for designing a mascot. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: what qualities make a good mascot
what to consider when choosing a mascot for the Cross Harbour Race
whether you would recommend using any of the proposed characters
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Are sports events popular in Hong Kong?
Do you like watching sports events?
Is the Cross Harbour Race suitable for people of all ages?
Why do people like to buy toys and other souvenirs at sports events?
How else could the Cross Harbour Race be promoted in Hong Kong?

Do mascots appeal to people of all ages?

title: Instant Noodles Have Changed the World
source_note: 2024 HKDSE English Language Paper 4 past-paper topic. Title, Part A task and prompts, and Part B question order were cross-checked against a scanned full paper; official HKEAA sample-performance material independently confirms selected versions. context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style practice article based on the verified 2024 Paper 4 topic (not the official passage):
context.title: A Small Invention with Global Reach
body: Instant noodles began as a practical answer to a simple problem: how to make a familiar meal quick to store, transport and prepare. Drying cooked noodles allowed them to last, while packaging them in a cup later made the product even easier to eat. Low cost, long shelf life and many flavours helped the idea spread across countries and social groups.

An exhibition could use instant noodles to show that inventions do not need to be large machines. Successful products often combine observation, repeated testing and an understanding of everyday needs. At the same time, the story has drawbacks. Many instant noodle products contain high levels of salt, and single-use cups and wrappers create waste.

Students could compare instant noodles with other inventions that changed daily routines, such as refrigeration, electronic payment or the reusable water bottle. The exhibit should neither advertise nor condemn the food. Instead, it can ask how convenience, health, cost and environmental impact shape whether an invention remains valuable over time.

part_a.instruction: Your school is holding an exhibition on inventions that changed the world. Your group is thinking about including instant noodles in the exhibition. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: why instant noodles are popular
whether instant noodles should be included in the exhibition
other inventions that could be included
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

Do you often eat fast food?

title: Space Tourism
source_note: 2024 HKDSE English Language Paper 4 past-paper topic. Title, Part A task and prompts, and Part B question order were cross-checked against a scanned full paper; official HKEAA sample-performance material independently confirms selected versions. context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style practice article based on the verified 2024 Paper 4 topic (not the official passage):
context.title: When Space Becomes a Private Journey
body: Private companies have begun carrying passengers high above Earth for short periods of weightlessness. Supporters argue that competition can speed up engineering, lower future costs and create new research opportunities. Images and personal accounts from travellers may also inspire interest in science and make space exploration feel less distant.

For now, tickets are available only to extremely wealthy people, and each launch uses energy and produces emissions. More flights could add debris to an already crowded area around Earth. Safety is another concern: passengers face risks, while accidents could affect people and property on the ground. Public resources may also be used to support private businesses.

Encouragement should therefore depend on strong safety rules, transparent environmental reporting and benefits beyond entertainment. Companies could fund scientific experiments and technology that serves people on Earth. Private travel may contribute to exploration, but excitement alone is not enough to justify every flight. The central question is who gains, who carries the risk and what wider purpose the journey serves.

part_a.instruction: You are members of your school's Science Club. You have gathered to discuss the issue of private space travel. You may want to talk about:

the disadvantages of private space travel
whether private space travel should be encouraged
anything else you think is important

title: Shopping on Social Media
source_note: 2024 HKDSE English Language Paper 4 past-paper topic. Title, Part A task and prompts, and Part B question order were cross-checked against a scanned full paper; official HKEAA sample-performance material independently confirms selected versions. The context below is original practice material, not the official passage.

context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style practice article based on the verified 2024 Paper 4 topic (not the official passage):
context.title: From Post to Purchase
body: Social-media platforms now let users discover and buy products without leaving an app. A video can demonstrate an item, a customer can ask questions in comments and a direct link can complete the purchase. Small sellers gain access to large audiences without opening a physical shop, while buyers receive recommendations connected to their interests.

The same speed can make careful judgement difficult. Sponsored posts may look like personal advice, reviews can be false and an attractive video may hide poor quality. Some shoppers are uncomfortable sharing payment details, and it can be difficult to return goods to a seller with no clear address. Constant personalised advertising may also encourage unnecessary spending.

Traditional shops can respond by combining physical service with online communication, allowing customers to inspect items and order later. Platforms should verify sellers, identify paid promotions and provide clear complaint procedures. Social shopping is likely to grow, but trust will determine whether it becomes a normal part of retail rather than a place associated with scams.

how shopping through social media may affect traditional businesses
anything else you think is important

title: Unmanned Convenience Stores
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.1 topic:
context.title: A Store with No Cashier
body: A convenience-store chain is testing a small branch inside a busy railway station. Cameras and shelf sensors record what customers pick up, while a payment screen prepares the bill automatically. Shoppers can pay by card, phone or cash before an exit gate opens. One employee remains on site to restock shelves, answer questions and help customers when the system fails.

Supporters say the shop can operate for longer hours and reduce queues, especially when commuters are in a hurry. The company can also use sales data to keep popular products in stock. However, the branch offers fewer products than a normal store, and some customers worry about privacy, inaccurate bills and what happens if they need help. Others fear that automated stores will reduce entry-level jobs.

Retail analysts add that Hong Kong presents special challenges: shops are crowded, customers include tourists and elderly people, and electronic systems must cope with several payment methods. A successful unmanned shop may therefore need clear instructions, reliable security and staff who can respond quickly from nearby.

discussion_points.text: the benefits of unmanned convenience stores

whether unmanned convenience stores are a good idea for Hong Kong
anything else you think is important

title: Cinemas vs Streaming Services
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.2 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.2 topic:
context.title: Is This the End of Cinemas?
body: Movie streaming has changed how audiences choose entertainment. For one monthly fee, viewers can watch a large library of films at home or on a mobile device. They can pause a film, choose subtitles and avoid travel. New releases also reach online platforms more quickly than before, so some people visit cinemas less often.

Cinemas still offer an experience that a living room cannot easily copy. A large screen, powerful sound and a shared audience can make a film feel like a special event. Friends may also combine a cinema visit with a meal or shopping. Yet tickets and snacks are expensive, popular screenings sell out, and travelling home after a late film can be inconvenient.

Local cinema operators are experimenting with loyalty programmes, student prices, comfortable seats and special screenings. Some show classic films, sports events or question-and-answer sessions with filmmakers. Their challenge is to give audiences a reason to leave home while keeping prices affordable and ensuring that smaller, less commercial films can still reach the public.

title: Plant-Based Meats
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.3 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.3 topic:
context.title: Plant-Based Food Meets Cantonese Cooking
body: Plant-based meat is now appearing in dishes that once depended on pork, beef or seafood. A Hong Kong restaurant has tested meat-free versions of familiar Cantonese dishes, using products made from beans, grains and vegetable oils. Its chefs say that flavour and texture are important because diners may reject a sustainable choice if it does not feel satisfying.

Interest in these products is driven by several concerns. Some consumers want more vegetarian choices, while others hope to reduce the environmental impact of livestock farming. Health is another reason, although nutritionists warn that plant-based products can still contain high levels of salt or fat. They should be compared carefully rather than assumed to be healthy.

A secondary school is considering serving plant-based meals in its canteen on Green Mondays. Supporters believe students could discover new food and think about climate change. Critics worry about price, food waste and whether the dishes respect students’ cultural preferences. The school must decide whether to encourage participation, require it or offer plant-based food beside the usual menu.

title: Night Owls
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.1 topic:
context.title: Different Body Clocks at Work
body: Some people feel most alert early in the morning, while others naturally become energetic late at night. These patterns are partly influenced by habits and partly by the body’s internal clock. Problems arise when a person’s preferred schedule does not match school or work. A night owl who must start at eight o’clock may lose sleep even when trying to go to bed earlier.

Regular sleep matters. Too little sleep can affect concentration, mood and long-term health. Early risers may find it easier to follow normal timetables and exercise before the day becomes busy. Night owls, however, may enjoy quiet hours for creative work and can be highly productive when interruptions are limited.

Some employers are testing flexible starting times or allowing staff to work from home. Supporters say performance should matter more than the hour at which someone arrives. Managers worry that different schedules may make teamwork and customer service harder. Any flexible system would need shared meeting hours, clear deadlines and rules to prevent employees from working late and starting early at the same time.

discussion_points.text: the advantages of being a night owl
the advantages of getting up early
whether companies should offer flexible working hours for people with different sleeping patterns
anything else you think is important

title: Teachers and Students on Social Media
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.2 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.2 topic:
context.title: Should Teachers and Students Be Online Friends?
body: Social media can make communication between teachers and students quick and familiar. A teacher may post reminders, share useful links or answer simple questions after school. Some students also feel more comfortable asking for help online than speaking in front of a class. Used carefully, a class account can strengthen learning and allow positive role models to reach students where they already spend time.

Personal accounts create different problems. Informal messages can blur the boundary between friendship and professional communication. Students may see private photographs or opinions that were never intended for a school audience, while teachers may learn more about students’ social lives than is appropriate. Screenshots can spread beyond the intended group, and a late-night message may create unrealistic expectations about when teachers must reply.

A school is considering a policy that would stop teachers and students from connecting through personal accounts. Official class accounts would remain available and all messages would be visible to the school. The proposal may protect both sides, but it could also remove a useful channel unless the school offers a practical alternative.

part_a.instruction: Your school is considering a policy that would not allow teachers and students to be friends on social media. Discuss the proposal.

discussion_points.text: why students like to connect with teachers on social media
problems that may result from connecting with teachers on social media
whether you agree with the proposed policy
anything else you think is important

context.title: Three Unusual Graduation Ideas
body: A local events company has suggested three experiences for a class graduation celebration. The first is a short helicopter flight over Victoria Harbour and the Geopark. It offers excellent photographs but is expensive and can take only a few students at a time. Bad weather may also cause a last-minute cancellation.

The second option is a cooking lesson with a well-known chef. Students would prepare a meal together and then hold a dinner party. The activity is social and can include teachers, although the restaurant has limited space and must know about allergies in advance. The third option is an outdoor zip-line experience. Trained guides provide safety equipment, but participants must travel to the site and some may be afraid of heights.

The class has a fixed budget and wants the celebration to be memorable without excluding anyone. Organisers must consider cost, safety, transport, group size and the meaning of graduation. They may choose one of the suggested activities or design a simpler event at school that allows every student to participate.

title: Fashion after the Pandemic
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.1 topic:
context.title: How Staying Home Changed Fashion
body: Periods of working and studying from home changed what many people expected from clothes. Instead of formal outfits, shoppers looked for soft fabrics, loose shapes and items that could be worn for both a video meeting and an evening at home. Some consumers bought fewer clothes because they had fewer social events, while others spent more time browsing online shops.

Social media became an important source of fashion ideas. Short videos showed viewers how to combine comfortable clothes or turn old items into new outfits. At the same time, fast-moving online trends encouraged impulse buying. Customers could order several sizes, return unwanted items and expect rapid delivery, creating extra packaging and transport.

Fashion companies now face mixed expectations. Customers want comfort and low prices, but many also ask for durable products, fair working conditions and less waste. Shops can respond with clearer size information, repair services, recycled materials and collections suitable for flexible work. The challenge is to remain profitable without encouraging people to buy clothes they will rarely wear.
