title: Student Cleaning Sessions
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.2 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.2 topic:
context.title: What Students Learn from Cleaning
body: At some Japanese schools, students spend about twenty minutes cleaning classrooms and shared areas after lunch. Each class receives specific duties, and students work in small groups. The practice is not intended to replace professional cleaners. Instead, it teaches students to care for spaces that everyone uses and to notice the work required to keep a school comfortable.

Teachers say cleaning can develop responsibility, cooperation and respect. A student who must sweep a corridor may be less likely to drop litter there later. Similar benefits can come from household chores: young people feel that they make a useful contribution and learn practical skills. However, poorly organised sessions may become unfair if responsible students do most of the work or if younger pupils are given unsafe tasks.

A Hong Kong school is considering adding short cleaning sessions to its timetable as part of an environmental campaign. It must decide how often sessions should occur, which duties suit different forms and how to provide equipment and supervision. The plan should improve habits without reducing lesson time or allowing cleaning to be used as punishment.

title: Growing Plants at School
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.3 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.3 topic:
context.title: Gardening as a Way to Feel Better
body: Horticultural therapy uses plants and gardening activities to support physical and mental health. Participants may water seedlings, arrange flowers or grow vegetables. These simple tasks provide a clear routine and a visible result. Time spent in green spaces can also reduce stress, encourage gentle movement and give people a break from screens and crowded indoor environments.

Schools can use gardening in several ways. A small herb garden can support science lessons, while flowers can improve an unattractive corner of the campus. Students may learn patience because plants need regular care, not attention only when an event is approaching. Produce can be used in cooking activities or sold for charity. However, gardens require space, tools, water and a plan for weekends and holidays.

One school wants to develop students’ interest in growing plants as part of a well-being programme. Some students may prefer sports, music or art, so participation should offer different roles such as design, photography and record keeping. The school must decide whether gardening will attract enough interest and how it can complement other activities rather than replace them.

title: Wearable Smart Devices
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.1 topic:
context.title: More than a Smartwatch
body: Wearable technology now includes rings, bracelets, clothing and shoes as well as smartwatches. A smart ring can collect information about sleep, movement and heart rate without displaying messages. Sensor-equipped clothing covers more of the body and may provide useful information about breathing, posture or exercise technique. Athletes and patients may therefore benefit from data collected throughout the day.

The same devices raise questions. Measurements are not always accurate, and users may worry unnecessarily about a single unusual result. Companies can collect location and health data that people would normally keep private. Wearables are also expensive and may become outdated quickly. In schools, a watch that receives messages can distract students or provide unfair help during a test.

Supporters argue that simple fitness trackers can motivate students to move and help physical-education classes set personal goals. A complete ban may treat every device as if it were a phone. Schools could instead require communication features to be disabled, prohibit devices during tests and explain how health information should be protected.

title: Wearable Smart Devices — Privacy and Health
source_note: Original hidden mock inspired by the officially confirmed 2023 Paper 4 version 4.1 theme. This is not an HKEAA question paper.

context.source_line: Original mock context for internal practice:
context.title: When Your Watch Knows More About You
body: Smartwatches, rings and sensor-equipped clothing can count steps, measure heart rate and estimate sleep quality. Some devices remind users to move after long periods of sitting, while others send an alert when they detect an unusual pattern. Athletes may use the data to plan training, and patients can show a longer record to a doctor. Continuous information can reveal changes that a short clinic visit might miss.

Wearable data is not always accurate or easy to interpret. A low sleep score may create anxiety even when the user feels well. Personal information may be stored by technology companies, shared with other services or exposed in a data breach. Users may not understand what they accepted when they first set up the device.

Schools face an additional problem because a smartwatch can receive messages and may be used unfairly during tests. A sensible policy could distinguish a basic health tracker from a communication device, restrict wearables during assessments and prohibit schools from collecting fitness data without clear consent. Students should also remember that a gadget offers useful clues, not a medical diagnosis.

whether they should be allowed at school
anything else you think is important

title: Adaptability Quotient
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.2 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.2 topic:
context.title: AQ: Learning to Handle Change
body: People often talk about IQ and emotional intelligence, but employers increasingly discuss adaptability quotient, or AQ. It describes a person’s ability to learn, adjust and keep working when circumstances change. New technology, unexpected events and changing customer needs mean that knowledge learned once may not remain useful for an entire career.

Adaptability does not mean accepting every change without question. It involves noticing what is different, asking for information and testing a sensible response. People can develop it by varying routines, learning unfamiliar skills and listening to viewpoints outside their usual circle. Reflection is also important: after a plan fails, an adaptable person identifies what can be improved instead of simply repeating the same action.

A school is planning an AQ workshop. Some teachers want problem-solving games and surprise challenges, while others prefer talks by people who changed careers or overcame setbacks. Students may feel uncomfortable if activities reward risk-taking without providing support. The workshop therefore needs a safe way to practise change and a clear explanation of how adaptability differs from intelligence, confidence and obedience.

title: Social Media and Well-being
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.3 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.title: Using Social Media with Purpose
body: Social media can spread useful knowledge, encourage creativity and help people find communities. It can also fill every quiet moment with comparison, advertising and upsetting news. A feed is selected by both the user and the platform, so it may give a distorted picture of other people’s lives. Popular accounts often show carefully edited highlights rather than ordinary experiences.

Digital-well-being advisers suggest using social media with a purpose. Before opening an app, a user can ask what they need to do and close it afterwards. Unfollowing accounts that create anger or pressure can improve the experience. Turning off unnecessary notifications and keeping phones away during study or sleep also reduces automatic checking. If a platform seriously affects someone’s mood, taking a temporary break may be sensible.

A school Mental Health and Wellness Club wants to promote healthier habits without presenting all social media as harmful. It could run a feed-cleaning workshop, a notification-free challenge or a campaign about realistic posting. The club must make activities supportive rather than judgmental and explain when students should seek help from an adult.

title: Family History and DNA Tests

context.title: Finding Family Stories through DNA
body: Home DNA kits have made family-history research easier to begin. A customer sends a small sample to a company and later receives an estimate of where their ancestors may have lived. The result can challenge family assumptions and lead users to old records or distant relatives. For some people, the search provides a stronger sense of identity and preserves stories that might otherwise disappear.

The result is not a complete family history. Estimates depend on the company’s database and may change as more samples are added. Unexpected relatives or information about parentage can cause distress. DNA is also highly personal: once data is stored, users may not fully control whether it is used for research, shared with another company or requested by authorities.

A class project is examining whether DNA tests are a good way to research family history. Alternatives include interviewing relatives, collecting photographs, reading public records and mapping important family events. These methods take time but provide names, choices and experiences that a percentage on a DNA report cannot explain. A careful project should combine evidence and respect relatives who prefer not to participate.

context.title: From Unwanted Items to a School Fund
body: Online marketplaces allow people to photograph an item, write a short description and offer it for sale within minutes. Buyers can compare prices, ask questions and arrange delivery or collection. Second-hand trading may reduce waste because clothes, books and electronics remain useful instead of being thrown away. It can also help a small organisation reach more customers than a physical sale.

A school plans to sell items donated by students to raise money. The organising team must inspect each item, record who donated it and decide on a fair price. Clear photographs and honest descriptions will reduce complaints. Valuable items may need secure storage, while unsold goods require a plan. Students should not publish personal phone numbers or meet unknown buyers alone.

Online selling also creates risks. A buyer may disappear, claim an item is damaged or send a false payment message. Delivery costs can remove much of the profit from a cheap product. The school therefore needs one official account, adult supervision and rules for payment, collection and refunds. Good organisation will determine whether convenience leads to useful income or a confusing dispute.

The package includes ten lessons, a mat and a water bottle. Supporters say the service saves travel time and lets people exercise even when weather, illness or a busy schedule keeps them at home.

Online classes are not suitable for everyone. An instructor may not see a student’s posture clearly, especially in a small room or with a poor connection. Participants need enough space to move safely and must decide whether the class level matches their ability. Some people are motivated by exercising with others in a studio, while others feel less embarrassed at home.

Before joining, customers should compare the instructor’s qualifications, timetable, class size, price and safety support. They should also check whether recordings are made and how camera images are used. Online fitness may remain popular as one option, but gyms can still provide equipment, direct correction and a stronger sense of community.

title: Storytelling in Advertising
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 6.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 6.1 topic:
context.title: Why a Story Can Sell a Product
body: Some of the most memorable advertisements do more than list a product’s features. They present a character, a problem and a satisfying ending. Viewers may remember a funny mistake, an unexpected act of kindness or a small personal victory long after they forget the price. If the product helps the story reach its conclusion, the brand becomes connected with that emotion.

Storytelling can also fail. A dramatic story may attract attention while leaving viewers unsure what is being sold. An emotional message can feel dishonest if the product has little connection to it. Celebrities may dominate the advertisement, and a joke that works for one audience may offend another. A good campaign therefore needs a simple idea, a clear audience and a believable role for the product.

A Business Studies class must advertise a new sports drink called Champion. The group could show a student preparing for a difficult race, a team recovering from a mistake or an ordinary person completing a personal challenge. Sound, colour, humour and a short slogan can make the advertisement memorable, but the claims about the drink must remain accurate.

title: Good Habits for S.4 Students

context.title: Habits That Make Senior Forms Manageable
body: Moving into the senior forms brings more demanding subjects, longer assignments and decisions about future study. Successful students do not depend only on last-minute effort. They organise deadlines, divide large tasks into smaller steps and choose a regular time and place to work. A realistic plan includes rest and other activities, because an impossible timetable is quickly abandoned.

Active study is more effective than simply rereading a textbook. Students can take concise notes, test themselves, explain an idea to a classmate and ask questions before confusion grows. Study groups are useful when members arrive prepared and remain focused. Good sleep also supports memory and concentration; staying awake all night to revise may reduce the benefit of the extra hours.

A group of senior students is preparing a sharing session for S.4. The session should recognise both academic and personal challenges, including time management, changing friendships and pressure about subject choices. Advice will be more convincing if speakers describe mistakes they made, practical habits that helped and places where younger students can seek support.

Comedy is affordable and easy to arrange, although jokes must be suitable for students, parents and former pupils. The third option is a lion-dance group offering traditional, LED and hip-hop performances. It costs $7,000 for fifteen minutes and requires a large space plus meals for eight performers.

The organising team must consider audience appeal, cultural meaning, length, safety, space and value for money. The most popular act is not automatically the best choice if it excludes part of the school community or leaves too little budget for other anniversary activities.

title: Time in Different Cultures
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 7.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 7.1 topic:
context.title: Is Being Late Always Disrespectful?
body: Ideas about time differ across cultures and situations. In some places, arriving late for a business meeting suggests poor preparation or disrespect. Daily life is organised around calendars, deadlines and exact transport schedules. In other places, relationships and changing circumstances may matter more than a fixed starting time, so an event begins when the necessary people have arrived.

Researchers often describe cultures as fast-paced or slow-paced, but these labels can become stereotypes. A country may value punctual trains while allowing long social meals. Age, occupation and city life also influence behaviour. Mobile phones have changed expectations because people can update one another immediately, yet constant messages may make schedules feel even more demanding.

Hong Kong is often associated with speed, long working hours and the idea that time is money. This can support efficiency, but it may also leave little room for rest, family and unplanned conversation. A slower life does not require ignoring responsibilities. People can protect meal times, reduce unnecessary appointments, walk without checking a phone and agree on which deadlines truly matter.

source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 7.3 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 7.3 topic:
context.title: When an Online Trend Threatens Wildlife
body: Videos of small wild animals in cafés and private homes can receive millions of views. Their large eyes and unusual behaviour make them appear harmless, and viewers may want the same experience. Wildlife groups warn that online popularity can increase demand, encouraging traders to remove animals from natural habitats and transport them in poor conditions.

A wild animal may survive in a home without living well. It can need a specialised diet, a large territory, contact with its own species and activity at times when an owner wants to sleep. Even a caring person may not recognise illness or stress. Some animals can bite, spread disease or be abandoned when they become difficult to manage. The trade also adds pressure to species already affected by habitat loss.

Social media platforms, cafés and pet sellers all influence what people consider an acceptable pet. Clear labels, restrictions on harmful content and public education may reduce impulsive purchases. Schools can help students distinguish between admiring wildlife and owning it. A responsible choice should consider animal welfare, public safety, conservation and whether a domestic animal can meet the owner’s needs instead.

context.title: Could Insects Become Everyday Food?
body: As the world population grows, producing enough protein without using more land and water will become difficult. In many countries, insects have been eaten for generations. Crickets, beetle larvae and other species can contain protein, vitamins and minerals. They also require less space and feed than cattle and can produce far fewer greenhouse-gas emissions.

These advantages do not make insect food an easy choice. People who did not grow up eating insects may feel disgust or worry about safety. Farms need hygiene standards, clear labelling and controls on species and feed. Allergy risks must also be studied. Products may be easier to accept when insects are ground into flour for noodles, snack bars or dumpling fillings rather than served whole.

A group is considering the food people may eat in the future. Promotion could begin with small tastings, chef demonstrations and honest information about nutrition and environmental impact. Price and flavour will matter as much as education. Insect products should be offered as another option, not presented as a punishment or as the only responsible diet.

title: Walking-Friendly Cities
source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 8.2 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 8.2 topic:
context.title: Why City Design Changes How Much We Walk
body: A large step-count study found that people in Hong Kong walk more than residents of many other cities. Dense neighbourhoods, frequent public transport and nearby shops mean that walking is often part of an ordinary journey. Research also links regular walking with better heart health, lower stress and a reduced risk of several long-term illnesses. It is free and requires no special equipment.

High average figures can hide important differences. Some districts have steep slopes, narrow pavements or roads that are difficult to cross. Summer heat, heavy rain, poor air quality and crowded streets discourage longer walks. Elderly people, wheelchair users and parents with young children may face broken surfaces or missing lifts that other pedestrians barely notice.

A walking-friendly city needs connected pavements, shade, seating, safe crossings, clear signs and routes that lead somewhere useful. Schools and workplaces can support walking through maps, step challenges and secure places for belongings, but activity should not become unhealthy competition. The group must decide whether Hong Kong’s environment encourages genuine choice or simply makes residents walk out of necessity.

title: Screen-time Controls for Teenagers
source_note: Original internal 2019-themed mock practice set. It is not an HKDSE past-paper question and must remain hidden from the past-paper library unless deliberately published as a mock.

context.source_line: Original mock practice article (not an official HKDSE examination text):
context.title: Can a Phone Teach Us When to Put It Down?
body: Most smartphones now show how much time users spend on different apps. They can block selected services after a daily limit, silence notifications during study periods and produce weekly reports. Supporters say the data turns an invisible habit into something measurable and helps families notice patterns that would otherwise be ignored.

Limits do not automatically create self-control. Users can press an “ignore” button, change settings or move to another device. Strict monitoring may damage trust and encourage secretive behaviour, especially when adults do not follow the same rules. The purpose of online activity also matters: an hour of homework is different from an hour of endless short videos.

Some families prefer a shared agreement in which everyone keeps phones away during meals, study sessions and before bedtime. Schools can teach students to manage notifications and recognise persuasive app design. Technology can provide reminders, but lasting change depends on motivation, realistic routines and honest conversations about sleep, learning and relationships.

title: Translation Apps and Language Learning

context.source_line: Original mock practice article (not an official HKDSE examination text):
context.title: A Helpful Language Partner — or a Dangerous Shortcut?
body: Translation apps are fast, inexpensive and easy to use. A traveller can point a phone camera at a menu, while a student can listen to the pronunciation of an unfamiliar phrase. The apps reduce anxiety and may help people communicate in an emergency when no interpreter is available.

A smooth translation can still be misleading. Software may miss humour, cultural references, specialist meanings and the speaker’s tone. Students who paste an entire assignment into an app may submit unnatural sentences without understanding the grammar. Constant dependence can also prevent learners from thinking directly in the language they are studying.

Used carefully, an app can act as a dictionary, pronunciation guide and checking tool. Students should compare uncertain results, declare when substantial help was used and keep a record of their own corrections. Schools need rules that distinguish learning support from work that falsely appears to be the student’s own language.

context.title: Redevelopment: Questions and Trade-offs
body: New railway stations and private investment can quickly change an older district. Better transport may bring visitors, jobs and safer buildings, while new cafés and shops can make an area feel more lively. Owners may also welcome the chance to repair properties that have been neglected for years.

The same changes can be painful for long-term residents. When rents rise, small family businesses may close and tenants may be forced to move. Bars and restaurants can create noise late at night, and a neighbourhood may lose the services, relationships and character that once made it feel like home.

Redevelopment therefore needs more than new buildings. Residents could be consulted fairly and transparently before plans are approved, while affordable housing, compensation and support for traditional shops could reduce disruption. The central question is how Hong Kong can improve old districts without treating the people who already live there as an obstacle.

context.title: Wedding Photography: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Wedding photographs are expected to preserve an important day, but couples now have many styles to choose from. Creative photographs use unusual ideas, glamorous shoots depend on impressive locations, storytelling photography records natural emotions, and studio sessions offer privacy and control over lighting and weather.

Each style involves trade-offs. Travelling overseas may produce striking pictures but costs more and takes time. Studio portraits are reliable but can look formal, while candid photographs may capture genuine feelings yet miss the carefully planned details of the ceremony. Family members may also have different ideas about what a wedding album should show.

A couple should decide whether the priority is personality, tradition, scenery or the relationships shared with guests. The best photographs may combine several approaches instead of following one fashion. Cost, comfort, privacy and the meaning the pictures will have many years later should all guide the choice for both partners involved.

context.title: Online Crime: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Online scams can reach people through shopping sites, social media, dating platforms, email and text messages. A false seller may take payment without delivering the promised product, while a criminal may pretend to be a bank or a trusted friend in order to collect passwords, account details or money.

Students may believe they are unlikely targets because they have limited savings, but their identities, photographs and online accounts still have value. Reusing one password across several services makes a single mistake more serious. A friendly message can also create false trust before the sender asks for money or private information.

Protection begins with simple habits: use different passwords, turn on two-step verification, check web addresses and avoid rushed payments. Suspicious requests should be confirmed through another channel and reported to an adult, the platform or the police. Schools can help students practise recognising warning signs rather than merely telling them to be careful.

context.title: Fortune Telling: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Fortune telling remains visible in parts of Hong Kong, especially around temples and traditional market streets. Visitors may have their palms or faces read, consult the Chinese zodiac or ask about relationships, careers and health. For some people the experience is entertainment; for others it is a serious cultural practice.

Its appeal comes partly from uncertainty. A confident prediction can make a person feel understood and may offer a way to organise difficult choices. Family customs and curiosity also attract customers. Critics, however, question whether vague statements only seem accurate and worry that vulnerable people may pay repeatedly for advice they cannot verify.

Modern technology may change the service rather than end it. Online readings can reach younger audiences, while traditional practitioners may continue to attract people who value face-to-face contact. Its future will depend on whether it is treated as cultural heritage, commercial entertainment or professional advice, and on how customers are protected from dishonest claims.

context.title: Apple Screen Time Control: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Screen-time tools allow parents to see how long children use particular apps and to set periods when games, videos or social media are unavailable. Essential services, such as school materials or emergency messages, can remain open. Supporters say these controls make family rules clear and reduce arguments about late-night phone use.

The software cannot solve every problem. A strict limit may interrupt useful work, and young people may feel that constant monitoring invades their privacy. They can also move to another device or focus on reaching the limit instead of learning self-control. Parents who spend hours on their own phones may find their rules difficult to defend.

Controls work best when families agree on the purpose of each rule and review it as children become more responsible. Device-free meals, sensible bedtimes and adults setting a good example can support the technology. The question is not only how much time students spend online, but what they do there and what offline activities are being displaced.

context.title: International Sport: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Small countries can succeed in international sport when they invest in facilities, qualified coaches and opportunities for young players. Iceland’s rise in football attracted attention because its population is limited, yet a long-term training system helped local athletes compete with much larger nations. Hong Kong faces similar limits on land and player numbers.

Sending coaches or youth teams overseas may expose them to new methods and a different sporting culture. Such exchanges can inspire athletes, but a short visit will not repair weak local leagues, limited school time or poor support for competitors. Money spent on officials and publicity may also be criticised if athletes lack medical or training resources.

Hong Kong must decide what success means: medals, public participation, healthier citizens or a stronger professional system. Learning from another country requires adapting its ideas rather than copying them. Schools, sports associations and government need clear responsibilities, patient funding and ways for talented young people to continue training.

context.title: Facebook: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Facebook once appeared to be the natural place for young people to share photographs, messages and news, but many users have moved to newer platforms. Older relatives, community groups and event organisers may still rely on it, so leaving completely can mean losing useful connections and information.

The service also raises questions about privacy and trust. Employers may look at public posts, false accounts can deceive users, and misleading stories may spread faster than corrections. A joke written for friends can remain searchable years later. People who compare their lives with carefully edited posts may also feel isolated rather than connected.

Users should review privacy settings, check the source of surprising claims and think before posting information about themselves or others. Social media is likely to remain popular even if individual brands rise and fall, because the desire to communicate will continue. The more important issue is whether future platforms give users meaningful control over their data and attention.

context.title: Sex Discrimination: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Pay differences between men and women cannot be explained simply by ability. Women and men can perform the same professional tasks, yet promotion decisions, occupational stereotypes and unequal caring responsibilities may shape their careers. A worker who takes time away to care for family members may lose experience, income and opportunities to advance.

Some employers assume that men are more suitable for competitive leadership or long working hours, while women are directed towards lower-paid caring and support roles. Even when the work is comparable, secrecy around salaries makes unfair differences hard to identify. These patterns can influence students before they enter the workplace.

Possible responses include transparent salary ranges, equal-pay reviews, affordable childcare and flexible arrangements available to all parents. Schools can challenge the idea that particular careers belong to one gender. Laws matter, but organisations must also examine how they recruit, evaluate and promote staff so that performance is judged by evidence rather than expectations.

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 3.3 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Cheating: Questions and Trade-offs
body: When two homework assignments look almost identical, a school must find out what happened before deciding on a punishment. One student may have copied, both may have used the same online source, or they may have worked together when collaboration was not allowed. Similar work is a warning sign, not complete proof.

Students cheat for different reasons, including fear of failure, heavy workloads, unclear instructions and the belief that everyone else is doing it. Technology makes copied essays and automatic translation easy to obtain, but it can also help teachers compare drafts and understand how work developed. Punishment alone may hide the cause without changing behaviour.

A fair response should distinguish a first minor offence from repeated or organised dishonesty. Students need clear rules, a chance to explain and support if they lack skills or time management. Rewriting the task, meeting parents or detention may be appropriate, while serious cases require stronger action. Prevention should make honest work achievable as well as expected.

context.title: Living in a Densely Populated Urban Area: Questions and Trade-offs
body: A small action in a crowded city can reveal very different ideas about courtesy. One lift passenger may hold the door for someone approaching, while another presses “close” because every second matters. The first person sees patience and consideration; the second sees an unnecessary delay for everyone already inside.

Similar conflicts occur on pavements, escalators, trains and in queues. Limited space and long working hours can make people hurried, but crowding does not excuse blocking doors, pushing or ignoring those who need a seat. At the same time, rules that sound polite may be impractical if they slow a busy system or create danger.

Better behaviour depends on clear expectations and awareness of other people. Signs, station announcements and school education can help, but design matters too: wider passages, visible queues and enough time for lift doors to close reduce conflict. Urban courtesy is not about performing one fixed gesture; it is about judging how an action affects others in that moment.

context.title: Unusual English Names: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Many Hong Kong people use an English name at school or work. Some choose a familiar name because it is easy for teachers and colleagues to remember, while others select a word, brand or invented spelling that expresses individuality. A name may also resemble the sound or meaning of a person’s Chinese name.

Unusual names can be memorable and personally meaningful, but they may create unexpected problems. Listeners may not know how to pronounce them, computer forms may reject punctuation, and an employer may make unfair assumptions before meeting the applicant. A name that seems amusing to one culture may have an unwanted meaning in another.

Students should be free to decide how they wish to be addressed, yet it helps to check pronunciation, spelling and possible associations. They can use different names in informal and professional settings or simply use their Chinese name. Respect works both ways: the person choosing a name should consider its audience, and others should avoid mocking a choice they do not understand.

context.title: Person of the Year: Questions and Trade-offs
body: A school’s Person of the Year award can show students what kinds of achievement and behaviour the community values. Famous candidates may include artists, athletes, businesspeople or public officials, each representing a different route to success. Their stories can demonstrate perseverance, talent, service or the ability to overcome disadvantage.

Popularity alone is not a reliable standard. Students may know little about some nominees, disagree with their decisions or feel that celebrity receives more attention than quiet service. A person can also be successful without being a suitable role model in every part of life. The selection process should therefore explain which qualities are being recognised.

The school could invite nominations from students and require evidence of positive impact. Local volunteers, former students, teachers or young innovators may feel more relevant than internationally known figures. A balanced choice should inspire effort without suggesting that wealth or fame is the only measure of success, and should allow respectful disagreement about the final result.

context.title: CCTV: Questions and Trade-offs
body: CCTV cameras can help a school investigate theft, bullying or damage and may discourage some unsafe behaviour. Recordings from entrances and public corridors can provide evidence when witnesses disagree. Parents may also feel reassured that incidents can be reviewed rather than decided only by rumour.

Constant recording, however, changes how a school feels. Cameras may capture private conversations, be placed where they are not necessary or create suspicion between students and staff. A recording can cause further harm if too many people can view it, if it is kept indefinitely or if it is used for a purpose students were never told about.

Any system needs rules before cameras are installed. The school should identify specific risks, avoid sensitive areas, limit access to authorised staff and delete recordings after a stated period unless an incident is being investigated. Students and parents should know where cameras are and how to complain. Security should be improved without treating everyone as a potential offender.

context.title: The HKUST Campus in Guangzhou: Questions and Trade-offs
body: A Hong Kong university may open a campus in mainland China to gain more space, reach a wider group of students and build research partnerships. New laboratories and government support can allow programmes that are difficult to develop on a crowded Hong Kong campus. Cross-border study may also connect graduates with opportunities in the Greater Bay Area.

Hong Kong students could benefit from new friendships and a better understanding of mainland life, but adjustment may be demanding. Teaching methods, internet services, payment systems, healthcare arrangements and daily language use may differ. Students also need clear information about qualifications, fees, accommodation and whether courses are shared between campuses.

Before applying, students should visit if possible, compare curricula and speak with current learners. Universities should provide orientation, academic advice and support for emergencies. Expansion is worthwhile only if the new campus protects teaching quality and student welfare rather than serving mainly as a way to increase enrolment or improve an institution’s image.

context.title: Space Travel: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Private companies have proposed sending wealthy passengers and invited artists around the Moon. Supporters say seeing Earth from space could inspire paintings, films and ideas that reach millions of people. Commercial missions may also test equipment, create jobs and reduce the cost of future launches without depending entirely on government programmes.

The price remains enormous and the journey carries serious risks. Critics ask whether one passenger’s experience justifies resources that could support health, education or environmental work on Earth. Rocket launches also have environmental effects, while ordinary people are unlikely to afford space tourism for many years. Public excitement can hide these trade-offs.

Spending choices depend on who pays and who benefits. A privately funded flight is different from a government project, yet both use shared scientific knowledge and regulation. Space travel may become more common if safety improves and costs fall, but popularity should not be confused with public value. Clear goals and transparent costs are needed before calling it a good use of money.

context.title: The Killing of Animals: Questions and Trade-offs
body: When wild animal numbers increase near homes, residents may report damaged property, stolen food or dangerous encounters. Governments sometimes use selective killing, or culling, to reduce a population quickly. Supporters argue that this protects people and prevents animals from starving when an area cannot support them.

Animal-welfare groups question whether culling addresses the cause. Feeding by visitors, easy access to rubbish and the loss of natural habitat can draw animals into urban areas. Relocating them may only move the conflict, while birth control is slower and needs long-term monitoring. No single method works equally well for every species or location.

A responsible programme should use reliable population data and consider non-lethal measures first. Secure bins, public education, enforcement against feeding and habitat management can reduce contact. If killing is proposed, authorities must explain why alternatives are insufficient and how suffering will be minimised. The debate requires both concern for human safety and respect for animal welfare.

context.title: Translation Apps: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Translation devices can turn speech or writing into another language within seconds. Travellers may use them at hotels and restaurants, while students can check the general meaning of unfamiliar text or listen to pronunciation. They reduce anxiety when people need basic communication and no human interpreter is available.

A fluent-looking translation can still be wrong. Apps may miss humour, tone, technical meanings or cultural references, and users who do not know the target language may not notice the error. Allowing unrestricted use at school could help understanding, but it could also prevent students from practising vocabulary, grammar and independent expression.

Schools need rules based on the purpose of a task. A device may be useful for research, accessibility or checking a draft, but not when the aim is to assess the student’s own language. Learning languages remains valuable for relationships, cultural understanding and judging whether technology is accurate. The strongest users will treat translation tools as assistance rather than a substitute for thought.

context.title: Selfies: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Selfies make it easy to record an experience and share it immediately. A striking photograph can attract attention online, help friends feel connected and give travellers a personal memory. The search for an unusual background, however, can move attention away from what is happening around the photographer.

Accidents occur when people stand near cliffs, roads, trains, water or wild animals while concentrating on a screen. Social pressure may encourage a person to take greater risks for likes or to copy an image that appears safe online. Problems also include disturbing other visitors, revealing someone’s location and photographing people without permission.

Warnings and barriers are useful at known danger spots, but a complete ban may be difficult to enforce. Platforms, schools and tourist sites can explain how risky images are created and avoid rewarding dangerous behaviour. Before taking a photograph, users should stop, check the surroundings and decide whether the picture is worth the risk to themselves or anyone nearby.

body: Yuenyeung is a Hong Kong drink that combines coffee with milk tea and can be served hot or cold. Its Cantonese name refers to mandarin ducks, a traditional symbol of a pair. Local customers recognise it immediately, but visitors may not know how to pronounce the name or understand what the drink contains.

An English name could make menus and tourism advertising easier to understand. A simple description might explain the ingredients, while a creative name could be more memorable. Yet replacing the local name completely could remove the cultural story that makes the drink distinctive. A poor name might also suggest the wrong flavour or make it sound like an imported product.

Promotion could combine the original name with a clear explanation and consistent spelling. Cafés might offer tasting events, demonstrations or maps of traditional shops, while tourism campaigns could link the drink to Hong Kong’s café culture. The most suitable choice should be accurate, easy to say and strong enough to represent both the drink and its local identity.

context.title: Electronic Lai See: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Electronic payments allow people to send lai see through a phone in seconds, even when relatives cannot meet in person. Digital packets can include greetings, animations and group games, and users do not need to visit a bank for new notes. For busy or overseas families, the convenience is clear.

Many people still value the physical red packet. Choosing an envelope, offering it with both hands and meeting relatives give the gift warmth that a notification may not provide. Older family members may find payment apps difficult, while users of any age may worry about fraud, data collection or sending money to the wrong account.

Traditions often change without disappearing. Families could use electronic lai see when distance makes it helpful and keep physical packets for face-to-face visits. Other Lunar New Year customs may also be affected by online shopping, shorter holidays and virtual greetings. The important question is whether technology supports relationships or merely makes an obligation faster to complete.

context.title: Inequality in Hong Kong: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Hong Kong offers efficient transport, public services and opportunities in an international economy, yet residents do not share these benefits equally. High housing costs, different school resources and gaps between wages can shape where people live, what they can study and how secure they feel about the future.

Some inequality reflects different choices, skills and responsibilities, but very large gaps can reduce social mobility. Families with fewer resources may struggle to afford tutoring, suitable housing or time for training. When people believe that effort cannot improve their position, trust in institutions and other social groups may weaken.

Policies can address barriers without promising that every outcome will be identical. Affordable housing, accessible childcare, well-funded schools, job training and fair wages may widen opportunity. Taxes and benefits also require careful design so that help reaches those who need it without creating unnecessary complexity. A more equal society should be judged by dignity, opportunity and participation as well as income.

context.title: Co-living: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Co-living developments give residents a private sleeping area while kitchens, lounges, workspaces or laundry facilities are shared. Short leases and included furniture can suit students and young workers who move frequently. Sharing expensive facilities may reduce costs and create opportunities to meet people in an unfamiliar city.

The arrangement also brings difficulties. Residents may disagree about noise, guests, cleaning and the use of common areas. Limited private space can be stressful, especially when strangers have different schedules. Advertised rents may not be cheaper once service charges are included, and frequent changes of residents can prevent a stable community from forming.

Clear rules should cover quiet hours, visitors, shared expenses, security and ways to resolve conflict. Residents need honest information about room size, fees and who manages complaints before signing an agreement. Co-living can add another housing option, but it should not be presented as a complete answer to high rents or a reason to accept unsafe and overcrowded accommodation.

context.title: McSleepers: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Some people without secure housing spend the night in twenty-four-hour fast-food restaurants and have become known as “McSleepers”. Bright lighting, air conditioning, toilets and the presence of staff can feel safer than sleeping outdoors. Buying a small item may also allow a person to remain indoors for several hours.

The arrangement is not a real home. Sleep is interrupted, personal belongings are difficult to protect and washing facilities are limited. Other customers may feel uncomfortable, while employees must handle complaints without training as social workers. Removing people may protect the business in the short term but leave vulnerable individuals in a more dangerous place.

Restaurants can set reasonable behaviour rules and connect customers with outreach services, but private companies cannot solve homelessness alone. Government and community groups need emergency shelters, affordable housing, mental-health care and help with employment or documents. The presence of McSleepers should be treated as evidence of a wider housing problem, not simply as poor customer behaviour.

context.title: Age Limit for Political Leaders: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Political leadership requires judgement, communication, integrity and the ability to respond to change. Older leaders may offer long experience, knowledge of institutions and established relationships. Younger leaders may bring different priorities, greater familiarity with new technology and a longer personal stake in decisions about the future.

Age does not guarantee either wisdom or innovation. Health and energy vary greatly between individuals, and a young leader can be inflexible just as an older leader can adapt quickly. A strict upper age limit might remove capable candidates and encourage discrimination, while ignoring age completely may leave legitimate questions about stamina and succession unanswered.

Voters and organisations should examine evidence of competence, health, ethics and recent performance rather than rely on a number alone. Term limits, transparent medical information and leadership teams with different generations may address some concerns more fairly. The goal is not to choose the youngest or oldest person, but to create accountable leadership that understands a changing society.

context.title: A Helper at Home: Promise and Practical Questions
body: A proposed care scheme would give older public-housing tenants who live alone financial help to employ a domestic helper. Supporters say daily assistance could allow more people to remain in familiar neighbourhoods instead of entering residential homes. A helper might prepare meals, keep the flat clean, collect medicine and notice quickly when an elderly person becomes unwell.

The arrangement is not as simple as paying a salary. Some tenants may struggle to interview workers, complete paperwork or communicate across a language barrier. Sharing a very small flat can reduce privacy for both people. Families also want safeguards against neglect, financial abuse and sudden contract disputes, while helpers need reasonable hours, training and somewhere suitable to sleep.

Community nurses, meal deliveries, emergency alarms and regular visits from social workers could support those who do not want a live-in helper. Neighbourhood volunteers may reduce loneliness, but they cannot replace professional care. Before launching the scheme widely, officials should ask elderly residents what they prefer and explain who will monitor each placement when problems arise.

context.title: Can Hong Kong’s Leading Broadcaster Win Viewers Back?
body: For decades, families planned their evenings around the same television dramas, variety shows and news bulletins. TVB stars became household names, and popular series gave people common jokes and stories to discuss at school or work. That shared audience made the station an important part of local entertainment and helped advertisers reach almost every age group.

Viewing habits have changed sharply. Young people can stream Korean, mainland Chinese, Western and independent local programmes whenever they choose. Some former fans complain that familiar plots, repeated locations and a small circle of actors make new dramas feel predictable. Online platforms also release complete seasons at once, while traditional schedules require viewers to wait for the next episode.

The broadcaster still owns a valuable archive and understands Cantonese audiences. A recovery might depend on investing in new writers, giving unfamiliar performers a chance and producing stories that reflect present-day Hong Kong. Short online editions, reliable subtitles and legal international streaming could reach viewers beyond free-to-air television. Success will require more than nostalgia; audiences must feel that the programmes deserve their time again.

source_note: Past-paper practice based on the verified 2018 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.3 task. context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2018 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.3; this is not HKEAA text:
context.title: When School Messages Follow Teachers Home
body: Class messaging groups make it easy to announce a timetable change, share a missing worksheet or check whether a student arrived safely. Parents appreciate receiving information quickly, and shy students sometimes find it easier to type a short question than approach a teacher in a crowded corridor. During an emergency, instant contact can prevent confusion.

Problems begin when every message is treated as urgent. A teacher may receive homework questions late at night, repeated reminders from parents and complaints that have already been answered. Group chats can expose phone numbers, spread rumours or embarrass a student in front of the whole class. Fast replies may also create an expectation that staff are permanently on duty.

One school is considering a single official platform with weekday contact hours. Teachers would answer routine questions on the next working day, while genuine safety matters would go through an emergency channel. Sensitive concerns would move to a private meeting rather than remain in a chat. Clear rules for students, parents and staff could preserve the convenience of messaging without allowing it to replace respectful face-to-face communication.

Shared bicycles could reduce car journeys, provide inexpensive exercise and help residents who have no room to store a bike. Yet early trials have produced familiar complaints: damaged bicycles, blocked pavements, careless parking and riders entering busy roads without helmets. Users may also worry about deposits, personal data and whether a broken bicycle will be repaired promptly.

District councils could mark parking bays, expand safe cycling routes and fine operators that fail to remove abandoned bikes. The app should report faults and prevent new rentals from unsafe locations. If the model works, other neighbourhood schemes might lend umbrellas, tools, sports equipment or small vehicles. Organisers hope newcomers will recognise friendly faces on their first morning and feel more confident asking for help.

A camp can build belonging, but compulsory cheering, late-night games or public performances may frighten quieter students. Fees could exclude some families, and children with disabilities, food allergies or religious needs may require adjustments. Anyone unable to attend should not begin the year feeling that every friendship group has already formed without them.

Suggested activities include a photo-free campus trail, a cooperative puzzle, a club fair and a relaxed picnic with form teachers. Students could choose between energetic and quiet sessions instead of being forced onto a stage. The school would need consent forms, trained leaders, first-aid cover, transport arrangements and a bad-weather plan. A follow-up lunch in the first week could welcome absentees and help staff check whether the camp achieved its purpose.

Some students may use it carefully, while others could spend it on entertainment or expensive gadgets. Limiting the first round to a few districts is easy to administer, yet candidates with similar financial difficulties elsewhere may see the arrangement as unfair.

The pilot could include a short, optional money-management workshop and confidential advice for students facing debt at home. After the examination, anonymous surveys could show which expenses mattered most without policing every purchase. If the programme expands, the foundation must choose between a universal grant and support based on household need. context.title: Why an Empty Hour May Not Be Wasted
body: Many teenagers move directly from lessons to tutorials, music practice, sport and homework. Parents often arrange these activities with good intentions, believing that every hour should develop a useful skill. A school counsellor, however, has suggested that students also need unplanned time in which nobody sets a target or measures their performance.

Quiet periods can allow the mind to wander, recover from stress and connect ideas in unexpected ways. A bored student may begin drawing, reading, repairing something or simply thinking through a difficult day. Doing nothing is not automatically healthy: endless scrolling, avoiding responsibilities or staying isolated for long periods can leave a young person more tired than before.

The school could trial one homework-light evening and ask families to observe the effect on sleep, mood and creativity. Students would be free to rest or choose their own activity, preferably away from constant notifications. Explaining the experiment to parents with evidence and student reflections may be more convincing than telling them to abandon structure. The aim is balance, not laziness.

Physical strength matters, but recruits also need calm judgement, clear communication and the discipline to follow instructions when conditions change suddenly.

The career offers stable training, strong teamwork and the satisfaction of protecting strangers. No two shifts are identical, and experienced officers can move into rescue, prevention or public education. The disadvantages are serious: firefighters work nights and holidays, carry heavy equipment, witness distressing events and sometimes place their own safety at risk.

A school careers programme could arrange a station visit, a first-aid workshop and a timed fitness activity using safe training equipment. Students should also hear from a female firefighter, a control-room officer and someone responsible for fire prevention, rather than seeing only dramatic rescues. Honest discussion of academic requirements, probation, emotional resilience and family life would help students decide whether public service suits them.

Similar comments accuse teenagers of avoiding hard work, depending on parents and caring more about phones than real skills. Older listeners recognise the frustration, especially when they remember long apprenticeships and fewer shortcuts to publicity.

The criticism misses part of the picture. Young people face intense examinations, high housing costs and a job market in which technology can remove familiar careers. Many learn new software, run small online businesses or volunteer while studying. Their effort may look different from the routines of an earlier generation, and not every family can provide the same support.

The greatest challenge may be uncertainty: students are told to plan carefully even though industries and qualifications change quickly. Adults can help by offering practical mentoring, paid entry-level opportunities and honest accounts of failure. Teenagers, in return, should accept that talent still needs practice and reliability. A useful conversation begins when both generations replace stereotypes with specific examples.

Relocation also brought sacrifices. Salaries are lower, professional contacts are far away and some services operate differently. The children miss close friends and need time to adjust to new classroom routines. Grandparents in Hong Kong can join video calls, but screens do not replace weekend meals or help when someone becomes ill.

Anyone considering the same move should compare employment, housing, schooling, healthcare and residency rules rather than relying on holiday impressions. Language confidence and family support can matter as much as the cost of living. A temporary rental or extended trial may reveal whether the quieter lifestyle remains attractive after the excitement fades. body: A university department will no longer fail students automatically for missing a fixed percentage of lectures. Course materials and recorded explanations will be available online, while marks will depend on assignments, tests and demonstrated understanding. Supporters believe adults should decide how they learn and that lecturers must make classroom time genuinely valuable.

Greater freedom may help students balancing part-time work, illness or family duties. It can also encourage teachers to use lessons for discussion and feedback instead of repeating information from a slide. Critics warn that weak students may disappear quietly, group projects may suffer and practical subjects cannot be mastered by watching a screen alone.

The policy’s success should be judged through results, participation and student well-being, not simply the number of empty seats. Advisers could contact learners who miss several sessions, and laboratories or assessed workshops could still require attendance. Secondary students generally need more structure, yet older pupils might benefit from limited flexibility for selected lessons. Any school version would require parental communication, reliable online access and clear consequences for unfinished work.

Connecting the visit with a charity fitness challenge might make the event worthwhile for both Rex and the school.

Boxing can improve stamina, coordination, confidence and respect for rules, but head injuries and poorly supervised sparring are real concerns. A school programme should be optional, led by qualified coaches and focused first on footwork, pads and fitness. Protective equipment, medical guidance and clear behaviour standards are essential. Millions watched her performance, while viewers argued about whether a child should face such public attention. The excitement of discovery, dramatic judging and audience voting helps explain why these shows remain powerful entertainment.

Competitions can build confidence, provide professional feedback and open doors that ordinary lessons cannot. Children may learn to practise consistently and recover from disappointment. The same experience can bring long hours, harsh comments, pressure to please adults and contracts that a young performer does not understand. Schoolwork and friendships may suffer when every weekend becomes another audition.

Parents should listen carefully to the child rather than treating fame as a family project. Age limits, counselling, protected study time and independent advice about money could reduce exploitation. Schools can offer lower-pressure concerts or talent days where improvement matters more than elimination. Television producers also have a duty to control filming hours and prevent humiliating criticism from being marketed as entertainment.

New restaurants should not block views or turn every quiet corner into commercial property.

A simple route map could show accessible entrances, transport connections and free activities. Schools might adopt garden sections or hold harbour-history walks, and artists could lead trial events before permanent facilities are built. Promotion should target local neighbourhoods as well as tourists. Measuring repeat visits, heat, litter and public feedback would reveal whether improvements create a genuinely welcoming shared space.

Drones can photograph difficult locations, inspect roofs, map construction sites and help rescuers search dangerous ground. Film-makers value smooth aerial views, while scientists can monitor coastlines without sending people into risky places. The same aircraft may crash into crowds, disturb residents, invade privacy or interfere with emergency and passenger flights.

Clear no-fly maps should appear inside control apps and at popular launch sites. Registration, height limits, basic training and insurance could apply according to a drone’s weight and purpose. Police and rescue teams may use aerial cameras during searches or major traffic incidents, but official use still needs rules on data retention and surveillance. Responsible technology depends on both enforceable boundaries and informed operators.

context.title: A False Post Travels Faster Than the Correction
body: A message claiming that all schools would close appeared in several neighbourhood groups before sunrise. It used an old government logo and a dramatic headline, so thousands of users forwarded it without checking the date or source. By the time officials denied the claim, screenshots had already spread to other platforms.

False stories succeed because surprise and fear encourage quick sharing. Advertising rewards popular pages, and recommendation systems often show users more of what keeps them watching. Some people therefore support removing misleading material or punishing accounts that repeatedly manufacture harmful claims. Others fear that broad censorship would let authorities silence criticism or define every mistake as deliberate deception.

A safer response could combine independent fact-checking, visible correction notices and media-literacy lessons. Platforms should reveal who paid for political advertising and make reporting tools easier to use. Readers can pause, inspect the address, compare reliable outlets and search for the original statement. Regulation may be necessary for fraud or direct danger, but transparent appeals are essential whenever content is removed.

context.title: Should Schools Ban Teenage Dating?
body: Several schools have introduced strict rules intended to keep students from forming romantic relationships. Supporters believe dating distracts teenagers from examinations and can create jealousy, pressure or conflict on campus. A simple ban also appears easier for staff to explain than deciding which behaviour has crossed a line.

Blanket rules are difficult to enforce fairly. Students may hide ordinary friendships, rumours can become evidence, and teachers may intrude into private lives without solving genuine problems. Punishment can also discourage a young person from seeking help about controlling behaviour, unwanted contact or the sharing of personal images.

Schools could focus on conduct instead of trying to police feelings. Guidance should cover consent, respectful communication, online safety, study balance and where to find confidential counselling. Harassment and public disruption require clear consequences regardless of whether two students are dating. Parents should receive practical information, but teenagers also need trusted adults who will listen without immediate judgement. Education is more likely than prohibition to prepare students for responsible relationships.

Some people describe slower breathing and a dreamlike calm; others find the vibration uncomfortable or leave with a headache. Personal reactions are strong, while scientific evidence for specific health claims remains limited.

A school wellness room could test a short session after lessons, provided participation is voluntary and the volume is controlled. Students with hearing sensitivities, migraines or anxiety should have another option. A trained facilitator must explain that the activity supports relaxation rather than replacing medical care.

Other uses of music may suit a wider range of students: guided drumming, quiet playlist sessions, songwriting groups or breathing exercises matched to a steady rhythm. Promotion could begin with a small taster week, teacher referrals and honest descriptions of what each activity involves. Anonymous feedback on stress, comfort and attendance would help the school decide what to continue.

The trial aims to reduce piles of short-lived handouts while making materials searchable and easier to update.

Less printing could save storage space, paper and ink. Students who are absent may collect work immediately instead of waiting for a classmate. However, not every family owns a reliable device or fast connection. Long screen sessions can strain eyes, batteries fail, websites go offline and notifications tempt students away from the lesson. Art, mathematics and close reading may still work better on paper at times.

A successful plan needs loan devices, charging points, teacher training and downloadable copies for weak connections. Essential documents should have an emergency print option, and students with accessibility needs require suitable formats. The school will compare costs, paper use, completion rates and feedback after one term. “Paperless” should mean thoughtful reduction, not a ban that ignores how people actually learn.

Before any shift began, the “employer” demanded a training fee, a copy of the student’s identity card and access to a bank account. The contact disappeared after receiving the money. Similar traps can involve illegal deliveries, unsafe machinery or contracts with hidden deductions.

Genuine summer work can still be valuable. Students earn spending money, practise punctuality and discover what dealing with customers or colleagues is really like. Short placements in shops, libraries, tutoring centres, sports programmes or community organisations can build confidence when duties and hours suit the worker’s age.

A school awareness event could invite a labour officer, show suspicious advertisements and let students practise checking a contract. A one-page checklist should cover company records, pay, insurance, personal data and emergency contacts. Families need to know where to report fraud without blaming the victim. Schools may share verified opportunities, but students should remain free to choose and must understand that unusually easy money usually carries a hidden risk.

Bringing animals into school also creates obligations. Some students have allergies or strong fears, and even a friendly pet may scratch when stressed. Cages, food, veterinary care, cleaning and holiday arrangements cost money. The animal needs rest and an appropriate environment; it must not become a toy passed around whenever a class wants entertainment.

A visiting programme may be safer than keeping a permanent pet. Qualified handlers could select animals with suitable temperaments, supervise contact and provide hand-washing rules. Students should be able to opt out without embarrassment. If the school keeps any animal, a written care rota, named adult, veterinary plan and quiet retreat are essential. Benefits to people cannot justify poor welfare.

context.title: When a Phone Replaces the Wallet
body: At a busy lunch stall, customers now scan a code and collect their food within seconds. The owner handles less change, keeps an automatic sales record and worries less about cash being stolen overnight. Shoppers appreciate speed and can see each purchase in an app rather than searching through paper receipts.

A completely cash-free system would exclude some people. Older residents may not own smartphones, children may lack bank accounts and tourists may use unfamiliar services. A flat battery, network failure or frozen account can leave someone unable to buy essentials. Digital payments also create records of personal habits, encourage unnoticed spending and expose users to scams or unexpected fees.

Hong Kong could expand mobile payment without removing notes and coins in the near future. Shops should display prices and fees clearly, keep at least one accessible payment alternative and train staff to help customers without taking control of their devices. Strong fraud refunds, spending alerts and offline options would build trust. Technological progress is most useful when convenience does not become compulsion.

Interest may fade after the first visit. Farming involves heat, mud, insects and repeated jobs that do not produce instant results. Some students have allergies or weekend commitments, and the plot still needs attention during examinations and holidays. Transport, seeds, damaged tools and failed crops must fit a modest budget.

The class could begin with one term rather than a full-year contract. Small teams would rotate watering, weeding, measurements and photo records, with an adult checking safety. Hardy seasonal plants would reduce waste, and no chemical should be used without guidance. A shared calendar must cover school breaks. At the end, students can decide whether the learning, food and teamwork justify renewing the plot.

context.title: Giving money to parents: Discussion Context
body: In some Hong Kong families, adult children regularly give part of their income to their parents. The payment may help with household bills, medical expenses or retirement, but it can also be a symbolic way of expressing gratitude. Parents who supported their children for many years may value the gesture even when they do not depend on the money.

The custom can become difficult when young adults are paying rent, saving for a home or caring for children of their own. A fixed amount that seems reasonable in one household may create pressure in another. Problems are more likely when expectations are never discussed or when brothers and sisters contribute very different amounts.

Families could treat financial support as one possible form of care rather than a compulsory test of respect. Time, practical help, regular contact and support at medical appointments may be equally meaningful. An honest conversation about needs and affordability can help parents and children find an arrangement that protects both family relationships and financial security.

context.title: Cantonese: Discussion Context
body: People who settle in Hong Kong without speaking Cantonese can often manage at international workplaces, yet everyday situations may still be difficult. Talking to taxi drivers, understanding notices in small shops and joining conversations with neighbours can require local language skills. These barriers may leave newcomers dependent on friends or separated from parts of community life.

Learning Cantonese can make practical tasks easier and help people understand humour, television, food culture and local concerns. It may also widen employment choices and make friendships with Cantonese-speaking residents more natural. Progress can be slow because pronunciation and tones are unfamiliar, while many courses do not fit adults’ working hours.

Language classes are only one solution. Schools, employers and community groups could organise conversation partners, subtitled activities and neighbourhood visits where learners use simple Cantonese without embarrassment. Local speakers can help by being patient and avoiding switching languages immediately. Connection should be a shared effort rather than a test newcomers must pass alone.

Online campaigns can disappear quickly once a new trend arrives. A strong fundraiser therefore needs reliable information, transparent donation arrangements and a way to keep supporters involved after the videos stop circulating.

Students could design other digital activities such as a sponsored skills challenge, an online performance or a team quiz. The activity should be safe, easy to explain and suitable for people with different abilities. Popularity matters, but the group should also judge whether the idea raises useful awareness, protects participants and directs support to a trustworthy organisation.

body: Hong Kong uses a range of signals to warn the public about typhoons, heavy rain, thunderstorms and other dangerous conditions. The system gives schools, families and businesses a shared reference point for making safety decisions. Clear warnings can reduce travel during severe weather and allow emergency services to prepare before conditions become worse.

However, the same signal may affect districts differently. A warning can close schools even when the weather near some campuses appears calm, while transport disruption and childcare problems create difficulties for working families. Businesses also need to decide when staff should leave, and members of the public may misunderstand what each signal actually requires them to do.

Improvements could include more district-specific information, clearer mobile alerts and practical advice linked to each warning. Any change must remain simple enough to understand quickly and must not encourage people to ignore territory-wide risks. The Observatory, schools, employers and transport operators should communicate consistently so that safety messages do not compete with one another.
