body: Emotional intelligence, often called EQ, involves recognising feelings, managing reactions and responding appropriately to other people. Students may experience anxiety about examinations, disagreements with friends, family expectations or uncertainty about the future. If they cannot discuss these emotions or recover from setbacks, concentration and relationships may suffer even when their academic ability is strong.

A high EQ does not replace knowledge or reasoning, but it can help people cooperate, make decisions under pressure and ask for support. These skills develop through experience rather than a single lesson. Group work, sport, creative activities and family conversations can all give young people opportunities to listen, negotiate and understand different points of view.

Schools could teach students how to name emotions, handle conflict and recognise when professional help is needed. Peer-support programmes and trained counsellors may make help easier to seek. Activities should not force students to reveal private experiences in public. The aim is to build a respectful environment in which emotional skills are practised alongside academic learning.

context.title: Libraries: Discussion Context
body: Public libraries compete with smartphones, streaming services and the large amount of free information available online. Teenagers may still value quiet study space, reliable internet access and books they cannot afford to buy. Yet some see libraries as places with strict rules, outdated collections and few reasons to visit once schoolwork is finished.

Modern libraries can offer more than shelves of printed books. Digital lending, media-making equipment, reading clubs and talks with writers can connect traditional services with young people’s interests. Flexible seating and group areas may also help students who have little study space at home. These changes require funding, staff training and careful management of noise.

New activities should support the library’s educational purpose rather than turn it into another shopping centre. Teenagers could help choose events and recommend materials, while librarians could teach how to judge whether online information is trustworthy. A successful library would provide both quiet and collaborative zones and remain accessible to people who do not own expensive devices.

context.title: Road Safety: Discussion Context
body: Road accidents in Hong Kong have fallen over time as vehicles, roads and public education have improved. Seat belts, airbags, better lighting and safer junctions reduce some risks, while enforcement discourages dangerous driving. Technology can also warn drivers when they leave a lane or approach an obstacle.

Safety equipment cannot prevent every collision. Speeding, drink-driving, mobile-phone use and tiredness still depend on human choices. Pedestrians may cross between vehicles or look at screens instead of traffic, and cyclists can be vulnerable when roads do not provide enough space. Older people and children may need more time and clearer signals when crossing.

Reducing accidents requires drivers, passengers and pedestrians to share responsibility. Schools can teach practical road behaviour, the government can improve crossings and cycle routes, and police can target the most dangerous offences. Campaigns are most useful when they explain the consequences of risky behaviour and are supported by road design that makes the safer choice easier.

context.title: Keeping the Elderly Active: Discussion Context
body: Groups of older residents often gather in parks to sing, dance and play music. The activity is inexpensive, social and easy to join, so it can reduce loneliness and help participants remain physically and mentally active. Performers may also enjoy sharing songs that carry memories from earlier stages of their lives.

Outdoor performances can disturb nearby residents and other park users, especially when amplifiers are loud or several groups compete for space. Strict bans may reduce complaints, but they can also create conflict and remove an activity that many elderly people value. Building a costly performance venue will not help if it is inconvenient or difficult to book.

A balanced plan could set reasonable hours and sound limits, designate several performance areas and provide indoor alternatives during bad weather. Performers should help monitor noise, while officials should explain rules consistently. Community centres, underused sports facilities and sheltered public spaces could offer additional venues without excluding other users.

context.title: Legal age: Discussion Context
body: Hong Kong law sets different minimum ages for activities such as employment, driving, marriage and getting a tattoo. These limits are intended to protect young people and the public when a decision carries lasting consequences or requires mature judgement. Tattoo rules are especially strict because an unsafe procedure can cause infection and the result may be difficult to remove.

A single legal age cannot measure the maturity of every teenager. Some young people can manage responsibility earlier than others, while parental permission does not always remove health or safety risks. Different activities also involve different levels of danger, so it is reasonable for the limits not to be identical.

When reviewing an age limit, the government should consider evidence about harm, young people’s rights and whether the rule can be enforced. Education and access to trustworthy advice may work better than punishment alone. Any proposed change should explain why that age is suitable and what additional safeguards, supervision or consent would still be required.

context.title: Social Problems: Discussion Context
body: Some young people withdraw from face-to-face contact for long periods and spend most of their time alone at home. The causes can include anxiety, bullying, academic pressure, family conflict or fear of failure. Technology may make isolation easier to maintain, but using the internet is not itself proof that a person has a serious social problem.

Extended withdrawal can interrupt education, employment, sleep and physical health. Families may feel helpless if direct pressure leads to arguments or deeper avoidance. The young person may also lose confidence in ordinary activities, making it harder to return to school or reconnect with friends.

Support should begin with patient, non-judgemental contact and an effort to understand the individual’s circumstances. Families can seek advice from counsellors or health professionals, while schools can offer flexible return plans and a trusted adult to speak with. Small steps, such as regular routines and low-pressure activities, may be more effective than demanding an immediate return to normal life.

context.title: Boot camps: Discussion Context
body: Some parents send children to military-style boot camps because they believe modern family life has made young people dependent and unwilling to face difficulty. Campers may have to wake early, complete physical tasks, clean shared facilities and manage without domestic help. Supporters say the experience can teach discipline, teamwork and basic self-care.

A harsh programme may also humiliate children, create safety risks or confuse obedience with independence. Young people have different physical and emotional needs, and a short period of discomfort does not automatically change habits at home. Parents who solve every problem for their children may need to change their own behaviour as well.

Independence can be developed through ordinary responsibilities such as budgeting, cooking, planning travel, volunteering or joining a supervised outdoor programme. If a boot camp is considered, its staff, safety standards and methods should be checked carefully. The goal should be confidence and responsibility, not punishment or fear.

context.title: Food: Discussion Context
body: Food can influence energy, concentration and mood, although no single item guarantees that a person will feel happy. Meals containing protein, fruit, vegetables and whole grains may provide steadier energy than snacks high in sugar. Schools therefore have a reason to consider both nutrition and how appealing their menus are to students.

A menu offering only foods labelled healthy may be unpopular if choices are expensive, unfamiliar or badly prepared. Claims about mood-enhancing foods can also be exaggerated. Stress, sleep, exercise and relationships may affect emotions more strongly than one meal, and students with allergies or medical needs require suitable alternatives.

Schools could provide clear information, affordable balanced meals and smaller portions of less nutritious treats instead of imposing a complete ban. Students could taste-test new dishes and help improve presentation. The aim should be to make a healthy choice convenient and enjoyable while teaching students to evaluate health claims rather than follow fashionable advice.

context.title: Good teachers are the most important factor in educational success: Discussion Context
body: Good teachers can explain difficult ideas, notice when learners are confused and create a classroom where students are willing to participate. Their expectations and feedback may strongly influence confidence and progress. For students with limited support outside school, a skilled teacher can be especially important.

Educational success nevertheless depends on more than teaching. Students must practise, persist and take responsibility for their work. Family support, school resources, class size, health and prior knowledge also shape results. Even an excellent teacher cannot control every factor, while motivated learners sometimes succeed despite weak instruction.

A debate on this motion should first define both “good teachers” and “educational success”. One side may argue that teachers connect all other resources to the learner; the other may stress effort and circumstances beyond the classroom. The strongest conclusion will compare the relative influence of each factor rather than claiming that teachers either determine everything or make no difference.

context.title: The importance of smartphones in China: Discussion Context
body: Smartphones have changed how people in China communicate, pay for services, travel and obtain information. For many users, one device can replace a camera, wallet, map and computer. This convenience has helped mobile services grow quickly, but it also means that cost, data access and digital skills affect who receives the benefits.

A premium international brand may struggle when the economy slows and strong local competitors offer capable phones at lower prices. Fashion also changes: a device once treated as a status symbol may become less distinctive. Brand reputation, software, after-sales service and links with other products can still persuade some customers to pay more.

Future success will depend on whether new features solve real problems and whether prices match consumers’ expectations. The group should distinguish the importance of smartphones in general from the prospects of one company. It should also consider privacy, distraction, electronic waste and unequal access when judging whether wider smartphone use is entirely positive.

context.title: Online Games Day at school: Discussion Context
body: A study reported that teenagers who regularly played online games achieved slightly higher results in some school subjects. Many games require players to read instructions, solve puzzles, manage resources and cooperate with teammates. These skills could support learning, although the finding does not prove that gaming itself caused the better scores.

A school Online Games Day might include strategy tournaments, collaborative puzzles and student-designed educational games. Activities could interest students who do not usually join sports events and provide opportunities to discuss teamwork and digital citizenship. Organisers would still need suitable devices, a stable network and games that are appropriate for different ages.

Possible problems include excessive screen time, unfair access to equipment, online behaviour and competition becoming too intense. The school should set sensible time limits, provide non-digital breaks and avoid games that reward spending money. Success should be judged by participation and learning, not only by who wins.

context.title: Working Holidays: Discussion Context
body: A working holiday allows young adults to fund part of their travel by taking temporary jobs overseas. Advertisements may offer farm work, fruit picking or jobs on tourist boats. Participants can meet local people, improve language skills and learn to manage money and daily life away from home.

The experience can also involve long hours, basic accommodation, remote locations and work that is more physically demanding than expected. An attractive advertisement may not explain wages, insurance, transport or visa conditions clearly. Some students may be prepared for customer service work but not for operating equipment or living far from medical help.

Applicants should check employers, contracts and legal requirements before travelling. They also need emergency savings, health cover and a realistic plan for communication with family. Other suitable jobs might include hospitality, childcare or event support, depending on skills and local rules. A successful working holiday combines travel with safe, lawful employment rather than treating any overseas job as an adventure.

context.title: Giving blood: Discussion Context
body: Hong Kong hospitals need a reliable supply of donated blood for surgery, emergencies and the treatment of serious illness. Young first-time donors can help meet present needs and may continue donating as adults. A school collection can also show students how one voluntary action supports people they may never meet.

Some students are unable to donate because of age, health or eligibility rules, while others are anxious about needles, pain or feeling unwell. Pressure from classmates could make a voluntary event uncomfortable. Organisers therefore need accurate screening information, trained medical staff, privacy and a clear message that declining is acceptable.

The school could hold the event in a quiet, accessible hall at a time that does not conflict with examinations or strenuous activities. Talks from medical staff, donor stories and opportunities to ask questions may reduce fear. Students who cannot give blood could help with publicity or logistics, allowing the campaign to encourage participation without treating donation as compulsory.

body: A travel-book cover has to attract attention while giving readers an honest idea of Hong Kong. Harbour views and dense city streets show energy and an international skyline, while temples, country parks and geological landscapes reveal heritage and natural space that some visitors may not expect.

A familiar skyline is easy to recognise, but it can repeat an image already used by many travel guides. A less familiar photograph may create curiosity yet fail to communicate the city immediately. The choice also depends on the intended readers and whether the book focuses on culture, outdoor travel, architecture or a general introduction.

The group should compare what each image includes and what it leaves out. A strong cover needs visual impact, a clear connection with the book and enough originality to stand out. If one photograph cannot represent the city’s contrasts, the designer might use a carefully balanced composition, provided it remains simple and does not mislead visitors.

context.title: More bus lanes are needed in Hong Kong: Discussion Context
body: Buses carry a large share of Hong Kong passengers, but their journeys can become slow and unreliable in heavy traffic. Supporters of more bus lanes argue that giving priority to vehicles carrying many people would shorten travel times, make timetables more dependable and encourage drivers to leave private cars at home.

Opponents point out that road space is limited. Removing a general traffic lane could worsen congestion for taxis, delivery vehicles and people who must drive for work. A bus lane that is poorly located or active all day may remain underused at quieter times and move pollution rather than reduce it.

Possible compromises include peak-hour lanes, better enforcement, traffic-signal priority and regular reviews of passenger numbers. Other solutions could involve congestion charges, improved interchange between buses and rail, and better information for passengers. The group should judge proposals by how many people benefit, their effect on journey times and whether they reduce total traffic.

title: Discrimination against older people

context.title: Discrimination against older people: Discussion Context
body: Some capable employees are required to leave work at a fixed retirement age even when they wish to continue. Older workers may offer experience, reliability and knowledge that can be passed to younger colleagues. Continuing employment can also provide income, routine and social contact as people live longer.

Employers may worry about health, training costs or whether promotion opportunities for younger staff will be reduced. Yet decisions based only on age can ignore large differences between individuals. Keeping everyone in the same role indefinitely may not be suitable, but automatically excluding applicants over a certain age is also unfair.

Reducing discrimination could involve flexible hours, retraining, phased retirement and recruitment based on ability rather than stereotypes. Government guidance and legal protection may help, but workplaces also need practical ways to review performance and adapt duties. The aim should be genuine choice: older people should neither be forced out of suitable work nor pressured to continue when they prefer to retire.

discussion_points.text: Advantages of allowing older people to work
Advantages of not allowing older people to work
What can be done to reduce discrimination against older people
anything else you think is important

title: Keeping Hong Kong's Streets Clean

context.title: Keeping Hong Kong's Streets Clean: Discussion Context
body: An elderly cleaner on a modest wage was fined after pouring waste water onto a street. Her employer later offered to pay the penalty. The case led to debate about whether a standard fine treats everyone equally when the same amount creates very different hardship for people with different incomes.

Fines can communicate that littering and pollution are unacceptable, and simple fixed penalties are easy to understand. However, punishment may appear unfair when rules are unclear, enforcement is inconsistent or an offence happens during work. Very high penalties can create financial distress without changing the behaviour that caused the problem.

Clean streets also depend on convenient bins, public education, responsible employers and consistent enforcement. Alternatives such as warnings, community service or income-related penalties could be considered, but each may be harder to administer. A fair system should distinguish deliberate dumping from minor mistakes while still requiring individuals and companies to prevent waste from entering public spaces.

part_a.instruction: Discuss whether fines and penalties are an effective way to keep Hong Kong streets clean.

discussion_points.text: Whether the elderly cleaner should have been fined
Whether fines and penalties stop people littering

anything else you think is important

context.title: Planning a Safe Night Hike and Camp
body: A group of students is considering a night hike and overnight camp on a Hong Kong mountain to mark graduation. Walking after dark can feel adventurous, offer cooler temperatures and give hikers a chance to see the city lights or sunrise. Sharing the challenge may also strengthen friendships at the end of school.

Night travel makes familiar risks harder to manage. Paths can be difficult to follow, weather can change, and tired hikers may fall or become separated. Each participant needs suitable shoes, water, warm and waterproof clothing, a charged torch and emergency contact arrangements. Heavy bags and unnecessary equipment can make the route more difficult.

The group should choose a route that matches everyone’s experience, check official weather and trail information, and tell a responsible person about the plan. Camping must be allowed at the chosen site, and students should carry out all rubbish. A clear meeting system and a willingness to cancel in unsafe conditions are more important than reaching the summit on schedule.

discussion_points.text: Why night hiking has become popular with students

context.title: Practice context: Charity Work Outside Hong Kong
body: A Hong Kong secondary school is considering an overseas service trip in which students would help a community organisation with teaching, repairs and daily activities. The trip would expose students to living conditions different from their own, but each participant would have to pay for travel and accommodation.

Supporters believe direct service can build empathy, teamwork and a stronger understanding of global inequality. Critics question whether a short visit creates lasting benefit, whether students are properly trained and whether the money might be better spent supporting local charities.

The proposed seven-day visit would combine classroom support with practical jobs such as painting community facilities. A partner charity would supervise the work, arrange child-protection training and explain which projects local residents have requested.

The school must decide whether overseas service should become a graduation requirement. Subsidies could widen access, while a local alternative might help students who cannot travel and ensure that volunteering is motivated by service rather than a certificate.

context.title: Practice context: Starting Your Own Business
body: Many Hong Kong homes have limited storage space. A new business proposes delivering secure boxes to customers, collecting them after packing, keeping an online inventory and returning individual items on request. Customers would pay a monthly fee rather than rent a larger flat.

The service may be convenient for seasonal clothes, books and keepsakes, yet customers may worry about price, privacy, damage and the time needed to retrieve an item. A successful company would also need reliable collection, transparent insurance and advertising that explains why it is better than self-storage.

Spacebox would photograph and label every container before moving it to a warehouse. Users could request next-day delivery through an app, although urgent access and oversized objects would cost extra under the proposed price plan.

The founders are considering student discounts, shared family accounts and reusable packing materials. Before launching, they need to prove that the warehouse is secure and that customers can understand insurance limits, collection times and cancellation charges.

context.title: Practice context: Learning Through Play
body: Some educators argue that play is not a break from learning but one of the ways children learn. Building games can develop planning, outdoor exploration can encourage curiosity, and role-play can improve communication. However, Hong Kong schools often have tight timetables and strong pressure to show measurable academic progress.

Teachers must decide how much freedom children should have, what kinds of games are suitable and how learning can be observed without turning every activity into a test. Parents may welcome creative lessons but still worry about safety, discipline and whether play reduces time for reading, writing and mathematics.

One primary school has tested a weekly ninety-minute play session. Pupils choose from construction challenges, drama corners and supervised garden activities, then record what they discovered in a short learning journal.

The pilot has produced lively lessons, but teachers report that large classes make observation difficult. The school is deciding whether to expand the programme, reduce homework on play days and invite parents to see how apparently simple games develop useful skills.

context.title: Practice context: Phone Scams
body: Phone and online scams often create a false sense of urgency. A caller may pretend to represent a bank, a message may promise a prize, or an email may appear to come from a friend who needs money. Criminals rely on fear, trust and personal information to make victims act before checking.

Young people are not automatically safe simply because they use technology confidently. Useful precautions include refusing to share passwords, contacting an organisation through an official number and asking a trusted adult for advice. Public education must reach both frequent internet users and people who may be unfamiliar with changing scam methods.

A recent school survey found that suspicious calls were often ignored, but convincing messages from hacked accounts caused more confusion. Several students said they would transfer a small sum if the request appeared to come from a close friend.

The school plans a public-awareness presentation using recorded examples, a verification checklist and a demonstration of caller-ID manipulation. Organisers want advice that protects victims without making people afraid of every unfamiliar message or genuine request for help.

body: A school celebrating its anniversary has invited a Hong Kong street artist to paint a mural. Her work uses bold lines, local images and large public walls, so the mural could become a memorable feature of the campus and a focus for the Open Day.

The school must choose a visible but suitable location and decide which images represent its history, values and students. The artist might also give a demonstration or involve students in planning. At the same time, organisers need to consider cost, safety, maintenance and whether the design will remain meaningful after the celebration.

The artist has suggested a wall beside the main entrance, where the work would be visible to visitors but exposed to strong sun and rain. Her first sketch combines the old school building, neighbourhood shops and portraits designed from student photographs.

During Open Day, she could lead a stencil workshop and explain how a mural moves from research to final painting. The anniversary committee must decide how much creative control students should have and who will repair or replace the work in future.

context.title: Practice context: Living with Parents in Your Twenties
body: High housing costs mean many young adults in Hong Kong continue living with their parents after starting work. Staying at home can reduce expenses, allow family members to support one another and make daily life more convenient. It can also reflect a family tradition rather than a failure to become independent.

Sharing a home may nevertheless limit privacy and create disagreements about money, chores, visitors and personal schedules. Independence can still be developed through paying part of the household costs, making decisions responsibly and planning for the future. Families need expectations that respect both the young adult and the parents.

In one household, a working daughter pays rent, cooks twice a week and manages her own savings while sharing a flat with her parents. She values family company but finds it difficult when relatives expect to know all her plans.

Housing advisers say moving out is not the only sign of adulthood. Clear household agreements, private space and long-term financial goals can reduce tension, although both generations must be willing to treat the arrangement as a partnership between adults.

context.title: Practice context: Educational Apps for Students
body: A school Computer Club has been asked to recommend educational apps for new tablets. Possible choices include tools for practising languages, organising revision, exploring scientific models and checking understanding through quizzes. The most attractive app is not necessarily the one that produces the best learning.

Students should consider price, accessibility, privacy, accuracy and whether an app works without a fast internet connection. Too much screen time may distract learners, while a well-designed app can give immediate feedback and allow practice at an appropriate level. Teachers also need training and a clear purpose for using each tool.

The club has a fixed budget and can purchase only two subscriptions this year. Trial users liked the science model but found it demanding on older tablets; the language app was easier to use, although some feedback was inaccurate.

Members will test each option with students from different forms and collect teachers’ comments before recommending a purchase. They also want an offline mode and a policy that prevents advertising or unnecessary collection of pupils’ personal data.

context.title: Practice context: Complaints against Hong Kong Taxi Drivers
body: Complaints about Hong Kong taxis have increased, with passengers reporting overcharging, refusal of hire and poor behaviour. Because taxis are often used by visitors, one bad journey can damage the city’s reputation as well as trust in the industry. Drivers, however, also face congestion, long hours and rising operating costs.

Improvement could combine fair enforcement with better support. Clear fare information, easier complaint procedures, driver training and recognition for good service may all help. The industry must also respond to competition from app-based hire-car services while ensuring that passengers receive safe, reliable and courteous transport.

The Transport Department is considering mystery-passenger checks and a clearer digital receipt showing the route and fare. Driver groups support action against serious misconduct but want complaints investigated before penalties affect a licence.

Tourism representatives propose a multilingual booking guide and a voluntary service badge for trained drivers. Any reform will need enough taxis at busy times, simple reporting for visitors and rewards that make professional service worth maintaining.

context.title: Practice context: Protecting Wild Animals
body: Wild boars sometimes enter residential areas in search of food. Some residents fear damage or injury and call for the animals to be removed, while conservation groups argue that shooting should be a last resort. Feeding by people and easy access to rubbish can make encounters more frequent.

A balanced policy could include secure bins, public warnings, habitat management and trained teams that move animals away from crowded places. Any decision must consider human safety, animal welfare and the practical limits of non-lethal methods. The debate is about when protection should give way to control.

Wildlife officers have recorded more reports near housing estates after residents left food beside rubbish collection points. Most encounters ended without injury, but frightened animals can behave unpredictably when surrounded or chased for photographs.

A district trial will install animal-proof bins and send trained teams to crowded locations. Officials will review whether these measures reduce conflict before deciding when relocation, fertility control or lethal action can be justified.

context.title: Practice context: Computer Programming in Schools
body: Some schools are considering whether computer programming should receive more curriculum time. Programming can develop logical thinking, creativity and problem-solving, and these skills may be useful in many future jobs. Supporters even suggest reducing time for subjects such as history and geography.

Others argue that students need knowledge of society, place and the past in order to make responsible decisions. Programming may also be difficult to teach well without trained staff and suitable equipment. Schools must decide whether it should begin in primary school and how to balance technical skills with a broad education.

A proposed timetable would give every junior student one programming lesson a week. Rather than memorising code, classes would design simple games, test instructions and explain why a solution failed, but the change would reduce time available for other subjects.

The principal has asked departments to suggest a balanced curriculum. One option links programming with maps, historical data and creative projects, allowing digital skills to support existing subjects instead of replacing the knowledge those subjects provide.

context.title: Practice context: Socialising after School
body: After-school time gives teenagers a chance to relax and maintain friendships, but suitable meeting places can be difficult to find. Libraries are quiet and inexpensive, shopping centres are convenient but crowded, and activity centres may offer useful facilities but close early.

A good hangout should be safe, affordable, accessible and welcoming to young people. It should also allow conversation without disturbing others. Schools and communities may need to provide more spaces, while students must show that socialising can be responsible and does not prevent them from completing homework or family duties.

The Peer Counselling team surveyed students about three possible venues: a covered area on campus, a youth centre and a café offering a group discount. Cost and travel time mattered more to respondents than fashionable decoration.

The team hopes to propose a welcoming space with Wi-Fi, drinking water and some organised activities, while keeping areas for ordinary conversation. Rules on noise, closing time and respectful behaviour would be agreed with students rather than imposed without consultation.

context.title: Practice context: Private Kitchens
body: Private kitchens serve small groups in flats, studios or other spaces rather than in conventional restaurants. Customers may enjoy a personal atmosphere, unusual menus and direct contact with the cook. Operators can test creative ideas without paying for a large dining room.

The model raises concerns about licences, hygiene, fire safety, prices and consumer protection. Neighbours may also be affected by noise or frequent visitors. Private kitchens can add variety to Hong Kong’s food culture, but their success depends on trust, clear standards and honest information about what customers are paying for.

A local cook runs a twelve-seat private kitchen twice a week, serving one seasonal menu announced online. Guests appreciate meeting the chef, but first-time customers say it is difficult to check licences, allergy arrangements and refund terms.

Restaurant owners argue that all food businesses should meet comparable safety requirements. Private-kitchen operators reply that small bookings and limited menus are different from full restaurants. A sensible policy would protect diners without removing the experimentation that attracts them.

context.title: Practice context: Hong Kong Buskers
body: Buskers bring live music and performance into streets and public spaces. Supporters say they make the city more lively and give new artists a way to meet audiences. A performer can gain experience without first being invited to a concert hall.

Critics complain about noise, repeated songs, blocked walkways and performers who seem to pressure people for money. Improving busking may require suitable locations, reasonable time limits and a fair permit system. The government must encourage creativity without making public performance so controlled that its energy disappears.

A residents’ letter has asked the district to ban amplification after repeated evening performances below nearby flats. Musicians respond that a total restriction would silence skilled performers along with the small number who cause complaints.

The arts committee is considering marked pitches, audition-free registration and quiet hours near homes. It may also publish a public code covering volume, crowd management and voluntary donations, with warnings before a performer loses access to popular locations.

context.title: Practice context: History Week
body: A school plans to hold a History Week and wants one Events Day to bring a chosen period to life. Students could create an exhibition, perform scenes, prepare food, invite a speaker or design an interactive trail around the campus.

The organisers need a period with enough reliable information and features that can be shown respectfully. Activities should do more than provide costumes and decorations; they should help students understand how people lived and why events mattered. Cost, accuracy, participation and links to the curriculum all need to be considered.

Students have shortlisted the 1960s in Hong Kong, the age of maritime trade and the early development of railways. Each choice offers strong visual material, but borrowed objects and specialist speakers would affect the budget.

The Events Day could combine an evidence-based exhibition with oral histories, demonstrations and a problem-solving trail. Teachers want sources clearly labelled so that entertainment supports accurate learning, while organisers hope every class can contribute without repeating the same display.

context.title: Practice context: Electronic Devices and Social Skills
body: Electronic devices help young people study, communicate and organise daily life. Yet constant checking can interrupt face-to-face conversation, reduce attention and make quiet moments uncomfortable. Online contact may keep friendships active, but it does not always develop the same listening and social skills as meeting in person.

Schools and families must decide whether limits are needed and how they can be realistic. Device-free activities, agreed times and better role models may work better than a total ban. The goal is not to reject technology, but to help young people use it without weakening relationships or well-being.

The Student Union observed that lunchtime groups often sat together while every member looked at a separate screen. Students said devices helped arrange meetings, yet notifications continued interrupting conversations after friends had arrived.

A proposed Connection Week would provide phone-free tables, cooperative games and short workshops on attentive listening. Participation would be voluntary, and secure storage would be available, allowing the campaign to demonstrate alternatives instead of treating normal device use as wrongdoing.

context.title: Practice context: A More Walkable Hong Kong
body: Walking in Hong Kong can be difficult when pavements are narrow, crossings are inconvenient and construction or parked objects block the route. Heat, rain, traffic and poor signs also discourage people, especially children, older residents and wheelchair users.

A more walkable city would need shade, seating, safer crossings, connected paths and clear information. A campaign leaflet should identify real obstacles, explain practical improvements and show how walking benefits health, neighbourhood businesses and the environment. Its message must be organised so readers can act on it quickly.

A street audit around the school found missing dropped kerbs, delivery boxes across pavements and crossings that gave slower walkers too little time. Students also mapped shaded routes that already make short journeys pleasant.

The proposed leaflet will pair photographs of obstacles with a neighbourhood walking map and a channel for reporting hazards. Community groups want improvements tested with wheelchair users, parents and older residents before money is spent on decorative features.

context.title: Practice context: Singapore-style Public Conduct Laws
body: Singapore is known for strict public-conduct rules, including controls on littering, eating in some transport areas and the sale of chewing gum. Some people believe similar rules could make Hong Kong cleaner and more orderly. Others worry that copying penalties ignores differences between the two cities.

Effective rules must be understandable, proportionate and enforced consistently. Heavy fines may discourage behaviour, but they can also seem unfair if public facilities or education are inadequate. The government should consider whether each proposed law solves a genuine problem and whether less severe measures could work.

The proposal includes higher littering fines, restrictions on food in public transport and tighter control of chewing gum sales. Supporters expect visible rules to change habits quickly; civil-rights groups ask how warnings, appeals and enforcement records would work.

Officials will compare cleanliness data, enforcement costs and the effect on visitors before recommending legislation. They are also considering more bins and public education, because punishment may have little effect when facilities are inconvenient or rules appear arbitrary.

context.title: Practice context: A Hong Kong-themed Coffee Shop in Shanghai
body: A business course is developing a Hong Kong-themed coffee shop for Shanghai. The shop could serve local drinks and snacks, display familiar street signs or transport designs, and introduce stories about Hong Kong neighbourhoods and popular culture.

A strong theme should feel authentic without becoming a collection of stereotypes. The team must choose products that travel well, decorations that create atmosphere and prices suitable for local customers. They should also decide which aspects of Hong Kong to promote and how the shop can stand out from other themed cafés.

Market research in Shanghai suggests customers recognise milk tea, egg tarts and Hong Kong cinema, but know less about everyday neighbourhood culture. The team therefore plans rotating menus and small displays telling the stories behind selected objects.

Designers favour tiled walls and compact booth seating rather than filling the room with unrelated souvenirs. Local suppliers would prepare fresh ingredients, while guest events featuring music, illustration and travel stories could keep the theme changing after the opening publicity ends.

context.title: Practice context: Trophies for Losing Teams
body: Some schools give trophies to every child who takes part in a competition. Supporters say this protects confidence, recognises effort and encourages less experienced students to continue. Critics argue that a trophy loses meaning if it does not represent achievement.

Learning to lose can teach resilience, honesty and respect for stronger opponents, but constant pressure to win may encourage anxiety or cheating. Schools must decide which activities should remain competitive, how effort should be recognised and whether awards can celebrate progress without pretending that every result is the same.

A sports day committee has proposed participation medals for younger pupils and performance trophies for older teams. Coaches believe beginners need encouragement, whereas several students say honest results make improvement more satisfying.

The revised award system could recognise sportsmanship, persistence and personal progress alongside first place. Competitive events would remain, but teachers would review activities that repeatedly exclude less experienced players or place excessive pressure on a single child.

context.title: Practice context: Emoticons as Word of the Year
body: An emoticon was selected as a Word of the Year, reflecting how often people now use pictures in digital messages. Emoticons can show tone quickly, cross language barriers and make informal communication warmer. Their meaning, however, may change across cultures, age groups and situations.

A message made only of pictures can be unclear, and frequent informal use may not prepare students for careful writing. At the same time, languages have always changed as new tools appear. The question is whether picture-based communication supplements words or gradually replaces skills people still need.

Editors chose a “face with tears of joy” because it appeared in millions of messages and represented a major change in everyday communication. The decision was widely discussed precisely because the winning item was an image rather than a conventional word.

Teachers note that students already switch between formal essays and informal chats. Misunderstandings are most likely when an unfamiliar symbol carries different meanings for different readers, suggesting that context and audience remain important even in very short messages.

context.title: Practice context: Meditation in Secondary Schools
body: Meditation programmes teach students to sit quietly, focus on breathing and notice thoughts without reacting immediately. Some schools believe short sessions could reduce stress, improve concentration and help students manage emotions during demanding school days.

Results depend on good instruction and voluntary, respectful participation. Students may feel embarrassed, consider the practice a waste of time or connect it with beliefs they do not share. Schools also need time, space and trained staff. Meditation should therefore be judged as one possible well-being tool rather than a cure for every problem.

A six-week school trial would offer ten minutes of guided practice before afternoon lessons. Participation records would not affect grades, and students uncomfortable with closing their eyes could use a quiet breathing or listening exercise instead.

Counsellors will collect anonymous feedback on stress and concentration, while teachers record whether the transition into lessons becomes calmer. The trial will stop if sessions create discomfort or replace professional support needed by students with serious mental-health concerns.

context.title: Practice context: Twins in Schools
body: A school project is exploring the experiences of twins. Twins may share a close relationship and similar appearance, but they are still individuals with different interests, abilities and personalities. School practices can either recognise this individuality or encourage constant comparison.

The project could examine whether twins prefer the same class, how parents and teachers avoid confusing them and what advantages or difficulties they experience. Students will need reliable information from interviews, surveys and published research, then choose a presentation format that is informative without treating twins as a curiosity.

The project team plans confidential interviews with twins, parents and teachers from several year groups. Questions will cover classroom placement, mistaken identity, competition and whether people expect twins to share friends or interests.

Findings could be presented through paired audio clips, charts and short profiles in which each twin approves the final wording. Names and photographs would be optional, helping the exhibition challenge assumptions without exposing private family experiences.

context.title: Practice context: Students on Social Media
body: Students use social media to share photos, maintain friendships and express identity. A carefully chosen post can create a positive impression, but constant comparison and pressure for approval may affect confidence. Tags and images can also spread beyond the audience originally intended.

Acceptable behaviour includes asking permission, protecting private information and responding respectfully. Schools should help students think about lasting digital footprints without monitoring every conversation. Young people need practical strategies for dealing with unwanted tags, misleading images, online pressure and disagreements that move between screens and school life.

The counselling team has received reports of embarrassing photographs being reposted after the original uploader deleted them. Other students describe anxiety when popular classmates appear to have perfect social lives every day.

A peer-led campaign would demonstrate privacy settings, permission before tagging and ways to report harmful content. It would also remind viewers that edited posts show selected moments, not a complete measure of someone’s friendships, appearance or success.

context.title: Practice context: Bicycle Safety Gadgets
body: A Bicycle Club is preparing a safety talk and comparing several cycling gadgets. Lights, reflective equipment, helmets and wearable signals may reduce risk, but no product can replace attention, road knowledge and responsible behaviour. Some gadgets may be expensive or uncomfortable.

The club should judge each item by effectiveness, ease of use, price and suitability for Hong Kong conditions. Its two recommendations need clear reasons and should form part of wider advice about checking a bicycle, choosing safe routes, following traffic rules and responding to pedestrians and other road users.

Four advertised products include a bright wheel light, an inflatable helmet, a handlebar direction signal and a jacket with reflective panels. The products address different dangers, so choosing two requires attention to both visibility and head protection.

Club members will compare independent safety testing rather than promotional claims. Their talk will also cover braking distance, hand signals and route planning, because a gadget that is poorly fitted or distracts its rider can create a new hazard.

context.title: Practice context: Short Story Vending Machines
body: Short story vending machines print a brief story for someone waiting at a station or public building. They offer a quick alternative to looking at a phone and may introduce readers to writers they would not normally choose. The experience is simple, surprising and easy to share.

Machines alone will not solve declining interest in literature. Location, cost, story quality, language choice and environmental impact all matter. Reading clubs, live events and school recommendations may reach different audiences. The aim should be to make literature inviting while preserving the depth that longer reading can provide.

The council is considering installing a machine beside a busy ferry waiting area. Readers could select one-, three- or five-minute stories in Chinese or English, printed on recyclable paper without advertisements.

Local writers welcome a new way to reach the public but want clear payment and selection arrangements. Librarians suggest printing a code linking each extract to borrowed books, author events and accessible electronic versions for readers who need larger text.

context.title: Practice context: International Left-Handers Day
body: International Left-Handers Day draws attention to everyday objects and routines designed mainly for right-handed people. Desks, scissors, tools and sports instruction can create small but repeated frustrations. Awareness can help schools notice barriers that right-handed students may never see.

An event could include demonstrations, adapted equipment and activities in which participants try common tasks with their non-dominant hand. Organisers should avoid stereotypes that all left-handed people are more creative or athletic. The purpose is practical inclusion and understanding, not turning a natural difference into a performance.

Students have found that several classroom desks and computer mice are uncomfortable for left-handed users. The school can borrow adapted sports equipment and invite a designer to explain why products should be tested by people with different needs.

The organising team proposes a lunchtime exhibition, a handwriting station and a review of school equipment. Activities will focus on practical barriers and solutions; claims about personality or intelligence will be labelled as myths unless supported by reliable evidence.

context.title: Practice context: Texting Lanes
body: Some cities have experimented with marked lanes for people who text while walking. The idea attracts attention to distracted pedestrians, who may miss traffic signals, obstacles and other people. Yet a special lane may appear to approve the risky behaviour it is meant to reduce.

A texting lane is also difficult to enforce and may be ignored by the people paying least attention. Public messages, safer street design, school education and personal habits could be more effective. Any campaign should explain the danger clearly and encourage people to stop moving before using a phone.

A temporary lane in another city attracted photographs but little consistent use. Observers found that distracted walkers crossed the markings whenever crowds formed, while pedestrians without phones sometimes used the empty space.

The Student Union is considering floor signs at school exits, short videos based on real near-misses and designated stopping places away from crossings. Success would be measured by safer behaviour, not by how many people notice a colourful lane.

context.title: Four Ways to Improve a Selfie
body: A school photography club is comparing four tools for taking selfies. A small wireless shutter lets users place a phone at a distance and take a picture without touching it. A camera app offers a timer and simple editing features. A lightweight selfie stick can include more people or more of the background in a photograph.

The fourth option is a smartphone designed for self-portraits. Its rotating camera makes unusual angles easier, while a beauty setting changes skin tone and face shape. The products range from a low-cost app to an expensive phone, so price, portability and picture quality do not point to the same choice.

Club members must recommend only two items for students. They should consider why young people enjoy selfies, whether editing encourages creativity or unrealistic images, and whether a gadget will still be useful after the novelty disappears. A strong recommendation should identify the intended users and explain why each chosen tool offers good value.

Others prefer a theme about student life today, including lunchtime conversations, club activities and hopes for the future. Storage space is limited, so not every suggestion can be accepted.

The Student Union also wants the project to involve more than a small committee. Possible ideas include an online vote, a memory-collection week and recording booths at school. The final selection should represent different ages and experiences, protect personal privacy and remain understandable to someone who discovers it many years from now.

An international exhibition could reach a larger audience, although it would require more research, displays and volunteers.

The society must decide which activities suit secondary students and how people outside the school can take part. It could invite community coaches, organise mixed-age teams or connect activities with a charity. Whatever it chooses, the programme should welcome beginners, value sportsmanship as much as winning, and give participants a meaningful role rather than making them passive spectators.

Repairs can be slow and expensive because experienced workers must clean fragile materials, recreate missing parts and explain what can safely be restored. However, customers may value the emotional history of an object more than the price of buying a new toy.

Business Studies students are considering whether a similar service could succeed in Hong Kong. They need to identify likely customers, suitable prices and ways to build trust. Social-media before-and-after videos, partnerships with toy shops and repair workshops for families could attract attention, but rent, specialist training and a limited market may make the idea risky.

Business Law would explore contracts, consumer rights, employment and the legal responsibilities of individuals and companies. These subjects may connect school learning with future careers, but not every student will find the same course useful or attractive.

Only one course can begin next year. The Student Union must compare educational value, popularity, safety, cost and timetable pressure. It should also consider whether students without previous experience can participate fairly. A trial lesson or interest survey may provide evidence, but the final recommendation should explain how the course benefits students beyond simply being new or entertaining.

Supporters believe students could research information quickly, create multimedia work and use accessibility tools suited to their needs.

The policy also raises practical problems. Not every family can afford the same device or data plan, and students may become distracted by messages, games or social media. Teachers would need clear rules for appropriate use, secure charging and online safety. Printed materials should remain available when technology fails or is unsuitable.

Before making a recommendation, students should identify the subjects in which a personal device adds genuine learning value. They should also propose ways to lend equipment, protect privacy and respond to misuse without disrupting the whole class. The aim is not to replace teachers or books, but to decide when technology makes learning more effective and inclusive.

Supporters argue that vertical development could use scarce urban land more efficiently.

Living in one giant structure might reduce commuting and make services convenient. Shared gardens and gathering areas could also encourage contact between residents. On the other hand, the project may feel crowded or artificial, and people could become dependent on a complex building for transport, safety, energy and essential services.

The proposal is being considered as an idea for Hong Kong. The discussion should identify missing facilities, compare the benefits and drawbacks of daily life inside the building and judge whether residents would accept it. Publishing online gives new writers immediate access to readers without waiting for a traditional publisher. Feedback can help them improve and build a loyal audience. However, comments may be rude or personal, work can be copied easily, and pressure to post frequently may reduce quality. Writers must also decide how to handle mature or offensive material.

A school magazine is preparing advice for students who want to write online. body: Some countries require young adults, usually men, to complete military service. Service may also expose people from different backgrounds to teamwork and practical skills.

Critics argue that compulsory service interrupts education or employment and removes personal choice. Not everyone is suited to military life, and the effect can be especially unfair when rules differ by gender or wealth. Some systems therefore allow community service in hospitals, environmental projects or elderly care as an alternative.

A school debate must consider whether compulsory military service is justified, what responsibilities citizens owe society and how people who object should be treated. The group should examine arguments on both sides and discuss whether women should face the same requirement. context.title: When Robots Serve Customers
body: Restaurants and hotels are beginning to use robots to greet guests, deliver meals and carry luggage. A robot can repeat simple tasks for long hours, reduce some labour costs and work in places that are uncomfortable or risky. The novelty may also attract customers who want a different experience.

Service work, however, often requires judgement, empathy and flexible communication. A machine may struggle with an unusual request, a frightened child or a customer who needs reassurance. Robots also cost money to buy and maintain, and technical failures can interrupt the whole service. Employees may worry that automation will reduce jobs or make work less personal.

A school-magazine article should weigh these effects rather than treating robots as either a miracle or a threat. It should identify tasks that machines can perform well, explain why customers or workers may object and consider other industries where robots could help. Human oversight, retraining and clear responsibility for mistakes should form part of any recommendation.

The results suggested that technology is no longer seen only as entertainment; many people use it for work, directions, payments and social connection.

A similar survey in Hong Kong might produce a different order. Dense neighbourhoods, long school days, public transport and widespread mobile payment may increase the importance of a phone, travel card or portable charger. Age could also shape responses: teenagers, parents and older residents may define necessity in very different ways.

Students are comparing the survey with local experience. They should distinguish between items needed for safety or daily tasks and items that merely feel difficult to give up. The discussion should predict which choices would change in Hong Kong, explain how generations may differ and consider whether reliable Internet access has become a basic need or remains a luxury.

context.title: Choosing a Leadership Camp
body: A school can send students to one of two personal-development camps. The outdoor camp uses hiking, team challenges and practical problem-solving to build resilience and self-reliance. The indoor camp focuses on communication, public speaking, planning and conflict management through workshops and simulations. Both claim to develop leadership, but they do so in different ways.

Outdoor activities may create memorable pressure and reveal how participants behave in a team, yet weather, fitness and safety can limit access. Indoor training is easier to control and may connect directly with school projects, although students could find it less challenging or authentic. The quality of instructors matters as much as the location.

The selection process also needs careful thought. Academic results alone may exclude students who would benefit most, while an open lottery may ignore motivation and readiness. The group should recommend a camp, propose fair criteria and identify concerns about cost, safety and follow-up. It should explain how students will apply what they learn after returning to school.

These measures should expand choice without suggesting that every girl must follow the same path.

Parents may strongly influence subject decisions because they are concerned about workload, job security or whether a field will suit their daughter. body: News reports often give great attention to celebrities who break the law. Some receive fines, treatment programmes or community service and later rebuild their careers. Others believe fame creates unfair advantages. Expensive legal support, loyal fans and public sympathy may influence how a case is discussed, even when courts apply the same rules. At the same time, demanding a harsher sentence simply because someone is well known would also conflict with equal treatment under the law.

The Liberal Studies Society is considering punishment, public reaction and continued fan support. The group should separate legal penalties from moral expectations and avoid assuming that every case is alike. It should discuss whether celebrities have extra responsibility as role models, while recognising that admiration for a person’s work does not excuse harmful conduct.

body: Some education researchers argue that children under six need more time for play, movement and social development before beginning full classroom instruction. They warn that pressure to read, write and complete formal tasks too early may create anxiety and leave less time for curiosity, independence and learning through experience.

Other specialists point out that a well-designed early programme can provide language support, regular routines and access to trained adults. Children from families with fewer resources may particularly benefit. The important distinction may be between developmentally appropriate early education and a narrow programme dominated by worksheets, testing and long periods of sitting.

A debate on school starting age should therefore examine both timing and the kind of education offered. The group must present arguments for and against the motion, decide which side to support and respond to differences between children. Parental choice, government standards, equality of access and the meaning of “formal schooling” should all be clarified.

body: Many students and office workers spend most of the day sitting. Standing desks allow users to raise the work surface and change position without leaving a task. Supporters say alternating between sitting and standing can reduce stiffness, encourage movement and make people more aware of long periods of inactivity.

A standing desk is not a complete health solution. Standing for too long can cause discomfort, and desks may be expensive or difficult to fit into crowded rooms. Height must be adjusted correctly, while students with particular health needs may require other arrangements. Evidence about concentration and long-term benefits should not be exaggerated.

A class presentation should explain both advantages and disadvantages and show how the desks might be used safely. A short demonstration, posture comparison or audience poll could make the topic engaging. The key message should be flexible movement rather than replacing all sitting with standing, and any school trial should gather feedback from different users.

context.title: Young People Abandoning Email

context.title: Helicopter Parenting
body: A family magazine describes “helicopter parents” as adults who closely supervise almost every part of a child’s life. They may check homework repeatedly, select activities, contact teachers about small problems and try to prevent their children from making mistakes.

Such attention can provide safety and support, especially when children are young. Yet constant control may weaken confidence, independence and problem-solving skills, while also causing arguments at home.

The article asks how parents can remain caring and involved without preventing teenagers from learning through experience. One teenager in the article describes a parent who rewrote a school presentation without being asked; another appreciates being collected late at night but wants to choose her own friends. Family counsellors suggest agreeing in advance which decisions belong to the child. Advice is most useful when it helps a young person act, rather than replacing the action altogether. Regular family meetings can revisit those boundaries as trust and maturity develop.

context.title: Food Photography
body: A lifestyle website notes that photographing meals has become a normal part of eating out for many young people. Colourful dishes can be shared instantly with friends, used to record special occasions or collected as recommendations for other diners.

Restaurant owners may benefit from free publicity, and careful food photography can be creative. On the other hand, repeated photo-taking can delay a meal, disturb companions and encourage people to judge food mainly by appearance.

A successful food blog therefore needs attractive images, honest comments, clear organisation and respect for other diners. For the proposed student blog, each post could pair one carefully framed image with the dish name, price, location and a brief comment on taste. Bloggers should ask before photographing another person’s plate and avoid blocking restaurant aisles. Readers are more likely to trust a page that includes ordinary meals and disappointments, not only perfectly arranged desserts. A simple rating guide would make separate reviews easier to compare.

Some residents associate street groups with noise, damage or unsafe behaviour. Participants respond that most performers respect public space and that clear rules and suitable venues would reduce conflict.

Community events, demonstrations and cooperation with local organisations may help the public judge street culture by its actual behaviour rather than by stereotypes. A district youth centre has offered its outdoor wall for supervised mural sessions and marked a smooth corner for weekend skating. Residents can watch demonstrations, speak to performers and report genuine nuisance through one contact person. The arrangement does not excuse damage or dangerous tricks; it gives responsible participants a place to show that street activity can be skilled and organised. Evening closing times would also answer neighbours’ concerns about noise.

body: An international report places Switzerland among the world’s happiest societies while Hong Kong appears much lower in the table. The comparison highlights health care, education, innovation and infrastructure. Both places are prosperous and highly connected, but residents may experience public services, housing, work pressure and community life differently.

Rankings can reveal broad patterns, yet a single number cannot capture every person’s situation or every cultural view of happiness. Economic success may improve security without automatically creating leisure, trust or belonging.

Readers are invited to consider which Swiss strengths could transfer to Hong Kong and which local conditions require different solutions. Hong Kong already performs strongly in transport and digital connections, but long working hours and expensive housing affect daily satisfaction. A Swiss policy cannot simply be copied into a denser city with different public finances. Local experiments might begin with accessible health support, less pressured school routines and neighbourhood spaces where residents can meet without paying to enter.

context.title: Urban Dictionary
body: Online dictionaries allow users to submit new slang, abbreviations and expressions before they appear in traditional reference books. These entries can show how language changes through music, social media and youth culture, but definitions are written by volunteers and may be inaccurate, offensive or short-lived.

A student dictionary could collect authentic examples from conversations, songs and online posts while checking meaning with several speakers. Editors would also need rules on relevance, clarity and respectful language.

Images, example sentences and short notes about origin could make the final dictionary informative without suggesting that every popular expression belongs in formal English. Editors at one school propose accepting a word only after finding it in three independent examples and confirming its meaning with several students. Each entry would show pronunciation, context and a warning if the expression is rude or unsuitable for formal work. Monthly online updates would handle fast-changing slang, while a printed selection would preserve the most useful terms.

context.title: Finland's Education System
body: An education feature describes Finland’s later school starting age, limited standardised testing, mixed-ability classes and strong teacher training. The system is often praised for equality and professional trust. Hong Kong, by contrast, offers a broad school network, strong academic expectations and clear public examination routes.

Practices that succeed in one country depend on culture, resources, population and university admission systems. Removing examinations or homework without changing other structures may not produce the same results.

Rather than declaring one system superior, students should identify useful principles and decide which changes would be realistic and fair in Hong Kong. A Hong Kong principal visiting Helsinki is impressed by calm classrooms and the time teachers spend planning together. She also notes that local schools serve larger populations and prepare pupils for a competitive public examination. Her trial plan keeps regular assessment but replaces one homework exercise each week with guided reading, teacher feedback and mixed-ability problem solving.

Critics question whether Hong Kong should copy attractions in other cities and whether valuable public land could serve residents better as open space, cultural facilities or a waterfront park.

The decision depends on cost, originality, public access and the long-term value of the whole waterfront rather than on visitor numbers alone. Under one design, the wheel would occupy the site for a limited period and pay rent towards waterfront maintenance. A competing plan proposes lawns, a small performance stage, shaded seating and space for weekend markets. Public access between attractions and the harbour edge remains crucial: a landmark loses much of its value if queues, ticket barriers and shops dominate the promenade.

context.title: Communicating with Parents through Social Media
body: A survey finds that many parents monitor teenagers’ social-media use, sometimes by following them directly and sometimes by creating another account. Parents say they worry about strangers, bullying, harmful posts and the amount of personal information shared online. Teenagers may understand these risks but still want a private space to talk with friends.

Monitoring can reveal a serious problem early, yet secret checking may damage trust and encourage young people to hide more. Clear family rules and open conversations may be more effective than demanding passwords.

Families need to balance safety, privacy and respect while recognising that the right level of supervision changes as children grow older. A useful family agreement might specify which platforms a teenager may use, what information must stay private and when an adult should intervene. Parents would promise not to post embarrassing childhood photographs or comment on every conversation. Teenagers, in return, would report threats and unknown contacts. Such rules make online safety a shared responsibility rather than a secret investigation.

context.title: Couponing
body: Discount coupons now appear in newspapers, mobile applications, shop memberships and social-media promotions. Students may use them for meals, drinks, entertainment or online shopping. A good offer can reduce the cost of something they already planned to buy.

Couponing can become time-consuming, and limited-time deals may encourage unnecessary purchases. Conditions such as minimum spending, restricted dates and data collection can make a discount less valuable than it first appears.

Careful shoppers compare the final price, read the conditions and decide whether the product is genuinely needed before treating a coupon as a saving. A student comparing two lunch offers discovers that the larger discount requires buying a drink and travelling to another district. The cheaper-looking meal actually costs more. Consumer groups recommend keeping a list, calculating the full bill and deleting unused offers before they expire. A coupon works best as a reduction on a planned purchase, not as a reason to create one.

Popular characters could attract members quickly, but the society should offer more than film-watching. Drawing workshops, costume design, debates, charity projects and original-story competitions could involve students with different interests.

The organisers need a recognisable identity, an inclusive programme and clear reasons why a superhero club deserves a lasting place at school. For its first month, the society could hold a character-design workshop, a debate on whether heroes should hide their identities and a charity costume walk. Members who dislike acting could draw posters, write stories or manage sound. A school vote among the three proposed mascots would publicise the launch, while a trial membership period would keep the club open to curious newcomers.

International films can introduce unfamiliar places, social issues and styles of storytelling. Subtitles may also help students connect language learning with entertainment.

Some students may prefer familiar stars or fast-moving films, while others could find cultural references difficult. The opening choice therefore needs an accessible story, suitable content and enough interest to start discussion.

Short introductions, audience voting and post-film activities could turn the day into a shared cultural experience rather than a simple screening. The organisers could screen a lively, age-appropriate film first, then offer shorter choices in different rooms. Country maps, director notes and a lunchtime food stall would provide context without turning the event into a lesson. A short audience discussion should focus on one memorable scene or cultural difference, giving shy viewers an easy way to contribute after the credits.

Students may be interested in dangerous field conditions and famous finds, but the visit should also show the training, teamwork and uncertainty involved in scientific research.

A fossil-handling demonstration, question session and small identification activity could make the guest’s career understandable and encourage interest in science. Before Dr Xu arrives, science students could examine replica footprints and guess how size, movement and habitat are inferred from incomplete evidence. Interviewers might ask about his first discovery, the longest field trip and a mistake that changed his thinking. A display of field notebooks and tools would show that dinosaur research depends as much on careful recording as on dramatic fossils.

body: A health column lists everyday mistakes such as skipping breakfast, carrying heavy bags, sleeping too little, exercising incorrectly and trusting unverified advice. Busy students may repeat these habits because the effects are gradual or because conflicting online information makes healthy choices difficult.

A workshop cannot cover every issue well. Organisers should select common, preventable problems with clear practical advice and avoid frightening participants or presenting uncertain claims as medical facts.

Demonstrations, short self-checks and expert explanations could help students connect reliable health information with realistic changes to daily routines. The school nurse recommends focusing on sleep loss, heavy bags and skipped breakfasts because pupils encounter them daily and can test simple improvements. At three stations, visitors could adjust a backpack, build a quick breakfast and compare bedtime routines. Anonymous question cards would let students raise sensitive concerns, while printed sources would separate medical guidance from online rumours. Follow-up cards could invite pupils to track one small change for seven days.

body: A sports report compares activities in which players depend on a team with those in which athletes compete mainly as individuals. Team sports can develop communication, cooperation and a sense of belonging. They may also share pressure after a defeat and create regular social contact.

However, teams require enough players, facilities and coordinated schedules. Individual sports may provide greater flexibility and allow progress at a personal pace, although training can feel lonely.

Affordable facilities, school leagues and beginner-friendly community programmes could encourage participation if they welcome different ages and ability levels. Community centres could lend basic equipment and run short seasons so beginners are not committing to a full year. Mixed-skill teams should rotate positions instead of leaving weaker players on the side. Publicity might feature friendships and gradual improvement rather than only trophies.
