context.title: E-textbooks and Traditional Textbooks
body: Schools are considering whether more subjects should use electronic textbooks on tablets and computers. Digital books can include search tools, audio, video, updates and interactive exercises while reducing the number of heavy volumes students carry.

Printed books do not need batteries or internet access and may make sustained reading and note-taking easier for some learners. Devices also bring cost, distraction, eye-strain and technical-support concerns.

The strongest learning model may depend on subject, student needs and access rather than on replacing every printed page at once. A sensible trial could give one class the same chapter in both formats. Pupils would use the electronic version for animation and instant definitions, then the printed copy for extended reading and revision. Teachers could compare concentration, accessibility and technical problems before choosing a mixture. Spare devices and downloadable pages would prevent a weak connection from becoming missed homework. The trial should include students who use accessibility tools or share devices at home.

context.title: Financial Problems Facing Tertiary Students
body: A newspaper feature examines tuition fees, transport, food, equipment and living expenses faced by tertiary students. Loans allow some young people to continue studying, but repayments may shape early career choices and delay savings or independent living.

A degree can offer knowledge, networks and access to particular professions, yet benefits vary by course and employment conditions. Part-time work may reduce debt but can also reduce study time and rest.

Students need clear information about total costs, financial support and realistic career outcomes before deciding how much to borrow. The profile follows a student who works two restaurant shifts each week and borrows the rest of her tuition. She checks repayment estimates before choosing a course and applies for grants early. Universities could help by publishing realistic living budgets, expanding emergency funds and offering paid campus work connected to study, reducing the need for exhausting late-night employment. Free financial counselling would make unfamiliar loan conditions easier to understand.

body: A proposal calls for secondary schools to teach courtesy through formal lessons rather than relying only on family guidance and school rules. Possible topics include respectful conversation, behaviour on public transport, online manners, conflict resolution and consideration for people with different needs.

Supporters say shared lessons could improve the school climate. Critics argue that good manners are learned through daily examples and that compulsory classes may become artificial or take time from other subjects.

The value of the programme would depend on age, teaching method and whether students practise the behaviour beyond the classroom. Instead of lectures on saying “please”, one pilot lesson uses role-play: giving up a priority seat, disagreeing in a group chat and responding when a queue is broken. Junior students practise simple public behaviour, while older classes examine workplace and online situations. Teachers would judge the programme by fewer repeated conflicts and more considerate routines, not by a manners test.

Different facial expressions may support richer storytelling and emotional understanding, but angry or frightening characters could encourage aggressive play or concern younger children. Branded sets can also be expensive and less open-ended.

The project should consider creativity, age suitability and how toy design shapes the stories children choose to tell. A toy workshop gives groups identical bricks but figures with cheerful, worried or angry faces. The stories they build become noticeably different, showing how a small expression can guide play without deciding it completely. Parents could choose age-appropriate sets and mix themed pieces with ordinary bricks. The most valuable box is one that invites rebuilding after the instructions are finished.

body: Advertising pays for media, informs consumers about products and can introduce useful services or public campaigns. Creative advertisements may entertain audiences and help small companies reach customers. Competition can also encourage businesses to explain price, quality and new features.

The debate team selects three cases: a road-safety campaign, a sugary drink advertisement aimed at children and an online loan promotion that hides charges. These examples reveal why one rule cannot cover every message. Clear labelling and limits on audience targeting may protect consumers while allowing legitimate businesses to speak, whereas dangerous or deliberately deceptive products justify stronger restrictions.

Customers could choose a normal or challenge size, and untouched ingredients could be prepared only when ordered. A visible portion guide and reusable sharing trays would preserve the fun photograph while controlling waste, cost and pressure to overeat.

The workshop could open with a five-minute passing drill, followed by small groups examining moments when a plan failed. Students would ask how Lin trained while waiting for opportunities and how teammates earned one another’s trust. The closing activity asks each participant to turn one personal setback into a specific next step, bringing the visitor’s story back to school life. A student interviewer could collect the strongest questions before the visit.

context.title: Technology Addiction
body: A youth-health report warns that some teenagers spend many hours moving between computers, phones, games and social-media platforms. Technology supports study, entertainment and friendships, so heavy use alone does not prove addiction. Concern grows when use regularly interrupts sleep, schoolwork, exercise or face-to-face relationships.
Notifications, rewards in games and fear of missing out can make stopping difficult. Families may impose limits, but sudden bans can create conflict or ignore the reasons a young person stays online.

Tracking habits, turning off unnecessary alerts and planning offline activities may help users regain control while keeping the benefits of technology. One class tries a seven-day log and discovers that most late-night screen time begins with “just one” notification. Students move chargers outside bedrooms, set game stopping points and arrange a phone-free lunch with friends. Anyone whose use causes serious distress should speak to a counsellor rather than rely on willpower alone. The target is controlled use, not life without screens.

Customers may blame workers without considering low pay, long hours, staff shortages or rude behaviour from the public. Businesses still need clear standards, training and support for employees handling complaints.

Improvement requires respectful communication from both sides, realistic staffing and managers who respond to feedback instead of treating courtesy as a slogan. A restaurant in the feature begins each shift with one service problem and lets staff propose a response. Managers simplify complaint procedures and authorise employees to replace a poor dish without a long argument. Staff are also protected when customers become abusive. Within weeks, reviews mention faster solutions rather than forced smiles, showing that good systems support genuinely courteous behaviour.

Opponents question enforcement and fairness. Students have different learning needs, tutoring schedules, homes and responsibilities, while fixed evening study may reduce sleep, exercise and family time.

A voluntary scheme, school study spaces and guidance on planning might achieve the same goal without fines or a single timetable for every household. A two-week neighbourhood trial offers quiet rooms in libraries and schools during the proposed hours but does not punish families who follow another routine. Participants record concentration, sleep and unfinished work. If younger pupils benefit while older students feel constrained, the scheme could remain an optional support service instead of becoming a territory-wide rule backed by penalties. Weekend athletes and evening carers must also be included in the evaluation.

context.title: Discipline and Children in Hong Kong
body: A parenting feature compares child-centred decision-making with stricter family rules. Allowing children to express preferences can build confidence and responsibility, but adults still need to set boundaries on safety, money, study and respectful behaviour.

Consistent discipline may teach self-control and consequences. Harsh, unpredictable or unexplained punishment can instead create fear, secrecy and resentment, especially when children have no chance to explain themselves.

The central issue is not whether children should have a voice, but how families can combine age-appropriate freedom with clear and fair limits. In one family, children choose the weekend activity but adults decide the spending limit and return time. Broken rules lead to related consequences, such as losing use of an item that was misused, followed by a calm explanation. The arrangement gives children meaningful choices without making them responsible for adult matters. Discipline becomes teaching, not a contest over control. Parents must follow the agreed rules consistently if they expect children to respect them.

Some students worry about embarrassment, cost or lack of experience, while demanding rehearsals may conflict with study. Beginner sessions and different performance roles can make the group more welcoming.

Demonstrations, lunchtime workshops and student-created videos could attract interest if the campaign presents dance as both an art and an inclusive activity. The group plans an open rehearsal where visitors learn one short routine in ordinary sports clothes. A lunchtime showcase would combine a traditional piece, street dance and student choreography, followed by information on beginner practices. Filming should require performers’ consent. Showing the preparation behind a polished performance may persuade hesitant students that dance is learned step by step, not an inborn gift.

Print issues are easy to browse but require storage and can become dated. Online editions may provide searchable archives, yet access limits and screen reading can reduce their usefulness.

The library should consider student demand, reliability, educational value and whether one subscription can serve a broad range of readers. Librarians could display sample issues for a fortnight and record which sections pupils actually read. The final choice might include a digital archive if its licence allows many users, or a print title that circulates well between classes. Future subscriptions should fill gaps in science, current affairs, arts and practical hobbies rather than buying several magazines that repeat celebrity news.

context.title: English Learning Beyond School
body: Students once depended mainly on lessons, textbooks and homework to improve their English. Today, short videos, online comments and international communities offer far more contact with the language. A learner can watch a tutorial, compare subtitles, repeat a useful phrase and ask a question without waiting for the next school day.

Online learning is most useful when students take an active role. Simply watching entertainment may not lead to progress. Learners can keep a vocabulary notebook, follow reliable channels, write short comments and check corrections carefully. They can also listen to podcasts, read news for young people, join English-speaking activities or practise with a friend.

Studying alone brings freedom, but it also requires discipline and good judgement. New learners may choose material that is too difficult or trust inaccurate advice. A practical plan should therefore include realistic weekly goals, varied activities and occasional feedback from teachers or classmates. The aim is not to replace school, but to turn everyday media and experiences into regular language practice.

context.title: Should Every Student Learn to Cook?
body: Many teenagers can order food through an app but cannot prepare a simple meal. Long school hours, small kitchens and busy parents mean that fewer young people learn by helping at home. As a result, some students reach adulthood without knowing how to plan a balanced meal, read a food label or use basic kitchen equipment safely.

Compulsory cooking lessons could teach practical independence. Students might learn to cook rice, prepare vegetables, avoid food waste and compare the cost of home-made meals with takeaway food. Working in small teams could also build organisation and cooperation. However, schools would need suitable rooms, trained staff, ingredients and clear safety rules.

A useful course should not focus only on following recipes. It could cover nutrition, hygiene, budgeting, allergies and dishes from different cultures. Critics may argue that the timetable is already crowded or that cooking should be taught at home. Supporters reply that not every family has the time or knowledge to teach it. Schools must decide whether the benefits justify the cost.

context.title: Living Well for Longer
body: A long life is influenced by more than one habit. Health researchers often point to regular exercise, balanced meals, enough sleep, strong social relationships, limited stress, avoiding tobacco, sensible medical care and a sense of purpose. No single rule guarantees longevity, but small decisions repeated over many years can reduce risk and improve daily well-being.

Some advice is easier to follow than others. Walking and eating regular meals may be practical for most people, while expensive fitness programmes are not. Eight hours of sleep can be difficult for students or shift workers. Social contact is also important: older people who remain connected to family, neighbours or community groups may feel less lonely and stay more active.

A school Live Well Week could turn advice into experience. Possible activities include a healthy breakfast challenge, a sleep diary, simple exercise sessions, stress-management workshops and interviews with active older residents. Students should avoid presenting long life as a personal achievement alone, because genes and living conditions matter too. The strongest message is to build realistic habits that improve both length and quality of life.

context.title: Learning at Work and in Class
body: An apprenticeship combines classroom study with paid training under an experienced worker. Instead of learning only from books and examinations, apprentices practise skills in real workplaces. Programmes may cover construction, engineering, hospitality, design, technology or health services, and usually lead to a recognised qualification after several years.

Supporters say apprentices understand workplace expectations earlier and can see why their academic learning matters. Employers can also train future workers for skills that are in short supply. Yet many Hong Kong families may still prefer university routes, believing that vocational education offers lower status or fewer choices. Small companies may worry about the time and cost of supervision.

A successful programme would need cooperation among schools, employers and training bodies. Students should receive career guidance, safe working conditions, fair pay and a clear route to further study. Employers may need financial support or public recognition for providing quality placements. Apprenticeships should not become cheap labour; they should offer structured learning and regular assessment while leaving students able to change direction later.

context.title: New Life for Empty Shops
body: When shops close, dark windows and unused spaces can make a neighbourhood feel neglected. Some cities allow charities, artists and community groups to use vacant shops for a limited period. These “empty shop projects” can host exhibitions, repair workshops, youth activities, local history displays or temporary markets while a landlord waits for a permanent tenant.

The arrangement may bring visitors back to a quiet area and give small organisations an affordable place to try new ideas. Landlords benefit from having their property occupied and cared for. However, short leases create uncertainty, insurance can be complicated and successful events may disturb nearby residents. Organisers also need enough volunteers and money for utilities and basic repairs.

In Hong Kong, projects could work in older shopping centres or districts with several vacant street-level shops. Companies might provide sponsorship, while charities could design activities that respond to local needs. Clear agreements should cover safety, opening hours and responsibility for damage. The aim should be to strengthen community life, not simply provide free commercial promotion or replace long-term services.

context.title: A Visitor’s Guide to Unexpected Local Food
body: Hong Kong is known for dim sum and roast meat, but visitors may also notice foods that seem unfamiliar: chicken feet, snake soup, preserved eggs, pig’s blood curd or herbal jelly. Local diners may connect these dishes with family meals, particular seasons or traditional ideas about health, while tourists may react first to appearance, texture or ingredients.

A brochure should explain rather than shock. It could describe how each dish is prepared, what it tastes like and when people usually eat it. Clear photographs, short cultural stories and advice about where to try a small portion would make the information more inviting. Food allergies, vegetarian concerns and strong flavours should also be mentioned honestly.

Calling a dish “strange” may attract attention, but it can also sound disrespectful. The brochure should therefore present different food traditions with curiosity and humour without making local people or visitors feel foolish. It might include a tasting challenge, a map of specialist restaurants and quotations from first-time tasters. The goal is to encourage informed choice and show how food expresses Hong Kong’s history and identity.

context.title: Fitness Can Be Fun
body: Exercise does not have to mean running around a track or lifting weights in a gym. A photo race can send teams walking quickly between landmarks, household-chore challenges can turn cleaning into movement, and lion dancing combines balance, strength, rhythm and local culture. Unusual activities may attract students who normally avoid competitive sport.

A Health Awareness Fun Day could offer short sessions so participants can try several activities. Organisers would need safe routes, trained leaders, first-aid support and alternatives for students with different physical abilities. A photo race could create traffic risks, lion-dance equipment may be expensive, and a cleaning challenge needs to feel enjoyable rather than like punishment.

Other possibilities include a dance-dice game, a fitness treasure hunt, desk-stretch workshops or team challenges using recycled materials. Technology could record steps or provide clues, but phones should support activity rather than distract from it. Success should be judged by participation and enjoyment, not only speed. The event should show that regular movement can fit into ordinary life and that students can choose activities that suit them.

context.title: A Teenager’s Guide to Moving to Hong Kong
body: Moving to a new city involves more than finding a home and learning transport routes. Teenagers want to know how school life works, where they can meet people, what activities are affordable and how to get help when they feel lost. Practical information about public transport, healthcare, weather and local rules is useful, but it should be written from a young person’s point of view.

Hong Kong offers efficient transport, a mixture of old and new neighbourhoods, country parks, sports centres and many cultural festivals. A guide could explain common payment methods, school routines and simple Cantonese phrases. It should also discuss crowded spaces, expensive housing, typhoons and the challenge of making friends when classmates already have established groups.

An attractive website might use maps, short videos, checklists and stories from teenagers who have recently arrived. Information should be searchable and available on phones, with links to reliable public services. The tone should be honest rather than promotional. Newcomers need reassurance, but they also need realistic advice about homesickness, cultural differences and ways to join school or community activities.

title: Protecting Yourself from Cyber Crime

context.title: Small Steps for Better Online Security
body: Young people use online accounts for study, shopping, entertainment and communication. Criminals take advantage of weak passwords, fake messages, unsafe downloads and personal information shared in public. Some attacks are highly technical, but many succeed because a user is rushed, curious or persuaded to trust someone who appears familiar.

The effects can include stolen money, lost photographs, damaged reputations and accounts being used to deceive friends. Strong, unique passwords and two-step verification reduce risk. Users should update software, check website addresses, avoid unknown attachments and confirm unusual requests through another channel. Public Wi-Fi and shared devices also require care.

Security advice must be practical enough to follow. Telling students never to shop online or never to share anything is unrealistic. Schools can teach how scams create urgency, provide a simple reporting route and practise responding to suspicious messages. Students should know that being tricked is not a reason for shame; reporting quickly may limit harm. Good online safety combines technology, judgement and support from trusted adults.

context.title: What Is Hidden Behind a Meal?
body: A meal can arrive on the table without showing how an animal was raised or killed. Campaigners have criticised products such as shark’s fin, foie gras and meat from crowded factory farms. They argue that consumers should not support practices that cause avoidable suffering, especially when other foods are available.

Supporters of a ban say clear rules would protect animals and encourage producers to improve conditions. They also believe restaurants should tell customers where ingredients come from. Opponents point to cultural traditions, farmers’ livelihoods, higher prices and disagreement about what counts as cruelty. They may prefer education and labelling to a complete ban.

A fair debate should separate evidence from emotional images. Students need examples, a clear definition of humane treatment and responses to practical questions about enforcement. Taste, nutrition, affordability and cultural meaning all influence food choices, but they do not remove ethical responsibility. The strongest arguments will consider both animal welfare and the consequences for workers, businesses and consumers.

context.title: Contact, Risk and School Sport
body: In full contact sports such as rugby, boxing or martial arts, physical contact is part of the activity. Supporters say these sports build fitness, courage, discipline and trust. Players learn to follow rules under pressure and to protect teammates. For some teenagers, the challenge is more motivating than non-contact exercise.

Critics worry about concussion, broken bones, aggression and pressure to continue when injured. Risks may be greater when students differ greatly in size or experience. Schools also need trained coaches, protective equipment, suitable facilities and clear procedures for medical assessment. Parents may object even when a student wants to take part.

Removing all risk from sport is impossible, but risk can be managed. Age-appropriate rules, gradual skills training, matched groups and the right to stop are essential. Schools could offer contact sports as an optional activity rather than a compulsory lesson. The decision should compare benefits with evidence about injuries and should not assume that either contact or non-contact sport suits every teenager.

context.title: A Month with Less
body: Simple living means reducing unnecessary possessions and learning to meet everyday needs with fewer resources. During a countryside week, students might grow vegetables, cook basic meals, repair objects and plan how much water or electricity they use. The experience could reveal how strongly convenience and shopping shape urban routines.

Supporters say the course would build independence, environmental awareness and appreciation for manual work. Shared tasks could strengthen cooperation and give students a break from screens. However, rural accommodation, transport, hygiene and safety would require careful planning. Some students have medical or mobility needs, and a temporary experience should not romanticise poverty or difficult working conditions.

The rest of the month could include a no-buy challenge, a repair workshop, a decluttering project and interviews with people who live in different ways. Students should reflect on which changes are realistic in Hong Kong homes. Simple living is not about rejecting technology or money completely; it is about choosing deliberately, wasting less and deciding what actually contributes to a satisfying life.

context.title: Always Connected
body: Smartphones give students instant access to maps, messages, cameras, entertainment and schoolwork. They can help someone learn a language, organise a project or contact family in an emergency. Because so many functions are combined in one device, checking a phone has become an automatic part of waiting, travelling and socialising.

Constant alerts may make sustained attention more difficult, while late-night use can reduce sleep. People may interrupt conversations to read messages or compare themselves with carefully edited online lives. At the same time, group chats and video calls can maintain friendships across distance and give shy students another way to participate.

The key issue is not whether phones are simply good or bad, but how they are designed and used. Turning off non-essential notifications, creating phone-free meals and choosing purposeful screen time can help. Schools need rules that support learning without ignoring useful tools. Young people should also discuss privacy, respectful communication and whether the device is controlling their attention rather than serving their needs.

context.title: When Possessions Take Over
body: Old clothes, books, gifts and broken devices can slowly fill a room. People keep things because they may need them one day, because the objects carry memories or because deciding what to discard feels tiring. Cheap shopping and frequent online promotions make it easy to acquire more than a household can use.

Clutter can waste space, make cleaning difficult and create trip hazards. It may also cause stress when people cannot find important items or feel embarrassed about their home. Yet throwing everything away is not a responsible solution. Useful possessions can be sold, donated, repaired, recycled or shared, while private documents and electronic data need secure disposal.

Decluttering works best as a gradual decision-making process. A person can begin with one drawer, group similar objects and set clear rules about what to keep. Family members should not remove one another’s belongings without permission. The goal is not a perfectly empty room; it is a living space where valued items can be found, used and cared for without unnecessary waste.

context.title: A City of Global Brands
body: Hong Kong’s busy shopping districts attract international fashion, jewellery and lifestyle brands. Companies value the city’s transport links, visitors, financial services and reputation as a place where trends spread quickly. A prominent store can serve both local customers and travellers from other parts of Asia.

Luxury retail creates jobs and may strengthen tourism, property income and Hong Kong’s international image. However, high rents can push out small local businesses and make shopping areas look similar to those in other global cities. Advertising may also encourage young people to connect status with expensive possessions or spend beyond their means.

A balanced project should compare international and local brands, examine employment and rent, and ask shoppers what they value: quality, design, identity or prestige. It should also consider whether local products can compete through distinctive stories and craftsmanship. Global brands are not automatically harmful, but their success should not erase neighbourhood character or suggest that price is the only measure of value.

context.title: A Robot in Every Home?
body: Household robots already vacuum floors, monitor rooms and help people control appliances. Future machines may carry groceries, remind older residents to take medicine, translate conversations or provide basic companionship. Robots could make daily life safer and give carers more time for tasks that require human judgement.

The benefits come with limits. A machine may misunderstand a command, collect private information or fail at a dangerous moment. Advanced robots could be expensive to buy and repair, increasing inequality between households. People may also become less active or depend on a device for emotional support that it cannot truly provide.

Designers should focus on clear needs rather than impressive tricks. Users need to know what data a robot records, who can access it and how to stop it quickly. Robots can support children, older people and busy families, but they should not replace responsibility or human contact. The most valuable future robot may be the one that performs a modest task reliably, safely and affordably.

context.title: A One-Way Journey to Mars
body: The Mars One proposal attracted attention by suggesting that ordinary people could be selected for a permanent settlement on Mars. Supporters imagined a global project combining science, adventure and public interest. A one-way mission might avoid the cost of returning astronauts to Earth, while media coverage could help finance the programme.

The plan also raises serious questions. Settlers would face radiation, isolation, low gravity, equipment failure and delayed communication. Food, water, power and medical care would have to work for years without quick rescue. Choosing participants through a reality-style programme could reward popularity rather than the teamwork and technical ability needed for survival.

People may volunteer because they want discovery, fame, purpose or a place in history. Before any mission, organisers would need independent scientific review, transparent funding and long-term responsibility for the settlers. Governments and private companies could cooperate, but neither should treat human lives as entertainment. Exploring Mars is inspiring; promising a settlement before the technology is ready is very different.

context.title: More Than a Game?
body: Modern video games combine visual design, music, writing, acting and computer programming. Unlike films, they ask players to make decisions and experience a story through action. Supporters therefore argue that games can be a form of art, capable of creating emotion and exploring ideas from more than one point of view.

Playing can develop problem-solving, coordination, persistence and cooperation. Online games may connect friends, while creative games let users build worlds or tell stories. The risks are also real: excessive play can reduce sleep and exercise, some business models encourage overspending, and hostile online behaviour can harm players.

A convincing debate should not claim that every game is beneficial. The type of game, age of the player, time spent and social setting all matter. Parents can choose appropriate titles, discuss content and agree on limits instead of treating games as one category. Games deserve serious evaluation, just like books or films, because artistic quality and educational value vary widely.

context.title: When a Pet Becomes Part of the Family
body: For many Hong Kong owners, a dog is more than an animal kept at home. Dogs offer companionship, routine and affection, especially to people who live alone. Owners may walk them in parks, visit pet-friendly cafés, celebrate birthdays, arrange grooming or take part in training and charity events.

Caring for a dog can encourage exercise, patience and responsibility. It may also help family members spend time together. However, veterinary treatment, food and housing are expensive, and small flats may not suit every breed. Noise, waste and fear of dogs can create conflict with neighbours. Long working hours may leave a pet alone for too much of the day.

Treating a dog with kindness does not require pretending it is human. Owners must understand animal behaviour, provide exercise and make plans for its whole life. Schools can teach responsible pet ownership before students ask families to buy an animal. A pet can enrich a household, but it should never be purchased as a fashionable object or a simple substitute for human relationships.

context.title: What Cantopop Tells Us
body: Cantopop has provided a soundtrack to life in Hong Kong for decades. Songs appear in films, television programmes, concerts and karaoke, while lyrics reflect changing ideas about romance, work, identity and the city. A school project could use music to explore language, media, history and the relationship between performers and audiences.

The proposal might include a timeline, analysis of lyrics, interviews with listeners and comparisons between older and newer production styles. Students could examine how streaming platforms and social media help independent artists reach audiences. They should also discuss copyright and why sharing music online without permission can harm creators.

Some people say Cantopop has lost influence because K-pop, J-pop and global English-language music compete for attention. Others point to renewed interest in local performers and concerts. Popularity cannot be judged by one chart or age group alone. A strong project should present different evidence and show how music can change while still expressing experiences that are recognisably Hong Kong.

context.title: The Pressure to Fit In
body: Teenagers often look to friends for information about clothing, entertainment, study habits and acceptable behaviour. This influence can be direct, such as being challenged to try something, or indirect, such as noticing what receives approval in a group chat. Social media can make the pressure continue after the school day ends.

Peer influence is not always harmful. Friends may encourage one another to revise, exercise, volunteer or seek help. Problems arise when belonging seems to depend on spending money, hiding opinions, bullying someone or taking unsafe risks. A student may agree publicly even while feeling uncomfortable, because rejection appears more immediate than future consequences.

Useful responses include delaying a decision, giving a clear reason, suggesting an alternative and speaking to a trusted person. Schools can teach assertive communication without blaming students who struggle to resist. Strong friendships allow disagreement. The aim is not to live without influence, which is impossible, but to recognise it and make choices that match one’s values and safety.

context.title: Should Our Class Have a Blog?
body: A class blog could collect news, project updates, photographs, book reviews and reflections in one shared space. Students who are less confident speaking in class might contribute through writing, while families could see selected examples of school life. Maintaining a real audience may also encourage students to edit their work more carefully.

The blog would need clear responsibilities. Posts must protect privacy, use images with permission and avoid copying material from other sites. Comments could create useful discussion, but they also require moderation. If only a few enthusiastic students do all the work, the blog may quickly become inactive or represent the class unfairly.

A proposal should use survey results to show what classmates want to read and who is willing to contribute. Possible sections include study tips, interviews, event reports and creative work. An editorial team could rotate each month, with a teacher checking sensitive content before publication. The blog should have a clear purpose and realistic schedule rather than existing simply because other classes have one.

context.title: Making Group Work Work
body: Group projects bring together people with different skills, ideas and working styles. A team can divide a large task, check one another’s work and produce something no individual could manage alone. Yet groups also create frustration when responsibilities are unclear, decisions take too long or one member does very little.

Conflict is not always a sign of failure. Disagreement can reveal weak ideas and lead to a better solution if members listen and criticise the proposal rather than the person. Problems become harder when messages are ignored, anger is hidden or friendships influence how work is shared. Choosing friends does not guarantee an effective team.

Teams should agree on goals, roles, deadlines and a method for making decisions at the beginning. Short progress checks make it easier to address missed work before the final day. Members can record contributions and ask a teacher for help when a pattern continues. Successful teamwork requires both accountability and flexibility: people must complete their own tasks while helping the group adjust when circumstances change.

context.title: Who Decides What Is Beautiful?
body: Ideas about attractive faces and bodies change across cultures and time. Advertising, films and social media can make certain features appear normal or desirable simply because they are shown repeatedly. Coloured contact lenses and cosmetic procedures allow people to alter their appearance, including the colour or apparent size of their eyes.

Changing style can be playful and personal, but beauty products also create pressure. Young people may compare themselves with edited images or believe that Western features bring greater social acceptance. Medical procedures involve cost and risk, while contact lenses can damage eyes if they are poorly fitted or used without proper hygiene.

No single eye colour or facial feature determines whether someone is attractive. Families and friends may react strongly to permanent changes because appearance also carries cultural meaning. Schools and media can show a wider range of faces and discuss how images are altered. Personal choice matters, but a choice is not fully free when it is driven by discrimination or fear of not fitting an imported ideal.

context.title: Showing a Living Culture
body: Hong Kong culture can be seen in wet markets, festivals, neighbourhood shops, public transport, food, popular music and the mixture of languages used every day. An exhibition should not treat culture as a list of old objects. Traditions change as people move, technology develops and younger generations create new meanings.

Displays could combine photographs, short videos, sounds and personal stories. Visitors might compare an old market stall with modern online shopping, learn the origins of a festival or listen to expressions used by different generations. Humour can make the exhibition memorable, but jokes should not turn communities or customs into stereotypes.

The organisers must decide what can be represented fairly in limited space. Interviews with residents and craftspeople would add voices beyond textbooks. Interactive activities could include matching games, a tram-route challenge or designing a modern festival poster. Preserving culture does not mean freezing it. The exhibition should help visitors understand why practices matter, how they are changing and what people hope to carry forward.

context.title: Calculators: Shortcut or Learning Tool?
body: Calculators can handle long arithmetic quickly, allowing students to explore patterns, check estimates and solve realistic problems with large numbers. In everyday life, adults use digital tools for shopping, budgeting and work. Supporters argue that schools should teach children how to use such tools intelligently rather than pretend they do not exist.

Critics worry that early dependence may weaken number sense and confidence with basic operations. A child who enters every calculation without estimating may not notice an impossible answer. Unequal access and unsuitable calculator functions can also create problems. Mental arithmetic remains useful when making quick decisions or checking whether a result is reasonable.

The choice is not necessarily between unlimited use and a complete ban. Schools could require students to learn core facts and show methods before introducing calculators for selected tasks. Teachers can ask pupils to predict an answer, calculate and then explain the result. A good policy should match the student’s age and the purpose of the lesson, using technology where it deepens thinking rather than replacing it.

context.title: Choosing a Book for Everyone
body: A school Reading Club wants a book that is enjoyable, discussable and manageable for members with different levels of English. Hero on a Bicycle offers adventure and moral choices, but one title may not appeal to everyone. Setting, length, vocabulary and the age of the characters all affect whether students continue reading.

Fiction can develop imagination and empathy by placing readers inside experiences different from their own. It also shows vocabulary and grammar in meaningful contexts. Challenges include unfamiliar cultural references, slow openings and the time required to finish a longer story. A film adaptation may attract interest but can also replace careful reading if shown too early.

The club could offer a shortlist and let members read samples before voting. Choices might include mystery, science fiction, humour, historical stories or fiction set in Hong Kong. Reviews are helpful when they describe style and difficulty without revealing the ending. The best selection is not simply the easiest book; it should give members enough support while leaving ideas worth debating together.

context.title: Useful, Unusual and Almost Useless
body: Chindogu are inventions designed to solve small everyday problems in ways that are imaginative but often too awkward to use seriously. Examples include slippers with cleaning brushes, a tiny fan attached to chopsticks or an umbrella that covers the whole body. The humour comes from seeing a real need answered by an unexpectedly complicated object.

A school Chindogu Society could encourage students to observe ordinary frustrations, sketch solutions and build simple prototypes from safe recycled materials. Unlike a general science club, it would value playful thinking and the ability to explain why an invention is both useful and impractical. Members could learn design, presentation and teamwork without needing expensive equipment.

Promotion should make the idea clear rather than merely displaying strange objects. A live demonstration, invention challenge or short comic video could attract attention. The society must avoid copying dangerous internet ideas and should give credit for original designs. Its purpose is not to produce commercial products, but to loosen fixed thinking and show that creativity often begins by asking unusual questions.

context.title: Manners at a Changing Table
body: Table manners help people share food comfortably, but the rules differ across families and cultures. Some expectations concern hygiene and consideration, such as chewing quietly or waiting until everyone is served. Others depend on custom, including how chopsticks, knives and forks are held or whether dishes are shared.

Modern habits create new questions. Phones can interrupt conversation, while taking photographs may delay a meal. Formal Western dining uses rules that are unnecessary at a casual Chinese family dinner. Visitors can feel anxious if nobody explains what is expected, and strict correction may embarrass them more than the original mistake.

A workshop could compare situations instead of presenting one universal list. Students might role-play a family meal, a formal dinner and a meal with visitors from another culture. The most important principle is to notice other people: keep shared areas clean, avoid disturbing diners and follow the host’s guidance. Good manners should make people feel welcome, not become a test of wealth or social background.

context.title: What Does It Mean for a Child to Succeed?
body: Many Hong Kong parents invest time and money in tutoring, music lessons, sports and carefully planned school choices. They want children to have opportunities in a competitive society. Clear expectations and practical support can build confidence, especially when adults notice effort and help a young person recover from setbacks.

Pressure becomes harmful when every activity is measured by prizes, grades or future applications. Children may have little time for sleep, friendship or unstructured play, and rewards such as money can replace interest in learning. Young people are motivated in different ways: some enjoy competition, while others respond to independence, belonging or the chance to master a skill.

Parents can discuss goals with children, set limits on schedules and recognise progress beyond public achievement. Encouragement should not mean removing every difficulty, because solving manageable problems develops resilience. Success can include health, character, relationships and purpose as well as academic results. A balanced family plan leaves room for ambition while allowing the child’s own interests and definition of a good life to develop.

body: Summer internships allow students to enter a workplace before they make long-term career choices. A company may offer an unpaid placement in which an intern observes meetings, assists with simple projects and learns how staff communicate with customers. The experience can help a young person test an interest, collect examples for a future application and understand why punctuality, accuracy and teamwork matter.

However, an unpaid intern still gives time and effort. Transport and meal costs may make the placement difficult for students from less wealthy families. Some interns receive useful guidance, while others are asked to repeat routine tasks without proper training. Long working hours can also affect rest, study plans or a summer job that would provide income.

A worthwhile programme should therefore state the hours, duties, supervision and learning goals clearly. Schools could help students check whether a placement is safe and relevant. Interns should be curious, dependable and willing to ask questions, but employers should also provide feedback and treat them respectfully. The value of an internship depends not only on its name, but on what the student is genuinely allowed to learn.

context.source_line: Original mock preparation text for 2012 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.2; not official examination text:
context.title: Mooncakes and Mid-Autumn Festival
body: Mooncakes remain a familiar part of Mid-Autumn Festival in Hong Kong. Families, friends and businesses give them as symbols of reunion and goodwill. Yet a household may receive more boxes than it can eat, and elaborate tins, plastic trays and paper bags can create a large amount of waste after a short celebration.

Traditional lotus-seed-paste mooncakes carry cultural meaning, but many consumers now choose smaller portions, reduced-sugar recipes, ice-cream flavours or products made without animal ingredients. New versions may attract younger customers and people with different dietary needs. At the same time, replacing every traditional product could weaken a custom that connects generations.

The festival can be celebrated without treating gift-giving as a competition. Shops could offer simple packaging, allow customers to return boxes or sell mooncakes individually. Families might share one box, donate unopened products early, reuse lanterns and avoid disposable glow sticks. A balanced approach would preserve the meaning of the festival while reducing unnecessary food and packaging. The most valuable gift may be time spent together rather than the size or price of a box.

context.title: Cosplay
body: Cosplay involves dressing and performing as a character from animation, comics, games or films. In Hong Kong, participants meet at conventions, shopping centres and photo events. Some design costumes by hand, learn make-up techniques and practise poses or short performances. Online communities also allow beginners to share work and find advice.

Supporters see cosplay as a creative hobby that combines art, craft and drama. It can help shy people meet others with similar interests and express a side of their identity that is not visible at school or work. Critics may consider it childish, expensive or too focused on appearance. Public misunderstanding can make cosplayers uncomfortable, especially when photographs are taken without permission.

Experienced cosplayers can make the community safer and more welcoming. They can explain event rules, teach low-cost costume methods and remind newcomers about consent, copyright and suitable public behaviour. Organisers can provide changing areas and clear photography guidelines. Whether cosplay becomes more widely accepted will depend on how participants present their hobby and how respectfully the public responds to forms of creativity that may look unusual at first.

context.title: Stephen Chow Project
body: A school film club is planning a Stephen Chow festival to introduce students to an important figure in Hong Kong popular culture. Chow began as a television performer and later became known for a distinctive form of comedy that mixes wordplay, physical action and unlikely heroes. His development from actor to writer, director and producer gives the club several possible themes.

Students could research his early career, major films, comic style and influence on audiences in Hong Kong and overseas. Useful sources might include recorded interviews, film reviews, library archives and comments from people who worked in the local film industry. Information from fan sites should be checked against more reliable sources before it is used.

The festival could combine screenings with short introductions, a poster exhibition and a discussion about how comedy can communicate serious ideas. Students might recreate a scene, compare subtitles or vote for a film to show. The programme should not become a simple celebration of fame: it should help the audience understand how film-making choices, local language and changing social conditions shaped Chow’s work and its lasting popularity.

context.title: Technological Products
body: New technological products appear quickly in homes, schools and workplaces. People are attracted by devices that save time, provide entertainment or make communication easier. A smartphone can combine a camera, map, payment system and learning tool, while smart appliances can perform routine tasks with little effort from the user.

These products can improve access to information and support people with particular needs. Video calls connect distant relatives, translation tools reduce language barriers and health devices can remind users to exercise. However, a product is not automatically useful because it is new. Some devices are expensive, difficult to repair or designed for a problem that could be solved more simply.

There are also questions about privacy, electronic waste and dependence. If a service stops working, users may lose access to important information or basic functions. Before buying a product, consumers should consider its real purpose, expected life, energy use and the support offered by the company. The best technology is not always the most advanced one; it is the product that meets a genuine need without creating unnecessary cost or harm.

context.title: Keeping a Diary
body: Keeping a diary gives people a private place to record events, thoughts and feelings. A short entry can preserve details that might otherwise disappear, such as a conversation, a small success or a difficult decision. Looking back later may help a writer notice changes in habits, relationships and personal goals.

A diary does not have to be a formal daily essay. Writers can include photographs, sketches, tickets, lists or a few sentences about the most memorable moment of the day. Some prefer paper because it feels personal and has no notifications. Others use a password-protected digital diary because it is searchable and can include audio or images.

The habit is easier to continue when expectations are realistic. A writer might choose a regular time, use prompts and accept that some days will be missed. Privacy also matters: paper diaries need a safe place, while online accounts need strong passwords and careful backup settings. A school campaign promoting diary writing should present it as a flexible tool for reflection and creativity, not another piece of homework that must be perfect.

context.title: Swimming Across Victoria Harbour
body: Hong Kong’s cross-harbour swimming race returned after a long break, with competitors travelling from the Lei Yue Mun side towards Quarry Bay. Applicants had to show that they could complete a qualifying swim within a set time. Organisers limited the number of places and planned support boats, medical teams and a route separated from normal marine traffic.

Swimming is a popular form of exercise in public pools and at beaches, but an open-water race creates different risks. Currents can carry swimmers away from the route, and weather, tiredness or poor visibility can make rescue more difficult. Water quality must be checked because competitors may accidentally swallow polluted water. Even experienced pool swimmers need preparation for waves and close contact with other participants.

If managed safely, the race can offer a demanding personal goal, revive a local sporting tradition and draw attention to the harbour environment. It may also attract visitors and encourage more people to learn swimming. Whether it should become an annual event depends on safety records, environmental conditions and the organisers’ ability to protect both competitors and other harbour users.

context.title: Study Tours
body: A proposed summer study tour would place Hong Kong students with host families in Oxford. Weekday mornings would include intensive English classes, while afternoons would be divided between sports, local activities and visits to historic places. A full-day excursion would take place each Saturday, giving students opportunities to use English outside the classroom.

Living with a host family can develop confidence, independence and cultural awareness. Students may learn how another household organises meals, travel and daily routines. They can also practise listening to different accents. However, homesickness, unfamiliar food and misunderstandings about rules may cause stress. The cost of the programme could exclude some students unless financial support is available.

Before recommending the tour, a school should examine supervision, safeguarding, accommodation checks and emergency arrangements. Students need clear information about expectations and whom to contact if a problem occurs. A strong programme should balance lessons with meaningful interaction rather than fill every hour with sightseeing. Its success should be judged by what students learn and how well they adapt, not simply by the number of famous places they visit.

body: The Japanese Food Club wants to hold an event that will attract new members. One option is a hands-on sushi workshop led by an experienced chef. Participants would learn about sushi rice, safe food preparation, cutting and presentation before making simple rolls. Another option is a visit to a conveyor-belt restaurant to observe how food is prepared and served.

A practical workshop may be memorable and encourage teamwork, but it requires suitable equipment, hygiene rules and alternatives for students who do not eat seafood. A restaurant visit is easier to arrange, yet it may feel less active and could be costly. The club should consider safety, budget, group size and how much students will learn from each activity.

Promotion could include photographs, a short demonstration at lunchtime and an online booking form explaining ingredients and fees. Future events might compare regional Japanese dishes, explore healthy lunch design or invite members to prepare food for a cultural fair. The best event will not simply be the most fashionable one; it should be inclusive, educational and realistic for students to organise well.

context.title: Lack of Space in Hong Kong
body: Space is limited in many parts of Hong Kong, where homes, offices, shops and transport systems must serve a large population. Some families share small flats, and students may not have a quiet room for study or rest. Crowded pavements and public facilities can also increase stress and reduce privacy.

People respond creatively. Furniture is designed to fold or provide storage, public libraries offer study areas and families use parks, shopping centres and community facilities as extensions of the home. High-density development can place schools, services and transport close together, making daily travel shorter and allowing neighbourhood businesses to reach many customers.

However, efficiency should not be used to excuse unhealthy living conditions. Children need safe places to play, older residents need accessible public areas and everyone benefits from light, ventilation and moments of quiet. Government, developers and residents must decide how land should be shared between housing, transport, business and recreation. The real challenge is not only finding more space, but ensuring that limited space is designed and distributed in a way that supports a reasonable quality of life.

Reducing car use could lower emissions, ease traffic and help people build healthier routines. Students can contribute by recording how they travel, organising a car-free challenge and mapping safe walking routes near school. The scheme must still recognise that some people, including those with mobility needs or unusual working hours, may rely on private vehicles.

Promotion should make the goal practical rather than blame drivers. Schools could share class results, invite transport experts and reward groups that reduce journeys in measurable ways. Social media, posters and community partnerships may extend the campaign beyond the school gate. To remain credible, organisers should publish simple evidence of what changed. A successful environmental scheme gives people realistic alternatives and shows how many small decisions can create a larger public benefit.

context.title: 3D Movies
body: Three-dimensional films use separate images for each eye to create an impression of depth. Improved projectors and successful action and animated films have made the format more visible in Hong Kong cinemas. For some viewers, objects appearing to move towards the audience make a film feel more exciting and turn a cinema visit into a special event.

The effect does not suit every production. A quiet drama may depend more on acting and story than visual spectacle. Tickets can cost more, the glasses may be uncomfortable and some viewers experience headaches or motion sickness. Converting a film after it has been made can also produce weaker results than planning the effects during filming.

Cinemas could create a more realistic experience through sound design, larger screens, carefully controlled lighting or moving seats, but each effect should support the story. Too many distractions may make an audience notice the technology instead of the film. The decision to use 3D should therefore be made by considering the genre, artistic purpose, cost and comfort of viewers rather than assuming that every new film needs the same treatment.

context.title: Heritage Conservation
body: Old buildings can show how people in Hong Kong once lived, worked and travelled. Their materials, signs and layout may preserve details that photographs cannot fully communicate. A well-used historic building can give a neighbourhood identity and help younger residents connect local history with places they see every day.

Conservation can conflict with the need for housing, transport and safer facilities. Some structures are expensive to repair or cannot meet current accessibility and fire standards without major changes. Keeping only the outer wall while replacing everything inside may protect an appearance but lose much of the building’s meaning.

Decisions should consider historical importance, architectural value, community memory, physical condition and possible future use. Government could offer repair grants, require careful impact studies and invite residents to comment before demolition is approved. Adaptive reuse may turn a former market, police station or factory into a library, arts space or community centre. Not every old building can be preserved, but development should not erase valuable heritage simply because rebuilding is faster or more profitable.

context.title: Protecting Dolphins
body: Chinese white dolphins live in waters affected by shipping, construction, pollution and fishing activity. Their pink appearance has made them a familiar symbol of Hong Kong’s marine environment. Yet public recognition does not automatically protect the feeding and breeding areas that the animals need to survive.

Campaigns can explain threats through school visits, documentaries, harbour exhibitions and responsible dolphin-watching tours. Clear evidence is important because dramatic images may attract attention without helping people understand which actions make a difference. Boat operators can follow speed and distance rules, while researchers can monitor numbers, movement and water quality.

Protecting habitats may affect plans for bridges, reclamation or other infrastructure. The choice should not be presented as development versus doing nothing. Authorities can compare alternative routes, restrict noisy work during sensitive periods and create protected areas that are large enough to be useful. Environmental groups, businesses and government must also report whether measures work. Conservation is strongest when decisions are based on long-term evidence and when the public can see how protecting dolphins also supports the wider marine ecosystem.

context.title: Money Management Skills
body: Good money management involves more than saving every dollar. Young people need to understand how money is earned, how to separate needs from wants and how small choices affect a budget. They should also learn that spending, saving and donating can all be reasonable when they are planned responsibly.

A cartoon can introduce these ideas through characters and everyday situations, but watching alone may not change behaviour. Students learn more when they make decisions themselves. A class could plan a meal with a fixed budget, compare prices, divide imaginary income among several goals or discuss how advertising creates pressure to buy.

Activities should reflect real life without asking students to reveal private family finances. Schools might use games, a savings challenge or a small charity project, followed by reflection on the choices made. Digital payment should be included because cashless spending can make costs less visible. The purpose is not to tell everyone to make identical choices. It is to help students ask useful questions, recognise risk and make decisions they can explain before financial mistakes become difficult to correct.

part_a.instruction: Your group is discussing “Money Management Skills”. Discuss the following points.

discussion_points.text: Why it is necessary to teach good money management skills

anything else you think is important

context.source_line: Original mock preparation text for 2012 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 6.1; not official examination text:
context.title: Restaurant Reviews
body: Hong Kong restaurants offer food from many regions, from Cantonese dim sum and regional Chinese dishes to Japanese, South-East Asian and European cuisines. This variety gives reviewers many choices, but it also means that a fair review should understand what a restaurant is trying to provide rather than compare every place by the same standard.

A good restaurant usually combines fresh, well-prepared food with cleanliness, reasonable value and service that suits the setting. Decoration may shape the atmosphere, but an attractive room cannot make up for unsafe food or rude treatment. Reviewers should consider portion size, menu information, waiting time and whether dietary needs are handled clearly.

A useful review identifies the restaurant, location, price range and dishes ordered. It separates observation from personal preference and gives specific examples instead of simply calling the food “good” or “bad”. Reviewers should also disclose invitations or free meals and avoid judging an entire business from one minor mistake. Honest criticism can help customers choose and restaurants improve, provided it is accurate, balanced and respectful to the people whose work is being discussed.

context.source_line: Original mock preparation text for 2012 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 6.2; not official examination text:
context.title: Reality Shows
body: Reality shows place ordinary people, performers or celebrities in competitions and unscripted situations. Talent contests, cooking programmes and lifestyle challenges can attract viewers of different ages. Younger audiences may follow contestants online, while older viewers may prefer programmes that demonstrate skill or tell a clear personal story.

Supporters enjoy the suspense and the opportunity to watch people improve. Some programmes introduce new performers or raise awareness of unfamiliar jobs. Critics argue that scenes are edited to create conflict, and that embarrassing moments are used as entertainment. Contestants may receive sudden attention without being prepared for public criticism or the loss of privacy.

Popularity depends on the format, personalities and whether viewers believe the events are genuine. Producers should explain rules, protect vulnerable participants and avoid presenting humiliation as harmless fun. Audiences also need to remember that “reality” has been selected and edited. A programme can be entertaining without pretending to be completely natural, but it should not mislead viewers about what happened or ignore the long-term effect that public exposure may have on participants.

context.source_line: Original mock preparation text for 2012 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 6.3; not official examination text:
context.title: English Lessons with Video Games
body: English lessons can be memorable when students use the language for a clear purpose. Role-plays, songs, debates and collaborative tasks may feel more meaningful than completing isolated exercises. Lessons become less enjoyable when activities are too repetitive, instructions are unclear or students are afraid that every mistake will be criticised.

Video games could create opportunities to follow English instructions, solve problems and communicate with teammates. Story-based games provide vocabulary in context, while short design tasks can lead to speaking or writing. However, not every game contains accurate or suitable language. Equipment costs, screen time, unequal gaming experience and distraction may also reduce the learning value.

Teachers should choose a game because it supports a learning goal, not simply because students find it entertaining. Activities need time limits, accessible roles and a follow-up task that makes students use what they noticed. Alternatives should be available for students who cannot or do not want to play. Games can enrich an English lesson, but they work best as one carefully guided method among many rather than a replacement for explanation, reading, discussion and feedback.

context.title: Home Swapping
body: Home swapping allows two households to stay in each other’s homes during the same period. Travellers may avoid hotel costs and live in a residential area with a kitchen, neighbours and ordinary local services. This can provide a closer view of daily culture than visiting only tourist attractions.

The arrangement also involves trust. Property may be damaged, personal belongings can be exposed and expectations about cleaning, pets or the use of equipment may differ. Photographs may not show the true condition of a home, and insurance might not cover every problem. People in small Hong Kong flats may also feel that their homes are less attractive to overseas partners.

A safer exchange needs verified identities, honest descriptions, written house rules and a clear plan for emergencies. Participants should agree on dates, guests, keys, expenses and what happens if either side cancels. Reviews can help, but direct conversation is still important. Home swapping may offer value and cultural contact for some travellers, yet it is not automatically more authentic than a hotel stay. The experience depends on preparation, mutual respect and realistic expectations.

context.title: Toys and Games
body: Traditional toys and games such as kites, marbles, skipping ropes and board games remain part of childhood memories in Hong Kong. They are inexpensive, easy to share and often encourage movement or face-to-face interaction. Families and schools can also use them to connect children with local customs and older generations.

Modern toys include electronic games, programmable models and online worlds. They can offer detailed stories, instant feedback and contact with players in other places. Some develop problem-solving or digital skills. However, they may be costly, collect personal data or encourage long periods of screen use. Traditional toys can also be unsafe or uninteresting if they are presented without explanation.

Future products are likely to combine physical and digital play. Augmented reality, adaptive learning and environmentally friendly materials may become more common. The most successful toys will not necessarily use the most technology. Parents and children may continue to value durability, imagination, safety and the ability to play together. A project on toy trends should therefore compare what different forms of play allow children to do, rather than simply treating old toys as outdated and new ones as better.

context.source_line: Original mock preparation text for 2012 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 7.3; not official examination text:
context.title: Career Choices
body: Young people are asked to make career choices while jobs and required skills continue to change. Some know what interests them but are unsure whether it offers stable work. Others face pressure from family, compare themselves with classmates or lack direct experience of the occupations they are considering.

Salary and job security matter, but they are not the only criteria. Personal strengths, values, working conditions, training opportunities and work-life balance can affect long-term satisfaction. A highly paid job may not suit someone’s health or interests, while an enjoyable field may require years of preparation or carry financial uncertainty.

Students who are undecided can research several paths, speak with workers and try short courses, volunteering or internships. Career tests may suggest questions to explore, but they should not be treated as final answers. Advice should help a person understand options rather than force an immediate permanent choice. Many adults change roles or industries, so the first decision does not determine an entire life. Building transferable skills and learning how to reassess goals may be more useful than searching for one perfect job.

context.title: Outdoor Music Festivals
body: Outdoor music festivals are major cultural and commercial events in some cities, but Hong Kong has limited open space and many venues are close to homes. Organisers argue that audiences want to hear pop, jazz, independent music and other performances outdoors. Residents may worry about sound tests, late-night noise, crowds and transport disruption.

A festival can support local musicians, attract visitors and create a shared public experience. It can also fail if the site is too small, weather plans are weak or ticket prices exclude much of the community. Noise complaints are reasonable when organisers do not communicate or control sound, but a complete ban would prevent the city from developing new cultural events.

The West Kowloon Cultural District could use clear finishing times, sound monitoring, transport plans and advance notices to nearby residents. Other suitable events might include open-air theatre, dance, film, Chinese opera or community arts days. Decisions should consider artistic value, public access and the impact on the neighbourhood. A successful festival needs a space designed for performance and rules that allow culture and everyday life to coexist.

context.title: Plastic Surgery for Men
body: Plastic surgery is increasingly marketed to men as a way to change facial features, body shape or signs of ageing. Some clients seek treatment after injury or because a physical feature causes serious distress. Others believe appearance affects confidence, relationships or career opportunities. Advertising and images of male celebrities may make procedures seem more ordinary than before.

Surgery can produce the desired result, but it also carries medical risks, pain, recovery time and cost. Expectations may be unrealistic, and a person who remains dissatisfied could seek repeated procedures. Social pressure is especially concerning when people feel they must look a certain way to be accepted. Non-surgical treatments are not automatically risk-free either.

Anyone considering a procedure should receive independent medical advice, understand alternatives and check the qualifications of the practitioner. Clinics should explain complications honestly rather than promise perfect results. Men deserve the same freedom as women to make informed choices about their bodies, but rising popularity should not prevent careful discussion of health, self-image and commercial influence. Confidence may improve through surgery, yet appearance is only one part of a person’s well-being.

context.source_line: Original mock preparation text for 2012 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 8.3; not official examination text:
context.title: Memory Training
body: Memory supports learning, work and everyday independence. Remembering instructions, names and appointments can save time and build confidence. Students may benefit when they can connect new information with what they already know, while older adults may value strategies that help them manage daily routines.

Memory can be trained through active recall, spaced review, association and organising information into meaningful groups. Sleep, exercise and focused attention also affect how well information is stored. Repeating words without understanding may help for a short test but is less useful than explaining ideas, applying them and reviewing them over time.

Different people need different methods. A musician may remember sound patterns, a professional may use checklists and a student may create diagrams or practise questions. Training should not promise impossible results or suggest that forgetting is always a personal failure. Phones and reminders can support memory, but complete dependence on them may weaken attention to important details. A good programme combines practical techniques with realistic goals and recognises that judgement and creativity remain important even when facts can be remembered accurately.
